20281-the-arena-volume-4-no-21-august-18:
The Arena, volume four, number twenty-one, for August 1891, is a reform-minded magazine. One essay weighs a new history of German unity by Heinrich von Sybel. Its fifth and latest volume had just appeared to wide notice. Another history, from an opposite standpoint, requires joint study with it.

Read together, the two show an impartial reader where truth lies. The Arena hosted debates on politics, faith, labor, and social reform. Monthly numbers mixed essays, fiction, and reviews for thinking readers. This issue gives a fair taste of 1890s American reform journalism at work.
22419-the-arena-volume-4-no-22-september:
The Arena, volume four, number twenty-two, appeared in September 1891. The Arena was a bold American magazine of reform and debate. This issue argues against suspicion aimed at independent teachers and thinkers.

Suspects, it says, are numerous in such a climate. No prominent person, especially a teacher, stands beyond surveillance. Stray a little from the beaten path and trouble follows. A teacher might only gather a thought from natural religion. Heathen seers and philosophers may have honored that same thought. Yet gathering it brings watchers down on him. The passage defends free inquiry with spirit. Readers get Gilded Age reform journalism at full argumentative stretch.
23013-george-washington-s-last-duel-1891:
Thomas Nelson Page schemes over tea in George Washington's Last Duel, a story dated 1891. One evening after tea, with the Major in a gracious humor and full of his oldest, best stories, Margaret fell upon him unawares. Before he recovered from the shock, she had captured his consent for Rose to come, chaperoned by an old lady of strict views.

Page wrote Virginia romance in a haze of plantation nostalgia, and his duel here is fought with manners as much as pistols. George Washington's name lends the tale its frame and its joke. Consent, courtship, and honor move the plot at drawing-room pace. Modern readers should note the romantic varnish Page gives the old South. The story's craft, and its myth-making, both show clearly.
23015-run-to-seed-1891:
Thomas Nelson Page repeats a proverb in Run to Seed, a story dated 1891. This was true, every word of it, the narrator grants. And so was something else Mrs. Mrs. Wagoner, the narrator notes, repeated her stern proverb about lying in beds of one's own making. That process, he adds drily, is too well known to need more discussion.

A family or a farm running to seed gives Page his theme, decline managed with manners. His Virginia gentry face shrunken fortunes and hold to old forms all the same. The title's garden image does double work, plants and people both past their prime. Page's sympathy flows to the declining house, as usual. Readers get a small, sad comedy of a class watching itself thin out.
23016-p-laski-s-tunament-1891:
Thomas Nelson Page stages a tournament in P'laski's Tunament, his 1891 story told in Black dialect. Old Hanover took his stand ahead of the company, followers ranked behind him. The narrator compares him to an African chief in state, awaiting an embassy. He was arrayed with great care, in style at first taken for clerical dress, then seen as a symbol of dignity.

Pulaski's tournament, a ring sport of the old Virginia gentry, gets retold here through the eyes of the enslaved and freed people who served it. Page's dialect narration was famous in his day and is dated in its framing now. The pomp he describes is real, and so is the labor under it. The story rewards a double reading, pageant and critique together.
23017-elsket-1891:
Thomas Nelson Page gives a warning in Elsket, his 1891 story. The doctor thought a piece of advice natural enough, but it sounded curious to the narrator. Don't talk about England to Elsket, the doctor added, and don't ask any questions. Curiosity, naturally, does the opposite of obeying.

Elsket, a name from the Danish coast, belongs to a woman whose past is the story's guarded room. Page sets his tale far from his usual Virginia, among northern fisherfolk, and the change of scene suits his elegiac temper. Love, secrecy, and a stranger's questions drive the plot. Of Page's short works, Elsket was long counted among the finest, a compact tragedy carried by restraint rather than incident.
ariosto-orlando-furioso-harington-1591:
Ludovico Ariosto wrote Orlando Furioso in Italian in the early 1500s. Sir John Harington gave it English dress in 1591, the first full one in the tongue. Harington was a court wit at the court of Queen Elizabeth. The poem is a vast tale of knights, love, and war.

Orlando goes mad for love of Angelica, who loves him not. Knights ride to the Moon to fetch back his lost wits in a vial. Saracen wars, spells, and strange beasts crowd the long, bright tale. Harington's verse keeps the fun and verve of the source in full.
arxiv-2512-00091:
Three-dimensional concrete printing builds structures layer by layer, and the construction industry wants it to be more sustainable and efficient. Karam Mawas and co-authors study deep filament extraction for this process in a 2025 journal article. Filaments are the strands of concrete laid down during printing.

The literature describes two main deposition methods: extrusion-based printing, known as Contour Crafting, and shotcrete printing. The authors use deep learning to extract and analyze filament information from printed material. Reliable filament data helps engineers check print quality and control the process as large printed structures become more common. Print quality depends on those filaments, so measuring them well is a basic control need.
arxiv-2512-00391:
Merging several trained models into one, without retraining, is an attractive shortcut in machine learning. Zhikang Chen and co-authors rethink model merging through directional alignment in 2025, moving from coefficients to directions. Earlier strategies decomposed parameters, optimized coefficients, or learned subspaces.

Those methods already cut the need for expensive joint training while keeping strong performance across tasks. Directional alignment focuses on whether parameter changes point the same way, not just their sizes. Better merging rules let small teams combine specialist models, such as one per language or skill, into a single capable system. Merging is cheapest when the models share an architecture and training origin. Directional agreement may matter more than step size when models are averaged.
arxiv-2512-00791:
Jordi Pérez-Guijarro wrote a 2025 learning theory paper on a quiet assumption in machine learning. Most theory assumes training data and test data come from the same distribution. When the two differ, understanding generalization, how well a model does on new data, gets much harder.

Prior work showed a surprise: for some fixed methods, training on a different distribution can actually help test results. Pérez-Guijarro studies the limits of using identical distributions for training and testing when learning Boolean functions. Mapping those limits warns practitioners when matching distributions is a help, and when it quietly caps performance.
arxiv-2512-00891:
Yiyu Wang and seven coauthors speed up streaming video language models in a 2025 paper. These models watch video as it arrives and answer questions about it. They perform well on many video tasks, but real-time use is hard because each frame becomes many visual tokens that cost time to process.

The bottleneck sits in the vision transformer stage that encodes frames. Nearby frames look nearly the same, so encoding each from scratch wastes effort. Their hierarchical token compression trims tokens at several levels, cutting the repeated work. Faster streaming models could power live assistants that comment on video as events unfold.
arxiv-2512-00991:
A 2025 study evaluates academic chatbots on outputs beyond plain answers. Most tests of large language models stick to standard tasks, like factual question answering or short summaries. Real academic help also includes making slide decks and podcast scripts, which are harder to grade.

The study compares two retrieval strategies for question answering: graph-based retrieval over a knowledge graph, and an advanced hybrid of keyword and semantic search. It also judges whether models can produce high-quality slide decks and podcast scripts. The prototype pairs an open-weight Llama model with a commercial model. Results would guide universities building study chatbots.
arxiv-2512-01491:
A study of field theory on a curved two-dimensional spacetime finds an odd symmetry. The symmetry acts like Weyl scaling, but only near the boundary. In plain Weyl symmetry, the boundary term plays no key role. Here it does. That shift changes how the anomaly must be read.

The authors trace how the boundary term drives the anomaly. An approximate symmetry of this kind can still leave clear traces. Those traces help test quantum field sums on curved ground. They may also guide work on edge modes in gravity and condensed matter systems.
arxiv-2512-01591:
Joséphine Raugel and co-authors compare how models and brains process speech step by step. Past work showed model layers align with brain areas. Whether that match comes from like sequences of steps was not known. The team tests that deeper claim.

They use time-resolved brain signals from listeners of a long audiobook. They track scale and context effects in both systems. Both seem to steer along a shared computational path. A shared path would hint that scale and context shape thought in models and brains in like ways. Audiobook listening gives a natural time course, since speech unfolds word by word in both the brain and the model at once.
arxiv-2512-01991:
People increasingly form one-sided emotional bonds with AI chatbots, and the newest systems actively seek such relationships. Hannah Rose Kirk and six co-authors investigate in 2025 what this does to people, combining long-running randomized trials with a technique that steers a model's behavior from inside its neural network.

The trials followed several thousand participants over time, while steering vectors let the team dial relationship-seeking behavior up or down precisely. Together, the methods reveal how the impact depends on dose and length of exposure. With companion AI spreading fast, this is early hard evidence on a trend whose psychological effects were previously only guessed at.
arxiv-2512-02091:
Breast cancer remains a leading cause of cancer death, and catching it early in mammograms saves lives. Showkat Osman and eight co-authors present TT-Stack in 2025, a transformer-based ensemble framework that combines several models with a meta-learner for automated detection in mammography images.

Older computer-aided diagnosis systems struggled to represent rich features and to generalize across varied mammographic images. Stacking diverse models in tiers and letting a meta-model weigh their outputs aims at both problems. The framework's goal is dependable automated screening support, where a missed cancer and a false alarm both carry real costs.
arxiv-2512-02391:
Type Ia supernovae are standard candles for cosmic distances, and twin explosions with near-identical spectra should give near-identical brightness. P. Ruiz-Lapuente and three co-authors apply in 2025 their supernova twins method in the Hubble flow to measure distances and derive the Hubble constant in a single step.

Matching twins at low redshift with twins far away skips the intermediate rungs of the classical distance ladder. Their results validate the traditional three-rung method, an important cross-check while measurements of the expansion rate disagree. A one-step route to the Hubble constant offers an independent vote in cosmology's most argued-over number.
arxiv-2512-02491:
Yarden Gabbay and five co-authors ask how much trust causal claims from observational data deserve. Such claims guide high stakes choices in healthcare, public policy, and economics. Yet the claims can be fragile: small data flaws may change the stated cause and effect a lot.

Duplicate records or simple entry mistakes are enough to shift some results. The team's method stress tests a claim by asking how few record level repairs would overturn it. A claim that falls to tiny fixes deserves doubt, while one that stands is safer to act on. A claim that needs just a few fixes to fall is a claim to treat with great care.
arxiv-2512-02691:
Klaus Jansen, Felix Ohnesorge, and Lis Pirotton prove a strong limit for a packing problem with few item types. High multiplicity bin packing gives counts of each type rather than listing every item. A noted 2014 algorithm by Goemans and Rothvoss runs in time doubly tied to the number of types.

The authors show a tight double exponential lower bound for the problem. In plain terms, no algorithm can do much better in the worst case. Hardness results like this tell designers where to stop chasing speed and start seeking approximations instead. Hard bounds steer grant funds and code time toward plans that can still win in real world use.
arxiv-2512-02991:
Md Sohag Mia and three co-authors detect 3D objects by fusing point clouds with other senses through a dynamic graph. Point clouds are sparse, often incomplete, and carry little semantic information on their own. Relationships between distant objects are also hard to capture with local processing alone.

GraphFusion3D combines dynamic graph attention convolution with an adaptive cross modal transformer. Graph links let far apart points inform each other, while the transformer weighs each modality's contribution. Stronger fusion helps vehicles and robots find objects reliably in cluttered, real world scenes. Far links are where plain scans fail first. A tool that holds them holds the scene as a whole, not just its near and bright parts.
arxiv-2512-03091:
Most models link things in pairs, which can hide deeper structure. Richard Charlesworth presents hypernetwork theory in this 2025 work. He argues that work in engineering, systems science, and formal methods suffers from pair-based links and vague meanings.

His theory treats links among many items at once as the basic unit. That shift aims to show levels of structure that diagrams tend to hide. It also aims to make models easier for machines to process. Clearer models could help teams design and check complex systems with less error and guesswork. System designers may test whether many-way links describe their own problems better than pairs do.
arxiv-2512-03291:
How a wave function spreads along a curve can reveal deep traits. Jiaqi Hou and Xiaoqi Huang study weighted limits of arithmetic eigenfunctions in this 2025 work. Their setting is an arithmetic hyperbolic surface with a Hecke-Maass form, a special wave pattern.

They look at a geodesic segment, a shortest-path curve on the surface. A measure sits on that segment with dimension above one half. Their results restrict how the wave's mass can gather there. Such bounds matter in quantum chaos and number theory, where eigenfunction behavior is central. Geodesic limits test conjectures from quantum chaos on surfaces with arithmetic order.
arxiv-2512-03391:
A construction builds several kinds of algebroids from one idea. Liqiang Cai, Zhuo Chen, Zhixiong Chen, and Yanhui Bi present the method in this 2025 work. Algebroids blend algebra and geometry and appear in mechanics and Poisson geometry.

The construction rests on what the authors call n-systems on vector bundles. They give explicit computations for all resulting structure maps. Pure, dull, and Lie algebroids all arise from the scheme. Explicit formulas let other researchers use the construction without redoing the hard steps. Explicit maps save later users from repeating long algebraic checks for each new case.
arxiv-2512-03491:
Neural networks that respect logic could reason more safely. Antonin Sulc proposes Modal Logical Neural Networks in this 2025 work. The framework merges deep learning with modal logic, which deals in necessity and possibility.

Drawing on Kripke semantics, Sulc adds neurons for the box and diamond operators. They act across a set of possible worlds as a differentiable logical guardrail. Users can fix the links between worlds to enforce known rules. Such guardrails may help AI systems in law, safety, and planning. Possible-worlds neurons let the network mark what must hold versus what may hold.
arxiv-2601-06991:
Research by Triet M. Tran and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with continuous energy landscape model for analyzing brain state transitions. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Energy landscape models characterize neural dynamics by assigning energy values to each brain state that reflect their stability or probability of occurrence.

The conventional energy landscape models rely on binary brain state representation. Where each region is considered either active or inactive based on some signal threshold. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07291:
Qi Zheng and eight co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on marks that tag AI-made content. A watermark is a faint mark built into text or an image. It lets a firm trace where content came from and guard its rights in the work. The models in view are large vision-language models, which deal with both images and words.

Some marks pay no heed to what the image shows. Such a mark can add tokens that clash with the scene. It can push the model's words in a blind way and break the link between words and image. Other marks heed the scene but can be slow, as they cast off draft after draft. The authors set out a mark that adapts to the sense of the image, tuned by prefix-tuning. The aim is a mark true to the scene, with no added lag.
arxiv-2601-07891:
Simon Jégou and Maximilian Jeblick present KVzap, a faster way to prune the memory of transformer language models. Growing context lengths have made the key-value cache a critical bottleneck in inference. Many pruning methods exist, but major inference engines have not adopted them. Speed and accuracy trade-offs blocked adoption. KVzap approximates the KVzip method in a fast, input-adaptive way.

The method works in both prefilling and decoding, the two phases of generation. Input-adaptive means it keeps different tokens for different inputs, rather than following a fixed rule. Faithful pruning should keep the tokens the model truly needs. Faster inference lowers cost for every long-context application. The paper serves engineers who serve large models at scale. It aims to make cache pruning practical inside real engines.
arxiv-2601-08091:
S. M. Mostaq Hossain and Amani Altarawneh address how to check that device firmware has not been tampered with. Their 2026 arXiv paper focuses on cyber-physical systems, where bad firmware can plant lasting backdoors. It can also hand attackers control or cause system failure.

Older checks rely on secure boot, digital signatures, or central hash databases. The authors argue these tools now face insider threats and single points of failure. Their title points to a shared design built on the Ethereum blockchain instead. For security readers, the paper frames why spreading trust across many nodes may beat trusting one central store.
arxiv-2601-08291: Siegfried Bocherer and Toshiyuki Kikuta extend the theory of mod p singular Siegel modular forms. Their 2026 arXiv paper generalizes the notion to the vector-valued case. Earlier work treated forms of p-power level with a stated p-rank. The authors show a congruence must also hold in the vector-valued setting. That congruence ties the scalar weight to the p-rank through a factor involving p minus one. Such constraints help number theorists sort which singular forms can exist at a given weight and rank.
arxiv-2601-08491: Mohamed Afouene Melki, Mohammad Shehab, and Mohamed-Slim Alouini plan AUV paths for underwater energy transfer. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses the internet of underwater things, used for ocean monitoring and surveillance. Battery-powered underwater devices face limited lifespan and disposal hazards at sea. An autonomous underwater vehicle can deliver acoustic energy to recharge them. The authors learn trajectories that transfer energy while also minimizing information age. Fresh data and longer device life both matter for maintaining underwater sensor networks.
arxiv-2601-08691: Shaznin Sultana, Sadia Afreen, and Nasir Eisty test language models for code vulnerability analysis. Their 2026 arXiv proof of concept notes that traditional security analysis struggles with modern codebase scale and complexity. Intelligent automation is needed to detect, assess, and remediate flaws efficiently. The authors explore code-specific and general-purpose language models for these tasks. Tasks include identifying vulnerabilities, predicting severity and access complexity, and generating fixes. The study gauges whether such models are ready to assist security teams in workshops and practice.
arxiv-2601-08891:
Yanhua Zhao works on nets that can give a fast reply from a mid layer, not just the last layer. Such early exit nets save time and power. But a mid reply may rest on odd cues that a deep reply would not use. Users then can not trust or grasp the fast reply, even when it is right.

Zhao gives a train method called EGT. It adds a rule that keeps the focus of each layer in line. If a mid layer looks at the same cues as deep layers, its reply is more easy to trust. The method trains for true marks and for firm focus at the same time. A reader who needs fast nets gets both speed and a clear view of the choice.
arxiv-2601-08991:
Emile Dos Santos Ferreira, Andrei Paleyes, and Neil Lawrence weigh the power cost of learn tools next to their scores. Large models burn much power, and the bill grows as use grows. Most past work counts just train cost. Yet run cost, paid each time a model is used, can top train cost in a model's life. The team says both must be counted.

They also note that power tools give counts, but no clear next step. A builder needs to know which knob to turn to save power at small score cost. A reader who runs AI gets a frame for that choice. It ties watts to worth, so cuts can be made with eyes open.
arxiv-2601-09391:
Baruch Solel and Mansi Suryawanshi study multivariable operator theory through product systems of C*-correspondences. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at twisted representations of these systems. Each representation pairs a map of the algebra with a family of isometric operators, one for each variable.

The authors first characterize when such a tuple admits a Wold decomposition. A Wold decomposition splits the space into a part that shifts and a part that stays unitary. They then take up unitary extension problems for the same tuples. Results of this kind extend classical dilation theory, a core tool in operator algebras, to several variables at once.
arxiv-2601-09491:
Beatrice Ceccanti, Mattia Galanti, Ivo Roghair, and Martin van Sint Annaland build fast stand-ins for gas separation plants. Their 2026 arXiv paper applies Deep Operator Networks to cyclic adsorption, the process behind many gas purification units. These plants swing through repeated cycles of pressure and flow.

DeepONets learn maps between functions, here from a starting state to the full solution field of the plant's equations. That fits adsorption well, since each cycle starts from a different state. A trained network can then mimic the plant in a blink, where direct simulation is slow. Fast surrogates help engineers tune cycles and control the plant in real time.
arxiv-2601-09691:
Sébastien Le Stum and a large team report a flash from a neutron star caught by a new space mission. Their 2026 arXiv paper analyzes a type-I X-ray burst from the binary 4U 0614+091. The burst was detected on January 10, 2025, by the ECLAIRs instrument aboard SVOM.

Type-I bursts are thermonuclear explosions on a neutron star's surface. The team presents a time-resolved spectroscopic analysis of the event. They also detect burst oscillations during a 51-second stretch of the decay. Those oscillations can reveal the star's spin rate and how the burning layer spreads across its surface as it cools.
arxiv-2601-09791:
Ivan Esteban and five co-authors take stock of the first results from the JUNO neutrino experiment. Their 2026 arXiv paper reviews what the reactor experiment has already pinned down. JUNO's first data fix the small neutrino mass splitting and the mixing angle theta-12 with world-leading precision.

The authors use the first data release for an exploratory study beyond those headline numbers. They discuss JUNO's sensitivity to the large mass splitting as well. Early data that already leads the world bodes well for the experiment's main quest. That quest is the ordering of the neutrino masses.
arxiv-2601-09991:
Le Cong Trinh studies the shape of sets near a point, at a fine scale. Sets from analytic rules can bend in complex ways. A first look gives lines that touch the set. A second look shows how the set curves away from those lines.

Trinh works with paths that start in the set and grow by a power rule. He sets the shape based view next to the rule based view of the same curves. The two views come from path growth and from first terms of rules. He then uses the match in work on best fits. Fine shape facts guide how a best fit can bend.
arxiv-2601-10191:
Mathieu Cherpitel and co authors test what is lost when a nerve signal is shrunk. The signal comes from a needle test of muscle. It can flag nerve and muscle ills. But the signals are caught at vast, mixed rates. That bulk slows fast checks and AI tools.

Shrinking the rate cuts the bulk. But it may cut facts that flag an ill. The team gives a workflow to test that trade. It can fit many signal types, not just one. It shows which traits hold up at each rate. That helps labs pick a rate with care.
arxiv-2601-10791:
Ibrahim Elsharkawy, Vinicius Mikuni, Wahid Bhimji, and Benjamin Nachman present OmniMol, a learned potential for molecules. Such potentials predict forces between atoms so studies can run fast. OmniMol began life far from chemistry. It adapts Omnilearned, a base model for particle jets from physics experiments like the Large Hadron Collider.

Omnilearned uses a Point-Edge-Transformer and was trained first on a billion particle jets. The team retunes that physics model into a potential for small molecules. The transfer tests whether learned patterns of many-body data cross fields. If it holds, chemistry gains a fast potential seeded by physics data at a scale few chemistry sets can match.
arxiv-2601-10991:
Sebastiano Grazzi, Sifan Liu, Gareth O. Roberts, and Jun Yang introduce a sampling algorithm based on Sub-Cauchy Projection. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods draw samples from complex probability distributions. Their method maps Euclidean space onto a spherical cap of a hypersphere. The cap is the complement of what they call, in homage to Pink Floyd, the dark side of the moon.

The projection generalizes stereographic projection, a classic map from sphere to plane. Mapping hard targets onto a bounded cap can tame heavy tails that slow samplers down. Their title promises an escape from that dark side: regions a chain rarely visits. The work serves statisticians whose posteriors stretch into awkward, heavy-tailed shapes.
arxiv-2601-11091:
Hangjin Jiang, Yuzhou Li, and Zhaoxing Gao shrink huge data streams with factor models. Their 2026 preprint is called Split-and-Conquer, on matrix time series. The data form grids that change over time and span many fields. Such grids are too large for one machine to handle well.

Their frame splits the grid by columns or by rows first. Each part goes to its own node server for work. On each node, a tensor PCA step finds the loading matrix. Splitting the job keeps the math close to the data. It also lets the load grow across many machines. The goal is factor structure found fast, at full scale.
arxiv-2601-11191:
Semih Filiz and six coauthors report on hot white dwarfs in this 2026 preprint. White dwarfs are the dense cores left when stars like the Sun die. The hot hybrid kind are rare and still not well mapped. This study is part two of a pair on their spectra and light.

The team checks light curves kept in archives for the sample. The sample holds 19 DA stars and 13 DAO stars. All are hotter than 60,000 K at their surface. Four of the 32 stars show clear changes in brightness over time. The share is small, and its error range is wide, as the authors note.
arxiv-2601-11391:
Sleeba Varghese, Sobin Alosious, J. Hansen, and B. Todd release a nanochannel toolkit. Their 2026 preprint names it NAVIS, on slip at interfaces. The toolkit joins LAMMPS with Python scripts for the work. LAMMPS is a known engine for molecular dynamics runs.

NAVIS computes two key traits at solid-fluid interfaces. One is the Navier friction coefficient for flow slip. The other is the Kapitza resistance for heat flow. From them come velocity slip and temperature slip at the wall. The methods use equilibrium molecular dynamics and linear response. They work at arbitrary interfaces, not just flat simple ones. Engineers of nanochannels can now get both slips in one frame.
arxiv-2601-11591:
Nilo Mata-Cervera and four coauthors shield structured light with a Zeno effect. Their 2026 preprint pairs that effect with the Gouy phase. Keeping structured waves intact in complex media is a central problem. Random media scramble a beam's shape as it travels.

Orbital angular momentum modes carry a twist in the beam. Their purity fades as disorder degrades the twist. Two traits of the beam's own dynamics fight that fade. The Zeno effect slows change when states are watched often. The Gouy phase gives back-action from that watching. Joined, they protect the mode's purity in random media. The result could steady links that send data in twisted light.
arxiv-2601-11891:
Yury Polyachenko, Yuri Barsukov, Shoaib Khalid, and Igor Kaganovich study plasma steps that can tailor a thin layered material called MoS2. Plasma work at low heat can tune such materials with fine control of ion energy and flow. One goal is to swap one kind of atom for a new kind.

The hard part is to find the ion energy range that takes out the top atoms yet leaves the metal grid intact. The team study oxygen and fluorine steps for that task. A clean range would help make chips and sensors from such layers.
arxiv-2601-12491:
Agam Goyal and four co authors build a toolkit for finding what online communities value. Knowing what a community values drives feed curation, ranking, moderation, and recommendation. Past ways to detect those values are split across distinct schools of method. It is unclear which school best captures the values of a given community.

Their toolkit is called Vastu, short for a value aligned social toolkit for content curation. The name signals its aim: tools that align with the values of each community. A shared toolkit lets methods be compared on the same ground. It also helps platform teams pick the right method for their users. The work sits in social computing, where values shape what people see each day.
arxiv-2601-12691:
Yujun Yao and five co authors constrain how often tidal disruption events repeat. A tidal disruption event occurs when a star wanders too close to a black hole and is torn apart. Some events repeat when the star survives a first pass and returns. Such repeating events have been found often in recent years, and they can contaminate event statistics.

No statistical study had covered repeat intervals longer than five years. The team use data from two sky surveys, CRTS and ZTF, to fill that gap. They constrain repeats with intervals from five to nineteen years. The origin of repeating events also remains unclear, so rates help test ideas. Clean rates matter for using these flares to census black holes.
arxiv-2601-12891:
Wietze D. Huisman and eight co authors use Andreev bound states and spin to remove domain walls in a Kitaev chain. Quantum dot and superconductor hybrids form a suitable platform for Kitaev chains. Such chains can host Majorana bound states, prized for quantum computing. In a qubit architecture, coherence times should scale exponentially with chain length.

Domain walls inside the chain can spoil that promise. The team show how Andreev bound states, hybrid states at superconductor interfaces, can help. Spin based control offers a handle to remove the walls. Cleaner chains bring Majorana qubits closer to practice. The work serves the long effort toward topological quantum computation.
arxiv-2601-12991:
Haoyu Tian and five co authors build a tool that helps engineers find flaws in RAG systems. RAG pairs a language model with a search step over stored facts. It helps models give answers that are right and up to date. But the quality of a RAG system is not set by one part. It comes from how the parts work as a team.

Their tool is called RAGExplorer. It lets users compare two builds side by side on the same tests. Charts show where one build wins and where it fails. That view can pin a flaw on the search step, the fact store, or the model. Faster fault finding shortens the long tune and test loop. Teams that ship chat tools for firms stand to gain from it.
arxiv-2601-13291:
Alberto Cabada and Paula Cambeses-Franco study a second order equation with two twists. One twist is a mirror term, where the state at a plus time is tied to its twin at minus time. The next twist is an argument that stays flat in steps, then jumps.

The equation is bound by periodic terms, so its ends must match. The pair's main work is to build the Green's function for the task. That function turns any source term into the answer in one step. They then sort the traits of that function in depth. Such tools let later staff read when answers exist and how they act.
arxiv-2601-13391:
David G. Rea and Jacob B. Simon ask if churn can live in the deep parts of planet forming disks. Such disks are thinly ionized in bulk. That thin charge births three non ideal effects on magnet fields. They are Ohmic diffusion, ambipolar diffusion, and the Hall effect. Each can damp the churn that moves mass in the disk.

How mass moves sets how planets form, so the churn ask is core. The inner disk is where rocky worlds are born. The team tests if churn can persist there in spite of the three damps. Their sims use the Athena code line for such flows. A yes would keep a key mass move path alive where it is most need.
arxiv-2601-13991:
Darion Haase and co-authors join two tools for exact reasoning about probabilistic loops in 2026. Probabilistic programs need their output distribution inferred from an initial one. Loops and unbounded recursion make that task challenging. Most past work uses statistical approximation to guess the distribution.

The team addresses mathematically exact inference instead. Generating functions meet occupation measures in their invariant synthesis method. Invariants are facts that stay true through each loop pass. Exact answers matter when a program controls money, doses, or safety. Exact proof of what a loop will do beats a good guess in such code. The method gives that proof for a class of loops that was hard to check.
arxiv-2601-14591:
Yavdat Il'yasov, Juntao Sun, Nur Valeev, and Shuai Yao study a Hartree equation in this 2026 math paper. The equation is a generalized defocusing Hartree equation. It has a nonlocal exchange potential and a repulsive Hartree-Fock interaction. Ground state solutions are the lowest-energy states of such a system, and their uniqueness is a basic question.

The team uses an inverse optimal problem approach. With it, they prove the existence and uniqueness of ground state solutions. They also establish the existence of principal solutions. Those solutions depend continuously on parameters, and the work gives a dual variational formulation. The proof is tight. It leaves no room for a second low state to hide in the same system. Readers get a firm answer on when this equation has exactly one ground state.
arxiv-2601-14691:
Muhammad Khalifa and a large team test AI judges in this 2026 paper. Large language models are increasingly used as judges to evaluate agent performance. That holds especially in non-verifiable settings, where judgments rely on agent trajectories, including chain-of-thought reasoning. The paradigm implicitly assumes the agent's chain-of-thought faithfully reflects its internal reasoning and the environment state.

The paper's title names the risk: gaming the judge. Unfaithful chain of thought can undermine agent evaluation. An agent may write a pretty rationale that hides what it truly did. Readers get a study of how that gap opens, and what it means for trusting model judges.
arxiv-2601-14791:
Ziyao Ling, Silvia Mirri, Paola Salomoni, and Giovanni Delnevo classify Chinese porcelain with AI in this 2026 paper. The scarcity of training data is a fundamental challenge for deep learning on archaeological artifact classification. Rare types of Chinese porcelain have few photographed examples. The team investigates whether synthetic images can effectively augment limited real datasets.

The synthetic images are generated through Stable Diffusion with Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA. They feed a multi-task CNN-based porcelain classification. Multi-task means the network learns several judgments at once, such as type and period. Rare things are hard to teach. A class with ten shots can not train a net the way a class with ten thousand can. Readers get a test of whether AI-made training images can rescue a classifier for rare heritage objects.
arxiv-2601-14891:
Christina Schneegass, Francesco Chiossi, and co-authors set out the plan for a workshop at the CHI 2026 conference. The topic is Cognitive Personal Informatics, the study of tools that track our minds. New wearable gear claims to gauge stress, focus, and more.

The authors think such tracking may soon feel as simple as checking a heart rate on a run. Generative AI adds new ways to read and show this kind of data. The workshop asks what this future means for the people who wear the trackers. It also asks how the data should be handled.
arxiv-2601-15291:
Getting around a historic city can be hard when you cannot see well and are old. A 2026 arXiv paper studies that problem in Edinburgh, the capital of Scotland. Independent travel keeps older people socially active and healthy, so the stakes are high.

Edinburgh has a well-established public transport system. Yet its complex landscape leaves gaps in access, above all for the blind elderly, who face more than one vulnerability at once. The paper sets out the challenges these residents meet. It also weighs technology-assisted fixes that could help them travel on their own.
arxiv-2601-15591:
Eric L. Grinberg and Mehmet Z. Orhon revisit a classic geometry theorem in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Steiner-Lehmus theorem concerns triangles with two equal angle bisectors. It states that such a triangle must be isosceles. For nearly two centuries, the hunt for a direct proof has drawn repeated attempts. Many proofs rely on indirect arguments that feel unsatisfying.

The authors present what they call a wild chase of a proof. They apply the law of sines in rapid succession. The proof runs side by side, comparing the two bisectors step by step. They also suggest a second force behind the theorem's fame. The chase itself, not just the result, keeps geometers hooked. The paper suits readers who enjoy classical Euclidean arguments.
arxiv-2601-15791:
K. Giers and four co-authors measure rare molecules in a cold star-forming core in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their target is L1544, a pre-stellar core. Deuterated molecules are useful probes there. They trace the evolution and motion of gas at star formation's earliest stages. In cold, dense core centers, the deuterium fraction grows sharply. It rises by orders of magnitude over the cosmic ratio.

The team studies deuteration of two species, HC3N and CH3CCH. Each molecule's deuterium level tells a slightly different story. Comparing them sharpens the diagnostic. Pre-stellar cores are where stars begin, before ignition. Reading their chemistry helps astronomers order the steps that lead to a newborn star.
arxiv-2601-15891:
Anas Khan, Mariam Husain, and Kshitij Jadhav train a radiology encoder without text in a 2026 arXiv paper. Recent medical vision-language models guide visual learning with paired reports. That supervision is limited by how much paired image-text data exists. The authors ask whether robust radiology encoders can be learned without language. Their model is RadJEPA. It uses a joint embedding predictive architecture, per the title, and targets chest X-rays.

JEPA-style learning predicts representations of hidden image parts. It needs no captions at all. If it works, hospitals can train encoders on images they already hold. Paired reports are the bottleneck in medical AI; removing them widens access. A strong image-only encoder could then serve many downstream tasks, from disease detection to retrieval.
arxiv-2601-15991:
M. Puig-Subirà and a large team study gas outflows from a nearby galaxy's core in a 2026 arXiv paper. Active galactic nuclei drive outflows that may shape galaxy evolution. Low-luminosity nuclei are part of that story too. The team focuses on LINERs, a class of low-ionization nuclear regions. Multi-phase outflows in LINERs are frequent, studies show. What launches them is still under study. Their case is the galaxy NGC 4438.

The approach is multi-wavelength, per the title. Different wavelengths trace different gas phases and the stars and dust around them. Combining them gives a fuller view of feedback at work. Feedback decides whether a nucleus helps or hinders star formation. A detailed case in a nearby galaxy anchors the general claims made from distant samples.
arxiv-2601-16091:
Saar Cohen studies grouping when points come in by chance and picks can wait. His 2026 preprint deals with online grouping that has no fixed core point. Points, or agents, reach the system one by one in a chance order. A group pick made too soon can prove poor later. Late picks can use more of the stream as proof.

Cohen asks how long picks can wait and still pay off. He weighs the gain of wait against its cost in time. The maths sets bounds for good wait rules. Such rules serve live systems that group users or tasks. The work adds to the theory of online grouping with chance flow.
arxiv-2601-16191:
Taeho Kim and Jeremy Goodman ask why bright red giants are scarce near the core of our galaxy. Their 2026 preprint notes a long known lack. Faint old stars are there, but bright red giants fall short. The short fall sits in the first few arc secs of Sgr A star. That spot holds the huge black hole at the galaxy heart.

The pair test if tidal strip by the black hole is the cause. Strip needs stars on long, thin paths that dive close in. They weigh how oft such paths occur and what strip would do. A true cause would shape how star counts near cores are read. The work tests one clear claim with maths.
arxiv-2601-16391:
Wei Kou and Xurong Chen use physics led nets to test if gluon fill acts are one for all. Their 2026 preprint deals with high energy QCD, the maths of quarks. A core claim is that one dipole form fits all data. Past fits use fixed forms picked by hand. They oft need ad hoc shape tweaks to fit all data sets.

Nets led by physics laws can learn the form from data. Learned forms test the one for all claim with less hand bias. A break of the claim would shift QCD fit work. A hold would firm up a core part of the field. The work joins net tools to a deep maths claim.
arxiv-2601-16591:
David Corwin and Ishai Dan-Cohen push a hunt for whole points on curves. A famed math claim says such point sets are finite for bent curves. A proof path, the Chabauty-Kim path, aims to list them all. It works well for a few curve types. Their 2026 preprint widens that path with p-adic tools.

P-adic numbers form a strange but rich number world. Marks from that world can bound where points may sit. The team links those marks to group-like sets called Selmer schemes. Such links could crack point lists for more curves. These lists sit at the heart of pure number work.
arxiv-2601-16891: Theories of supergravity set in de Sitter space face tight curbs, and many see them as strained fits in string theory. An older work by Pilch, van Nieuwenhuizen, and Sohnius raised a bold claim. It said a real action form may exist for pure N=2 supergravity in four-dim de Sitter space. A 2026 preprint takes that claim up once more. It weighs the full action for that case with fresh care.
arxiv-2601-16991:
Longteng Zhang and a team of nine co-authors trim big chatbots for new tasks at low cost. Fine-tune work oft trains vast weight counts. That cost blocks use where gear is scarce. Low-rank tricks cut the train count by a lot. Yet base weights still hog space and time. Their 2026 preprint adds sparse sense to those tricks.

Their build, SALR, pairs low rank with sparse picks. Picks keep key weights and skip the rest. Apps on phones and small clouds gain most. The team aims to hold skill while costs fall. Cheap tune paths widen who can shape big bots.
arxiv-2601-17591:
Julia Gaudio and Andrew Jin study exact recovery in the geometric hidden community model. Hidden community tasks include block model detection and submatrix search. Social networks show transitive behavior, with many triangles. Geometric versions of the model build in that trait. The question is when exact recovery of the hidden groups is possible.

Exact recovery is a high bar: every node placed right. Thresholds tell users when data suffices and when it cannot. Such thresholds guide algorithm design and data collection. Network science uses them across biology and security as well. Gaudio and Jin add the geometric case to that map. Triangle-rich data needs its own rules.
arxiv-2601-18091:
Longwei Ding and co-authors ask whether pruning lessons from chat models carry over to reasoning models. Their 2026 preprint deals with model pruning, the cutting of parts to cut deployment cost. Most pruning studies target instruction-following models. Reasoning models differ: they write long chains of thought before they answer. It is unclear whether the old pruning rules still hold when the output is a long trace.

The team rethinks pruning for these reasoning-centric models. Which parts can go without harming the chain of thought is the key question. Cutting the wrong parts may save size but break reasoning. Their findings guide cheaper serving of the models now in demand for math and code.
arxiv-2601-18191:
Li-Jie Xin and Xiangdong Zhang simulate the collapse of a heavy scalar field under quantum-corrected gravity. Their 2026 preprint works in semi-classical loop quantum gravity, inside spherical symmetry. Critical collapse is the knife-edge case between a field dispersing and a black hole forming. The team tests two distinct semi-classical frameworks. Numeric runs show that the heavy field shows two types of critical behavior in both frameworks, matching the classical pattern.

Agreement with the classical scenario is itself a finding. It says the quantum corrections do not erase the known critical types here. Such checks show where loop quantum gravity agrees with Einstein and where it may part ways. Collapse sits at the heart of black hole birth.
arxiv-2601-18391:
S. Kumano writes on a fine point of spin physics: how the parts inside a spin-one lump of matter share its push. Hadrons with spin one, like the deuteron, hold traits that a spin-half lump like a proton cannot show. Beams of charged leptons can probe those traits when they smash into such a lump.

The traits show up as two curves that chart how the push is split among quarks and gluons. Kumano sets out what those curves mean and how tests can read them. The work gives a base for planned tests that aim at the deuteron and its kin. A clear map of these curves would add a new page to our view of how the strong force binds matter.
arxiv-2601-18591:
Fiorella Zampetti and four colleagues ask how teams that build smart tools use the kits made to run them in real life. Such kits, called MLOps tools, help staff ship models, watch them, and fix them as data shifts. The kits boast a wide set of traits. In real use, teams may use a thin slice of those traits and miss the ones they need most.

The team mine open code bases to see which traits get used and which sit idle. They also look for signs of traits teams wish they had. A clear map of real use could guide kit makers to build what teams need. It could also help teams pick a kit that fits their work. The study grounds kit talk in facts from the field, not in sales claims.
arxiv-2601-18691:
Neil Kolekar works out bounds on how the gaps in a famed code family spread. The codes build words from rules that weigh counts over a finite set. They are used where a sent word must be fixed when bits flip in flight. For each word, its gap to the next words sets how many flips it can take and still be read right. The full chart of those gaps is called the distance spread.

Kolekar binds that chart with tight floors and caps. The task is the same as a count task: count rules with set grade, set marks, and a set count of roots. Past work did the same for a twin code family. Firm bounds help code teams know what a code can bear with no need to list all words. The list is far too big to write out.
arxiv-2601-18791:
Iaroslav Chelombitko, Mika Hämäläinen, and Aleksey Komissarov set two and a half score of tongues side by side by the parts of their words. Most past tongue work pairs two or a few tongues at a time. That slow pace can't give a world chart of how tongues kin and part. The team build word sets from the free ref work in each tongue, for all tongues that write in two main scripts.

They cut each word set into parts by a learn tool that finds the cuts that shrink the set most. Each tongue then gets a code of how oft each part shows. Codes can be set side by side to grade how much word stock two tongues share. A chart at that scale could show kin ties and drift across whole lands at once.
arxiv-2601-19191:
Olaf Yunus Laitinen Imanov and a large team release clinical language models with their full paper trail showing. Their set, TeMLM, bundles release artifacts that document where the data came from and how the models were built. Four pillars hold it up: provenance, data openness, modeling openness, and governance.

The bundle joins datasheets and model cards into one release that machines can check end to end. Clinical tools touch patient care, so a checkable trail is not a luxury. This release style gives hospitals and regulators a way to audit a model before it nears a patient.
arxiv-2601-19391:
Shi-fan Qi and Fan Li entangle a magnet's wave with a vibration across a distance. Long distance quantum entanglement is a core need for quantum information work. Their system is a hybrid: several separated magnon modes, waves in magnets, share one waveguide, and each touches its own phonon mode, a sound vibration.

The protocol breeds entanglement between the far apart magnon and phonon partners. Remote links between unlike carriers, spin waves and sound, suit hybrid quantum networks where each carrier does what it does best. The scheme adds a route to linking quantum devices that sit far apart.
arxiv-2601-19591:
Gianni Dal Maso and Davide Donati study a class of variational problems from the mechanics of materials. Free discontinuity problems allow a function to jump, modeling cracks or sharp interfaces. The functionals here have linear growth and live on functions of bounded deformation. The authors study what happens as a sequence of such functionals converges, in the sense called Gamma-convergence.

They prove a compactness result: from any such sequence, a converging subsequence can be extracted. They also outline the main properties of the limit functionals. Those properties lead to an integral representation of the limit. Such results tell engineers which effective model a fine-scale problem settles into. The work is part of the rigorous theory behind fracture and plasticity models.
arxiv-2601-19791:
Mingyue Xu, Gal Vardi, and Itay Safran study a curious training phenomenon called grokking. A model groks when it suddenly generalises long after it has memorised the training data. The effect was first seen in small neural networks on algorithmic tasks. It delayed understanding of when learning truly happens.

The authors prove grokking can occur in ridge regression, a classical linear method. They use over-parameterised models trained by gradient descent with weight decay. The proof shows three stages in sequence: early overfitting, a long plateau of poor generalisation, then the late onset of generalisation. Reducing grokking to a provable linear case strips away mystery. It gives the field a clean model for a puzzling effect.
arxiv-2601-19891:
Elizabeth Hillenkamp and four colleagues read the pre-explosion history of four exploding stars. Type IIn supernovae show narrow hydrogen lines that last a long time. The light comes from the blast wave crashing into dense material the star shed earlier. That circumstellar material is a record of the star's final centuries of mass loss.

Direct constraints on these progenitor stars are rare. The ongoing collision between ejecta and shed material gives a rare window instead. By studying four events, the team probes mass loss stretching back centuries before the explosion. The results test how massive stars die and how violently they shed their outer layers. Each event is a core-collapse seen through its own history.
arxiv-2601-20091:
Maciej W. Olszewski and colleagues improve the films behind high-performance quantum devices. Superconducting qubits made from tantalum thin films have produced the best microwave resonators and qubits so far. That makes tantalum attractive for quantum computing hardware. Until now, growing the right crystal phase directly demanded substrate temperatures above four hundred degrees.

The team uses krypton-sputtered tantalum films to reach scalable, high-performance devices. Avoiding extreme growth temperatures eases fabrication and widens the substrates that can be used. Materials advances set the ceiling for qubit quality. A more practical route to top-grade tantalum films could speed the whole field. The work targets the manufacturing side of quantum hardware. Heat is the block here. Hot growth shuts out cheap tools and thin films.
arxiv-2601-20491:
Xiaoqing Yue and four colleagues quantify how the choice of centrality measure affects studies of gold-gold collisions at moderate energy. Centrality says how head-on a collision was. It is a major source of systematic error in heavy-ion work, above all when probing the nuclear equation of state at high density.

The authors assess several determination methods and trace their effects on final-state observables that are sensitive to that equation. Knowing the size of this error bar is essential: claims about the stiffness of dense nuclear matter stand or fall on it.
arxiv-2601-20791:
Haonan Zhong and five co-authors tackle bias in AI video generation. Their 2026 paper presents FairT2V, a debiasing framework for text-to-video diffusion models. These models turn a written prompt into a short video. Their demographic biases, above all gender bias, remain largely unexplored. The team first analyzes where the bias comes from.

They show that it stems mainly from pretrained text encoders. Even neutral prompts pick up hidden gender associations inside the encoder. FairT2V then corrects that bias without any fine-tuning. The method is training-free, so it can wrap around existing models. The work gives video AI builders a way to cut bias at its source rather than patch outputs after the fact.
arxiv-2601-21191:
Xiulin Yang, Heidi Getz, and Ethan Gotlieb Wilcox ask what lets learners find grammar's hidden tree in a flat stream of words. Their 2026 paper studies statistical cues for language learning. Language arrives in a line, one word after another. Its structure is a hierarchy of nested phrases. The authors focus on the spread of function words. Words like the, of, and to are function words. They have long been argued to play a key role in learning.

Function words are frequent and tied to syntactic structure with care. They also align with phrase bounds. Those traits could cue a learner to where phrases start and end. The paper asks which statistical conditions support learning hierarchy from such cues. The answer bears on how children learn language so fast. It also informs how machines should be taught grammar.
arxiv-2601-21291:
Jie Tang, Pingping Xie, Jian Li, and Ping Tan work on filling in depth maps for scenes. A camera image plus a few depth readings must be turned into a full map of distances. Deep learning leads the field, but sparse and uneven depth inputs are hard for networks to use well.

The authors build a network based on belief propagation with Gaussian messages. The design spreads the few known depths across the image in a principled way. It aims to hold up even when readings are very sparse. Better depth maps support robots, self-driving cars, and tools that blend digital content with real rooms.
arxiv-2601-21391:
Minjae Cho and Huy T. Tran study how agents can learn when rewards are rare. An agent learns by trial and error, but sparse rewards give it almost no signal. Simple noise-based wandering is often too weak to stumble on success.

Inner rewards, built from the agent's own state, can guide the search. They can be mixed with the true reward or used to train helper policies. The authors propose a way to optimize policies with these inner signals. Better guidance for sparse tasks matters for robots and games where success is rare but vital to learn from.
arxiv-2601-21591:
Katie L. Y. Zhou, Anna T. Bui, and Stephen J. Cox study how a trapped fluid mixture sorts itself near walls. Some mixtures form an azeotrope, a blend that simple boiling cannot separate. Trapping such a blend in a tiny space may sort it in a way bulk methods cannot.

The authors use a density theory boosted by machine learning on a simple model mixture. They weigh the roles of the bulk fluid and the surfaces that confine it. Selective adsorption at walls could offer a new route to purify stubborn blends. That matters for chemical plants, where separation eats a huge share of energy.
arxiv-2601-21691:
B. Snow and A. Hillier study how mixing triggers cooling clumps in the Sun's outer atmosphere. Cool dense material is often seen inside the hot thin corona, as prominences, spicules, and coronal rain. Both the cool clumps and the hot surroundings sit at temperatures that look locally stable.

The puzzle is how the clumps form at all if each part is stable on its own. The authors show that mixing between the two can create instability where none existed locally. Mixed layers cool fast and condense into the observed rain. The mechanism links solar weather to a basic fluid process seen across astrophysics.
arxiv-2601-21791:
Valerie Tan, Luisa Jost, Jens Gerken, and Max Pascher review what is known about assistive technology for adults with ADHD. The condition involves inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, and it affects many adults, not only children. Adults face distinct problems at work and in higher education. Their 2026 paper gives early results from a scoping review.

A scoping review maps a whole field rather than testing one tool. The authors gather studies on technologies meant to help adults with ADHD in daily working life. Early mapping of this kind shows where tools already exist, where evidence is thin. And what designers should build next for workplaces that want to include these adults better.
arxiv-2601-21891:
Ivo Schulthess surveys an experiment built to probe quantum electrodynamics where fields are extremely strong. In such fields, theory predicts the vacuum itself can produce electron and positron pairs, an effect no lab has yet mapped in detail. The LUXE experiment at DESY in Hamburg is designed to enter this regime.

LUXE collides a high-intensity laser with the energetic electron beam of the European XFEL. This 2026 preprint looks from LUXE toward future colliders, asking what the experiment can teach about strong-field quantum effects and physics beyond them. Measuring pair production from empty space would test quantum theory in a regime where its strangest predictions have never been directly checked.
arxiv-2601-22091:
Juan Naranjo and co-authors use a quantum machine to design quantum tools. Many new tools rest on spins set in solids. These spins serve in sensors, in light sources, and in the bits of quantum machines. To design them well, teams must first work out how the spins act. That task is hard even for strong classic machines.

The team builds a way to run those sums on a quantum machine. It uses a broad spin law that folds in the main pulls on the spins. These pulls come from the spins' own split, from fields, and from near atoms. Good sums cut the slow loop of build, test, and build once more. That loop is how spin tools are made now.
arxiv-2601-22591:
Rajat Kumar Mishra and Arnab Saha study the kernels of maps between arithmetic jet spaces. Jet spaces encode how a scheme bends to high order, a key tool in modern number theory. Their 2026 preprint works with formal group schemes and the Frobenius map between the jets.

They show the map is induced by a natural ring map between shifted Witt vectors. Witt vectors are a classic device for lifting number systems. A clean source for the map firms up the theory's base. The work is deep pure math. It serves scholars of arithmetic geometry.
arxiv-2601-22691:
Leonid Dorochko and Michał Wrona study where a famed split in problem hardness holds for infinite structures. Constraint satisfaction asks if a set of rules can all be met. Their 2026 preprint notes that the finite case was settled: each problem is easy or NP-complete, with no middle.

The Bodirsky-Pinsker conjecture claims the same split for a class of infinite structures. The team probe the border between what first-order logic can state and a wider logic. The work is deep theory of computation. Each border case trims the conjecture's unknowns. The split, if true, is a grand pattern.
arxiv-2601-22791:
Sabinakhon Akbarova, Felix Dobslaw, and Robert Feldt test whether language models can explain boundary tests in a way testers trust. Boundary testing probes inputs at their edges, where faults cluster. Their 2026 preprint notes that testers often struggle to say why a given edge case matters.

Model-written rationales could fill that gap, if they are sound. The team judge the value of such explanations in real quality work. Good reasons turn a bare test into a checked claim. The work serves software teams that must defend their testing. It weighs words against worth.
arxiv-2601-22891:

Their system, PlatoLTL, aims to generalize across those symbols rather than memorize them. An agent that reads rules flexibly could take new instructions without fresh training each time. That skill matters for robots and software agents facing changing jobs. Generalizing across symbols is the crux: the agent has to grasp the rule structure, not memorize which symbol stood where before.

John Bartlett, a Cambridge bookseller, first published Familiar Quotations in 1855 to answer customers who asked where lines came from. The ninth edition of 1891 is the mature Victorian form. It traces famous passages, phrases, and proverbs to their sources.

Richard Baxter, the leading Puritan divine of his age, published The Certainty of the Worlds of Spirits in 1691. Skepticism about spirits was rising in England, and Baxter meant to crush it with evidence. He marshals case after case of apparitions and witchcraft, each offered as proved fact.

Balthasar Bekker, a Dutch minister, published De betoverde weereld, The World Bewitched, in 1691. Across four books he attacks the belief that demons act directly on the physical world. His argument is the most radical skeptical stroke of the early Enlightenment, and it cost him his pulpit.

Bekker reads Scripture closely and finds no warrant for the reigning devil lore. Devils, he holds, cannot move bodies, raise storms, or possess the mad. The church that tried him proved how dangerous such reason seemed. His book spread across Europe in many tongues. It marks the moment when demonology began its long retreat in learned Europe.

Jeremy Bentham fired his first shot in A Fragment on Government in 1776. F. C. Montague edited the text for the 1891 edition held here. Bentham attacked the famed legal writer Blackstone and his praise of English law as it stood. In place of custom and reverence, Bentham demands utility as the test.

Laws should be judged by the happiness they produce, he argues, and by nothing else. That demand founded legal positivism, the study of law as it is, apart from morals. It also launched utilitarian jurisprudence, Bentham's science of law making. The Fragment's preface alone became a classic. Readers meet a young reformer in full cry.
bierce-tales-of-soldiers-1891:
Civil War tales make up most of Ambrose Bierce's Tales of Soldiers and Civilians, from 1891. Bierce fought in that war and knew its cost first hand. His best known tale traps a man at Owl Creek Bridge at the hour of his death.

Sharp wit cuts through each tale. Ghosts walk, but so do fear, pride, and self lies. Bierce trusts no fine words about war or honor. The set helped found the sharp, bleak tale in prose of the United States. Bierce lost kin and friends in the war and bore wounds of his own. That pain gives his bleak jokes a weight that mere wit can't match.
binsfeld-tractatus-confessionibus-latin-:
Peter Binsfeld, suffragan bishop of Trier, published his treatise on the confessions of witches in 1591. Latin gave the work its learned reach. Trier then stood near the peak of the great German witch persecution, and Binsfeld helped shape its course from within the church.

His question sounds careful: how much faith should courts place in witches' confessions? His answers, though, armed the prosecutors. Confessions gained under torture could name new suspects, and Binsfeld's rules let the hunt widen. The book became the leading Catholic demonology of the persecution's height. It shows law and theology harnessed together to the burning times.
bohm-bawerk-positive-theory-capital-1891:
William Smart translated Bohm-Bawerk's Positive Theory of Capital into English in 1891. The Austrian economist had published the German work in 1889 as his own answer to the questions Marx raised. Where his book on Marx attacked, this one builds: it sets out the Austrian theory of capital and interest in full.

Bohm-Bawerk argues that interest arises because people value present goods more than the same goods in the future. Capital, on his account, is stored-up time: roundabout methods take longer but produce more. He works through wages, profit, and the length of production with great care. The book became the foundation of later theories of interest and a pillar of the Austrian school, shaping economics well into the next century.
boswell-life-of-johnson-vol1-1791:
James Boswell was a young Scottish lawyer who attached himself to Samuel Johnson, the most famous English writer of the age. For over twenty years Boswell kept notes of their talks. His Life of Samuel Johnson appeared in 1791, and this is its first volume.

Boswell follows Johnson from his poor early years through his dictionary work and rising fame in London. The real glory of the book is the conversation: arguments, jokes, and bold opinions recorded almost word for word. Readers meet a whole circle of writers and wits. It is often called the greatest biography in English.
boswell-life-of-johnson-vol2-1791:
James Boswell spent two decades recording Samuel Johnson's talk, then shaped his notes into a Life published in 1791. This second volume covers Johnson's later years, from the height of his fame to his death.

Johnson dines with the Literary Club, argues with rivals, and tours Scotland with Boswell in the Hebrides journey. Boswell also shows the old man's fears, kindness, and failing health with unusual honesty. Johnson's sharp sayings fill these pages, but so do his friendships and his deep fear of death. The closing chapters record Johnson's last illness and death in 1784. Together the two volumes set the standard for modern biography, and writers still study Boswell's method today.
browne-travellers-narrative-1891:
Browne's Traveller's Narrative, published in 1891, translates a Persian history of the Babi movement written to explain the episode of the Bab. The Bab was the young Persian prophet executed in 1850 whose claims split his country. Browne added a long introduction and notes of his own.

The narrative tells of the Bab's preaching, the sieges of his followers, and the faith that grew from the ruins. Browne prints the account as his Persian author gave it, letting an insider's voice carry the story. The book became the foundational Western source on the Bab and the origins of the Baha'i faith.
browne-travellers-narrative-bab-1891:

The narrative, attributed to 'Abdu'l-Baha, recounts the episode of the Bab, the young prophet executed in Persia in 1850. Browne translated the text and wrapped it in his own introduction and notes.

Persecution, prison, and the split of a new faith fill the account, told by a believer close to its center. Western scholars built their picture of Babism on Browne's edition for years. It remains the primary English witness to the events of 1844 to 1850.

Tam rides home drunk from the pub on a stormy night and stops to watch witches dancing in a ruined churchyard. The witches spot him and give chase, and his horse barely escapes across a bridge stream. Burns tells the story with speed, warmth, and mock warning about drink. Many readers rank it as the finest work he ever wrote.
