A status list was basic bookkeeping for officials following the fate of a fallen government.
cia-0000022491: Two American pilots shot down over North Vietnam were killed, a CIA record dated in 1971 reports. The catalog notes that only page one of the item is held. A single page can carry the worst news a family liaison ever passes on. The entry's brevity makes its fact stand bare, with no detail to soften it.
cia-0000022791: Three American military prisoners of war were sighted in Prey Veng Province, Cambodia, a CIA record dated in 1973 reports. Prey Veng lay near the border with South Vietnam, along routes the war had used for years. A sighting in Cambodia widened the search past Vietnam's own camps. The same province drew a follow up report two years later in this file.
cia-0000024491: Four American prisoners of war were sighted in Phuoc Ninh District, in Tay Ninh Province, a CIA record dated in 1972 reports. Tay Ninh, northwest of Saigon, held the great Cao Dai temple and a busy war zone. Four men seen together made a stronger lead than a lone glimpse. The report was checked against the prisoner lists like every other.
cia-0000028491: Cuba and Nicaragua gave support to Central American insurgencies, a CIA paper dated in 1980 reports, tagged Truth Commission in the catalog. Havana and Managua backed the Salvadoran rebels with arms, training, and safe ground, by Washington's account. Proving supply lines was key to the American case for aiding El Salvador's government. The paper maps those lines as analysts then read them.
cia-0000041391:
Pilot Emmet Kay's association with the CIA is the subject of a CIA record dated May 1, 1973. Kay flew in Laos, where American aviation worked in a gray and secret world. Pilots there served the war without the cover of open acknowledgment.

Inside, the file concerns one pilot and his tie to the agency. Such ties mattered when a pilot was lost, captured, or asked about later. The record preserves the paper link between a man and the service he flew for. It is a small file, but it shows how even quiet arrangements left traces in the archive.
cia-0000045191:
Archbishop Rivera y Damas said talks with the rebels were fruitful, in a CIA record dated September 3, 1985. The talks concerned the kidnapping of the president's daughter. Fruitful was a hopeful word in a season of dead ends.

Inside, the archbishop's judgment on the talks is preserved. His optimism gave the negotiations a public blessing. Church backing mattered greatly in that crisis, since the church was trusted in villages where parties and soldiers were not. The file holds that blessing at its giving, in the middle of a crisis that would test every hopeful word spoken about it in the weeks ahead.
cia-0000049091: The Romero murder case is the subject of a CIA item from 1984, kept with the Truth Commission records. Four years after the archbishop's assassination, the case still had no ending anyone accepted. Files like this one tracked the investigation's slow steps and the suspicions that never left it, in San Salvador or abroad.
cia-0000049291: A murder suspect's continued detention in El Salvador is recorded in a CIA item from 1984, kept with the Truth Commission records. Continued detention, noted in the files, meant a case was alive but stuck, its suspect held while proof was hunted. The item is one small marker of a prosecution's slow road.
cia-0000049391: Officers wanting the Jesuit murders solved in El Salvador are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049391, dated July 3, 1990. The item carries a Truth Commission note and records that wish among officers. Readers get a brief dated record whose heading gives an unusual angle on the case, preserved among the agency's Jesuit murder materials.
cia-0000095091: Views of a redacted source that Mexico's economic situation will continue to deteriorate fill declassified CIA document 0000095091, dated September 2, 1976. The source's name is deleted in the heading, misspelled there as well. The brief file records a gloomy forecast for Mexico's economy, kept as reported views rather than an agency estimate.
cia-0000105891: Estimate That Pku Activity Will Culmate with Mass Action Against U.S. is the first numbered heading, with culminate misspelled, on declassified CIA document 0000105891, dated April 5, 1965. The title forecasts that activity under the initials PKU would build toward mass action. The target named in the heading is the United States. The brief record is a forecast item from 1965 Indonesia reporting.
cia-0000107291: Diplomats Comment on Photo of Livng American Mia;s is the heading, with living misspelled and stray marks, on declassified CIA document 0000107291, dated June 6, 1991. The title gives a reaction: diplomats commenting on a photo said to show American MIAs. No diplomat or country is named in the heading. The brief record preserves the misspelling as released.
cia-0000107391: Soviet Dependence on Space Systems is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000107391, dated October 5, 1975. The heading names a reliance: the Soviet Union depending on its space systems. No single satellite or mission is named in the title itself. The brief record is a space systems study item from the mid-seventies Cold War reporting in the files.
cia-0000126891: A November 1970 CIA Weekly Review covers Vietnam and the fallout from Son Tay, part of the heading deleted before release. The Son Tay raid had tried to free American prisoners from a North Vietnamese camp. The review judges what that daring mission changed. The raiders found the camp empty of prisoners, a result that fed argument for years, and fallout papers like this review mark the start of that reckoning.
cia-0000132191: Situation report 508, from January 1991, covers France and the European Community smoothing relations with Israel, the heading breaking off at that name. Keeping Israel out of the fighting was the coalition's central diplomatic task. The report tracks that effort. France held a special place in the diplomacy, with old ties to Baghdad and a strong wish to be seen acting apart from Washington in the crisis.
cia-0000132291: Iraqis remaining defiant is the theme of Situation Report 600 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated January 6, 1991. It covers political developments, though the headline word is cut short in the record title. Reaching number 600 marked how large the daily crisis watch had grown. The short report records Baghdad's public posture as the deadline for Iraq to leave Kuwait drew near.
cia-0000132491: Trade and aid links between Cuba and the bloc fill a CIA paper dated April 4, 1960. Its headline misspells one word as relatios, a slip kept from the original. The paper covers a Soviet trade pact in detail. It also covers work by smaller bloc states and by China, though the title is cut short. Such links were growing tighter month by month. The short paper maps them as analysts saw them that spring.
cia-0000135291: A world peace assembly fills a CIA paper carrying an estimated publication date of May 3, 1983. Its full name was the World Assembly for Peace and Life, Against Nuclear War, though the title breaks off. Gatherings of this kind were a staple of Soviet-backed front work in those years. The short paper covers the assembly and the groups behind it.
cia-0000135891: A instruction dated 3 April 1954 is among the declassified CIA papers on tactical instructions, part two, with an attachment, a twin to the other April part two file. The wider file is PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation aimed at the Arbenz government in Guatemala before the June 1954 coup. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000135991: A CIA cable from 1 February 1954, now declassified, deals with how to put SYNCARP materials into use, working instructions sent from the Lincoln station. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136691: An estimated date of 3 January 1961 heads this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers, with the estimate flagged in the catalog. The brigade was in training for the invasion of Cuba. The record gives the document no subject, and the date itself is a reviewer's placement rather than a certainty. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, one of the brigade's early-January records.
cia-0000136891: Do not risk Venezuelan and Dominican support, headquarters warns LINCOLN in April 1954. Both are of great importance. A partner has some reservations. He was not allowed sufficient time. That is no reason to put their backing at risk. The cable also asks about a to-whom-it-may-concern letter. It matters less whether CALLIGERIS signs it. What matters is the impression it creates on both governments. Both signers should know of it. They should also know SKIMMER's intended use. Frank Wisner signed the message.
cia-0000140391: Hypnotized couriers are feasible in general, these June 1954 comments conclude, but unproven where it matters. The commenter did not invent the idea; the agency has carried out much more complex problems. However, there is no proof whatsoever on key questions, and the entire test has not yet been subjected to actual field conditions such as long travel and time. What happens to a hypnotized individual under third-degree tactics or when plied with chemicals, whether he will disclose hypnotic material, has not been determined. Further testing is the verdict.
cia-03161991: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1957/02/08, a CIA publication. The February briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-03177891: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1960/04/20, a CIA publication. The April briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06186291: O/NE CONSULTANTS' CONFERENCE, PRINCETON, 12-13 MARCH 1959, a CIA document. The 1959 meeting. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
cia-06215991: MODIFICATION FORTY TWO DATED 8 SEPT 2011, a CIA document. The 2011 amendment. The files keep it safe. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
cia-06627791: [SANITIZED] LATIN AMERICA REGIONAL AND POLITICAL ANALYSIS 18 AUGUST 1977, a CIA document. The redacted analysis. This file preserves that declassified paper. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
cia-06708891: IRAQ: REGIONAL RECONSTRUCTION TEAM KURDISH MEDIA SUMMARY 19 MAY 2015, a CIA document. The Kurdish press roundup. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
codrington-the-melanesians-1891:
Robert Henry Codrington gave the study of religion the word mana in The Melanesians, published in 1891 after long Pacific service. Codrington, a missionary-scholar in the Banks Islands and the Solomons, described the unseen power behind magic, luck, and success. Secret societies, ghosts, stones with power, and the spirits of the dead fill his studies in Melanesian life and folklore.

Mana entered the world's vocabulary from these pages and never left it, spreading into every tongue. Codrington wrote from long residence and real command of local languages, correcting travelers' tales as he went with care. His book founded the serious study of Melanesian religion and remains a delight to read today.
cowper-homer-iliad-1791:
Cowper's Iliad, printed in English blank verse in 1791, renders Homer's epic of the Trojan War. The story centers on the rage of Achilles in the last weeks of the long siege of Troy. An edition note shows Cowper revising his own work with care soon after it first appeared.

Readers follow fierce battles, Hector's sad farewell to his family, and the fall of heroes on both sides. Like his Odyssey, this version drops Pope's polished rhymes for a plainer line that tracks the Greek more closely. It was a bold bid against the most famous English Homer of the century, and scholars still weigh it.
cowper-homer-odyssey-1791:
Homer's Odyssey tells of Odysseus, called Ulysses here, and his long trip home after Troy fell. William Cowper turned the Greek epic into English blank verse, and his version came out in 1791. The title page of this edition names him plainly as translator, writing for J. M. Dent and Dutton.

Book one opens with the gods debating the hero's fate while his son Telemachus faces rude suitors at home. Cowper refused the rhyming couplets that Pope had made famous, aiming for a plainer sound closer to the Greek. Monsters, gods, and shipwrecks thus reached common readers in clear and direct English.
doe-osti-3367728-resubmitted-final-repor: SC0018091 got final-resubmitted, and this DOE report covers the resubmission. The pages detail the final findings. The researchers get their data. The report was resubmitted final. The data were researcher. The SC0018091 were report. The final were resubmitted. The researchers were data.
dorian-gray-1891:
Oscar Wilde's sole novel came out in book form in 1891, grown from the magazine text of the year past. He added new parts and a famed preface of sharp, bright lines on art. The book is the form in which most readers have met Dorian Gray since.

Dorian sells his soul, in effect, for youth that does not fade with the years. The portrait in his loft bears the marks of age and sin while he stays fair and young. The tale is the dark crown of the art for art's sake creed of its age.
eddy-retrospection-introspection-1891:
Mary Baker Eddy told her own story in Retrospection and Introspection, published in 1891 when her movement was already famous. The short book traces her path from a sickly New England childhood to the discovery she named Christian Science. She recounts her healing, her break with the healer Quimby, and the founding of her church and college.

Eddy writes to fix the record as she wished it kept, answering rivals in her own calm, firm voice. Readers meet the founder not through followers or foes, but through her chosen account of herself and her work. The memoir remains a first source for the movement's beginnings and for Eddy's mind.
europmc-pmc10277291:
Sun and colleagues review T cells in health and disease in a 2023 paper. T cells are white blood cells that mature in the thymus and form a core arm of the immune system. They develop in steps and split mainly into helper CD4 cells and killer CD8 cells, each with many subtypes tuned to different threats.

The review follows T cells from birth to action at sites of infection and cancer. It explains how their failures lead to immune deficiency, autoimmunity, and weak tumor defense. It also covers therapies that harness or replace them.
europmc-pmc10575791:
McCutcheon, Keefe, and McGuire reviewed thinking problems in schizophrenia in 2023. Such problems are a core part of the illness, not a side note. They drive much of the loss in daily function that patients face. Current drugs for the illness do not fix them.

The review first charts how the deficits look and unfold over time. Genes and life events that raise risk for schizophrenia also track with weaker thinking. McCutcheon then weighs brain paths behind the signs. Dopamine signals, a second signal called acetylcholine, and the balance of two nerve cell types all play a part. The close weighs care today and new drug leads in trials.
europmc-pmc10579091:
Mitchell led a phase 3 trial in 2023, with the MAPP2 Study Collaborator Group, on MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD. PTSD is a lasting stress disorder after trauma. Patients got therapy with MDMA, a drug that alters mood and trust, or therapy with a dummy pill. In all, 104 people with moderate to severe PTSD took part.

Symptom scores fell far more in the MDMA arm. Mitchell reports a mean drop of 23.7 points on the CAPS-5 scale, versus 14.8 with the dummy pill. Daily function scores also improved more with MDMA. Seven people had a severe event tied to care, five of them in the MDMA arm. No deaths or serious events of that kind occurred.
europmc-pmc1073691:
Geissmann and co-authors filmed immune cells on patrol inside mouse livers in 2005. The cells are natural killer T cells, or NKT cells, which sit in the liver's fine blood channels. A glow gene swap let the team watch them live under a microscope. Most of the watched cells carried a receptor called CXCR6.

The cells crawled along the channels at 10 to 20 micrometres per minute. They froze in place when their antigen receptor fired. Mice that lacked CXCR6 held far fewer of these cells in the liver. Geissmann found they also shook off a T-cell-driven hepatitis more easily. The receptor mainly sets cell counts, not their speed or path.
europmc-pmc11140691:
Shattock and a large team model 50 years of global vaccination impact in this 2024 study. The World Health Organization launched the Expanded Programme on Immunization in 1974 to make vaccines available to all. To mark the program's fiftieth year, the team quantified what vaccination has achieved since then. They modelled routine and extra campaigns against 14 pathogens.

Vaccination since 1974 has averted an estimated 154 million deaths, the models say. Of those, 146 million were children under five, and 101 million were infants. Each death averted gained an average of 66 years of full health. That sums to 10.2 billion years of full health gained. Vaccination accounts for 40 percent of the global fall in infant deaths over the period, they estimate. Gains were counted against a scenario with no vaccination at all.
europmc-pmc11309591:
Alduais, Zhang, Fan, Chen, and Chen review non-small cell lung cancer in this 2023 paper. Lung cancer still kills more people than any other cancer worldwide. Non-small cell lung cancer is its most frequent subtype. Care draws on surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and molecularly targeted therapy, chosen per patient.

Many patients who have surgery still develop spread or local recurrence, the authors note. Accurate sub-classification of the tumour, per the latest World Health Organization standards, is critical for tailored treatment. Smoking accounts for 85 to 90 percent of all lung cancer cases, the review states. Second-hand smoke and family history add further risk. Targeted treatments and immunotherapy have improved at a breakneck pace in recent years. The review covers risk factors, diagnosis, and treatment in sequence.
europmc-pmc1177991:
Kasai, Allen, Mason, Kamimura, and Zhang test whether a growth factor can convert lung lining cells into scar-type cells in this 2005 study. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a lethal lung scarring disease. Its hallmark, fibroblastic foci, are aggregates of mesenchymal cells under sites of unresolved epithelial injury. Where those cells originate was unclear.

The team treated A549 cells, a human alveolar epithelial cell line, with TGF-beta1, a potent fibrogenic cytokine. Treated cells changed shape and marker profile: they gained mesenchymal markers including a fibronectin form and lost the epithelial marker E-cadherin. Scar-related markers, such as collagens and connective tissue growth factor, were measured by RNA and protein tests. The shift is called epithelial to mesenchymal transition. The authors also investigated which signalling pathway carries the effect.
europmc-pmc1184591:
Conti and co-authors reported in 2005 that brain stem cells can grow alone. Stem cells in the body were thought to need a special home niche. In dishes they were grown in mixed balls with other cells. Pure stem cell cultures had stayed out of reach.

Two growth factors proved enough to keep pure cultures going. The cells copied themselves in equal pairs over long periods. They came first from mouse embryo stem cells. Conti shows the complex ball setting is not required. Pure cultures let scientists watch and test stem cells directly.
europmc-pmc11868591:
Ogulur and a large team reviewed allergy immunity in 2025. Their focus is type 2 immunity, one arm of the immune system. It guards against parasites and toxins in the body. When it misfires, asthma, hay fever, and eczema can follow.

Food and drug allergies also fall under this response type. Skin and airway linings start the response with alarm signals. Helper cells then drive antibody output and recruit other cells. Ogulur traces each step from first alarm to full reaction. That map points to spots where new drugs can intervene. New biologic drugs that block these pathways already help many patients with severe disease today.
europmc-pmc12124691:
Borba and colleagues ran a trial of chloroquine for severe COVID-19 in 2020. No proven antiviral drug existed for the new disease. Lab work hinted chloroquine could help at high doses. High doses also carry clear risks for patients.

The trial enrolled 81 hospitalized patients in Brazil. One group got a high dose for ten days, the other a low dose. A safety board flagged more toxic effects and deaths in the high-dose group. Heart rhythm changes stood out as a concern. Borba warns that high-dose chloroquine should not be used for severe cases.
europmc-pmc1241091:
Schönfelder and co-authors measured bisphenol A in pregnant women and fetuses in 2002. BPA is a hormone-like chemical in many consumer products. Rodent work suggested it alters developing reproductive organs. No data existed on human fetal exposure at the time.

Blood came from 37 mothers in late pregnancy, plus placenta and cord blood. A new sensitive method found BPA in all three compartments. Median levels were 3.1 nanograms per milliliter in maternal blood. Placenta held far more, at a median of 12.7 nanograms per gram. Male fetuses carried higher blood levels than females.
europmc-pmc1543691:
Loss of species weakens the life-support systems people rely on. Díaz, Fargione, Chapin, and Tilman made that case in 2006, reviewing fresh science and global assessments. Diversity of life drives the ecosystem processes behind clean water, food, and stability in the face of change.

Human acts that feed and clothe us also drive species loss, and the trend looks set to grow. The poor stand to suffer most from the damage. Díaz stresses that nature's variety is not just a store of medicines and fibers. It underpins basic needs like safe water and materials for a decent life.
europmc-pmc1934391:
Scuteri, Abecasis and co-authors ran in 2007 a genome-wide scan for genes behind obesity traits in Sardinia, a genetically isolated island population. Obesity drives diabetes and heart disease, and both environment and inheritance shape it. New mapping tools finally allowed a scan across the whole genome at once.

Variants in two genes stood out: FTO and PFKP. In FTO, one variant showed the strongest ties to body mass index, hip circumference, and weight. Sardinians carrying two copies of its rarer letter were 1.3 BMI units heavier than those with two copies of the common letter. That variant is carried by nearly half the population on one chromosome copy, on average. A PFKP variant also tied strongly to body mass index. The FTO hit became one of the first robust common obesity genes.
europmc-pmc2126691: A medical paper on the pathological changes in the testes in epidemic pneumonia. The diseased testes. This article preserves that pathology. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. Kept for study.
europmc-pmc212691:
Lee, Salic, Krüger, Heinrich and Kirschner built a mathematical model in 2003 of the Wnt signalling pathway. Wnt signals guide development and can drive cancer when overactive. Switching the pathway on stabilises beta-catenin, a protein that turns genes on. The team wrote differential equations for the core proteins and their reactions, using data from frog egg extracts as a reference state.

Model predictions were tested in experiments and used to refine the model further. One confirmed insight concerns the scaffold proteins axin and APC. They promote formation of beta-catenin destruction complexes in very different ways. Axin breakdown helps amplify and sharpen the Wnt signal. Its dependence on APC forms a regulatory loop that stops beta-catenin building up when APC is scarce. Control analysis also revealed the pathway's modular, robust design.
europmc-pmc2128291: A medical paper on experimental syphilis in the rabbit, cutaneous syphilis part two. The skin pox. This article preserves that venereology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2130991: A medical paper with blood sugar studies, changes in fatal bacterial anaphylaxis. The shocked sugar. This article preserves that physiology. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2131491: A medical paper with studies upon the effect of light on blood and tissue cells. The lit cells. This article preserves that photobiology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2131591: A medical paper on relation of varicella to herpes zoster, clinical and experimental observations. The chickenpox-shingles link. This article preserves that virology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140591: A biology paper with studies in the physical chemistry of the proteins. The protein physics. This article preserves that biochemistry. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2140691: A biology paper on photochemistry of visual purple, the relation between light intensity. The eye's chemistry. This article preserves that photobiology. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2140891: A biology paper on the geotropic conduct of young rats. The gravity-wise pups. This article preserves that animal behavior. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It retains its place in time. The text survives intact.
europmc-pmc2151091:
Kettler and a large team compared twelve genomes in 2007 of Prochlorococcus, a tiny marine cyanobacterium. It is the smallest known oxygen-making photosynthetic organism and dominates mid-latitude oceans. Strains split into high-light and low-light adapted groups. Earlier genomes numbered only four. Adding eight new ones let the team define the shared core genome and the flexible genes that come and go during evolution.

All twelve strains share 1,273 core genes, enough by reconstruction to run a living cell. Much variation sits between the most closely related strains, at the tree's leaves. Differences cluster in genes for outer membrane building and nutrient transport. Highly changeable genomic islands emerged from the gain-and-loss analysis. Some genes clearly mark the high-light and low-light lifestyles. Core and flexible gene frequencies matched patterns in global ocean survey data.
europmc-pmc2222591:
Suri, Fenniri and Singh reviewed nanotechnology-based drug delivery systems in 2007. Nanoparticles, particles under 100 nanometres in at least one dimension, can carry drugs inside their core or on their surface. Cells take them up more efficiently than larger molecules. The review covers recent systems for drug and gene delivery, and what governs targeting, release and stability inside the body.

Several cancer drugs, including paclitaxel, doxorubicin and 5-fluorouracil, have been formulated successfully in nanomaterials. Quantum dots, chitosan and biodegradable PLGA particles have delivered RNA interference in lab studies. Doxorubicin bound to nanomaterials crossed the intact blood-brain barrier and reached therapeutic levels in brain, a major hurdle in brain cancer. Peptide nanotubes targeting vessel growth receptors offer another route to control disease progression.
europmc-pmc2254191:
Hayashi and co-workers studied in 2008 whether microRNAs are required for mouse germ cell development. Germ cells also make another small RNA type, piRNAs, known to silence jumping genes during sperm production. MicroRNA function there was unclear. The team profiled 220 microRNAs across germ cell development, then deleted the microRNA-making enzyme Dicer only in germ cells of mice, and separately removed Argonaute2.

Two microRNA clusters tied to cell cycling were highly expressed in primordial germ cells and spermatogonia, the early sperm precursors. Without Dicer those cells proliferated poorly, and sperm production stalled early. Jumping-gene activity was unexpectedly suppressed in early germ cells, not raised. The model was a conditional knockout studied by the team. Argonaute2-deficient testes made sperm normally. Dicer's key role in spermatogenesis is therefore independent of Argonaute2.
europmc-pmc2335091:
Shaftel, Griffin, and O'Banion re-examined interleukin-1 in brain disease in 2008. Interleukin-1 is a signal protein that promotes inflammation. It rises in the brain after injury and in long-term diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, the most common cause of dementia.

For two decades, most work cast this rise as harmful, driving damage and drawing white blood cells into the brain. The authors summed up newer animal studies that challenge that view. In Alzheimer models, some effects of interleukin-1 looked helpful, not harmful. They argued the protein may support repair as well as worsen injury, depending on context. Boosting its helpful side, they suggested, might ease the disease burden rather than blocking the signal outright.
europmc-pmc2373291:
Qin and colleagues showed in 2008 that alcohol primes the brain and body for stronger inflammation. They worked with a bacterial toxin called endotoxin, or LPS, which triggers immune alarm signals named cytokines. Mice got alcohol by stomach tube for one day or ten days, then the toxin a day after the last dose.

The toxin alone raised alarm cytokines such as TNF-alpha in liver, blood, and brain within an hour. Ten days of alcohol changed the picture: toxin responses grew larger in all three places and lasted far longer in the brain. Liver and blood signals settled within a day, while brain signals stayed up. The alcohol-plus-toxin group also showed activated brain immune cells, fewer new brain cells, and more oxidative stress enzymes. A calming cytokine, IL-10, fell in brain but rose in liver.
europmc-pmc2374791:
Atkins and colleagues shared lessons from a meta-ethnography of tuberculosis research in 2008. Meta-ethnography is a method for merging findings from many interview-based studies into one bigger interpretation. The team used it on studies of why patients stick with, or stop, tuberculosis treatment, a course lasting many months.

Working through the method's seven stages, they hit problems the guides leave vague. Shaping a tight question, finding the right studies, and judging study quality all took extra steps they had to invent. Merging findings was hardest, since the primary studies came from many countries and research traditions. Still, they judged the method useful for building models that explain results across studies. Their paper offers practical fixes for future teams, and calls for more research on the method itself.
europmc-pmc2551591:
Francke, Smit, de Veer, and Mistiaen reviewed in 2008 what helps or hinders putting clinical guidelines into practice. Guidelines for health professionals multiply, yet writing one does not guarantee anyone follows it. The authors gathered existing systematic reviews on the subject, screened them in two steps, and rated their quality.

Twelve reviews qualified, and only two scored high for quality; the rest carried major flaws. Across them, multi-part strategies worked better than any single tactic such as reminders alone. Guidelines that were easy to understand, easy to try, and cheap in resources stood a better chance of use. Clinician awareness, patient factors such as having several illnesses, and workplace support also mattered, with lack of staff and time the main barriers.
europmc-pmc2583991:
Gu, Zhang, and Lupski reviewed in 2008 the mechanisms that produce large rearrangements of human DNA. Such changes, from a few hundred DNA letters to millions, cause a family of conditions called genomic disorders and also appear in cancers. The authors organise the evidence around three mechanisms that explain most events.

The first, non-allelic homologous recombination, misaligns repeated DNA stretches and produces the common, recurring rearrangements of shared size. The second, non-homologous end-joining, glues broken DNA ends back together imperfectly. The third, called FoSTeS, involves a stalled copying fork switching templates mid-replication. Which mechanism dominates at a given spot depends partly on the local genome layout. That is the arrangement of repeats nearby. The review covers events in both inherited cells and body cells.
europmc-pmc2607291:
Ponomarenko and colleagues built a web tool called ElliPro in 2008 for predicting antibody epitopes, the patches on a protein that antibodies grab. Knowing epitopes helps design vaccines and diagnostic tests, but predicting them reliably is hard. The tool implements Thornton's method, which looks for regions protruding from a protein's surface, since accessible, flexible, sticking-out areas tend to be antigenic.

ElliPro combines that geometry with residue clustering and the MODELLER program. A 3D viewer lets users see predictions on the structure. The team benchmarked it on discontinuous epitopes taken from known antibody-protein complexes. ElliPro beat six rival structure-based methods. It reached an accuracy score of 0.732 by the AUC measure. Its best prediction ranked in the top three for over 70 percent of proteins tested.
europmc-pmc2648991:
Rücker and colleagues warned in 2008 that a popular statistic can mislead people who combine study results. When researchers merge trials in a meta-analysis, they check how much the trials disagree, a problem called heterogeneity. Many report a measure called I-squared, read as the share of variation due to real differences between studies.

The team showed that this measure depends on study size in a hidden way. Using a real meta-analysis, they reran the numbers as if each trial had been much bigger. The actual spread of effects did not change, yet the I-squared value shot toward 100 percent. The same pattern showed in 157 published meta-analyses. Bigger studies inflate the score even when nothing else changes. europmc-pmc2689691:
Wilkinson and colleagues invented in 2008 a high-throughput way to read the folded shape of the HIV genome, which is made of RNA, not DNA. The method, SHAPE, probes how flexible the RNA backbone is at every single letter. Flexible spots are unpaired; stiff spots are locked in structure. The team read the genome in four states, including inside real virus particles.

Given countless shapes the RNA could take, the first tenth of the genome held one dominant form in all four states, a striking constancy. Control regions carried more structure than protein-coding stretches, which stay loose for the cell's protein factories. The method also caught the virus's nucleocapsid protein at work inside particles. Seven matching grip sites marked where it helps package the genome, and two other motifs marked where it loosens structure so copying and protein making can begin.
europmc-pmc2715191:
Aitken and Roman reviewed in 2008 how the testes guard sperm making against oxidative stress, damage from reactive oxygen forms. Making sperm is a fast, dividing process that uses much oxygen, yet the testes have poor blood flow and low oxygen by design. That low oxygen may itself shield the tissue, since both sperm making and hormone making are easily harmed.

Their review details layers of antioxidant enzymes and scavengers, chemicals that mop up reactive forms before they damage fats, proteins, and DNA. It also covers what weakens those defenses, from testicular twisting to diabetes and chemical exposure. Such damage is now seen as a leading cause of poor testicular function.
europmc-pmc2796391:
Grundmann and colleagues, with the European Staphylococcal Reference Laboratory Working Group, mapped invasive Staphylococcus aureus strains across Europe in 2010. This germ is a leading cause of severe infection, and drug-resistant forms known as MRSA worry hospitals across the continent.

Laboratories typed samples with a shared method based on one variable gene region, then pooled the results into the first Europe-wide snapshot taken at one time. The project also built a public web tool that plots each strain type on an interactive map. Comparing drug-resistant and drug-sensitive strains side by side shows where each clone rules, which helps clinics prepare for the strains most likely to arrive.
europmc-pmc2814091:
Bork and colleagues tracked chemical tags on DNA in human mesenchymal stromal cells as the cells aged in a dish in 2010. These stromal cells are repair precursors that enlarge, lose their range, and stop dividing after two to three months of growth. The team read tags at more than twenty-seven thousand sites and also compared cells from young and older donors.

Overall tag patterns held steady, but clear shifts appeared at set sites, many in homeobox genes that steer body development and cell fate. Tag changes from long culture overlapped strongly with changes seen in aging itself. That overlap supports the idea that dish aging and body aging follow shared, tag-driven programs.
europmc-pmc2820091:
Naumann and colleagues showed in 2010 that a puzzling receptor called CXCR7 works as a scavenger, quietly clearing two signaling molecules from their surroundings. The signals, CXCL12 and CXCL11, are chemokines that guide cell movement. CXCR7 binds both tightly yet triggers none of the usual chemokine responses, which left its job in doubt.

The team found that CXCR7 constantly loops between the cell surface and inner compartments, dragging captured chemokines inside for destruction. The cleanup never saturated, even as signal levels climbed. Real scavenging was caught in action in adult mouse heart valves and in human vein lining cells. By draining CXCL12, the receptor can fine-tune its famous partner receptor CXCR4 during development and tumor growth.
europmc-pmc2928191:
Sarin revisited in 2010 the classic theories of how fluid and proteins cross capillary walls, the exchange that feeds every tissue. One classic theory allows a single population of tiny pores around six nanometers wide. A rival dual-pore theory adds rare large leaks tens of nanometers across, inferred from how big proteins appear in lymph. The two were built from different experimental traditions and never fully reconciled.

Sarin reviews the size evidence capillary type by capillary type. The types run from continuous walls in muscle to fenestrated walls in glands. They end at open sinusoids in liver and spleen. For each type he sets a physiologic upper pore limit. Much of the supposed large-pore traffic, the analysis suggests, fits within the true ceilings of the leakier capillary types without invoking a universal second pore system.
europmc-pmc2936891:
Winkler, Bell, and Zlokovic mapped where a key growth factor receptor sits in the adult mouse brain in a 2010 study. Pericytes, small cells hugging brain capillaries, help build the blood-brain barrier, and signals from a vessel protein guide them there during development.

Using paired fluorescent labelling and a proximity test, they mapped the receptor PDGFR-beta. The test lights up only when two molecules touch. The receptor sat only on pericytes, not on neurons, support cells, or vessel lining cells. They also checked mice carrying weakened receptor variants. The precise map sharpens models for studying barrier breakdown in adults.
europmc-pmc3026691:
Sinha, Smyth, and Williamson reviewed in 2011 how research teams use group voting to agree on which outcomes every trial in a field should measure. Agreeing on such core outcome sets stops trialists from picking only results that favor them, and it lets later reviews combine studies cleanly. The method studied is the Delphi technique, which polls experts in rounds.

The team found fifteen studies that used Delphi for this purpose and judged how each was run and reported. Methods varied widely, and reporting was often thin. Their advice is direct: include patients as well as clinicians, keep facilitators from steering answers, and work to keep participants from dropping out. Clear reporting of each choice would let readers judge the sets for themselves.
europmc-pmc3049591:
Proctor and the Glasgow group tested in 2011 whether a simple inflammation score from routine blood tests predicts cancer survival across all tumor types. The score combines two blood measures, one that rises with inflammation and one that falls. The team followed more than twenty thousand patients whose blood was sampled around the time of a cancer diagnosis, and compared the score against liver tests and other blood markers.

A higher score predicted shorter overall and cancer specific survival at five years, whatever the tumor site and after accounting for age, sex, and deprivation. Several liver related measures also carried warning value, but the inflammation score stood out as consistently powerful. Because the tests are cheap and already routine, the score offers doctors a quick extra gauge of outlook. It may also help sort patients fairly in treatment trials.
europmc-pmc3084991:
Bruix and Sherman summarized in 2011 the updated practice guidelines for liver cell cancer from the American liver disease association, replacing the 2005 version. New evidence had accumulated on who to watch, how to diagnose, and how to stage and treat this cancer, which usually grows on a scarred liver. The summary highlights only what changed.

Blood marker testing was dropped from surveillance because it misses too much and cries wolf too often, leaving ultrasound every six months as the standard. Diagnosis now rests on one good dynamic scan showing the classic pattern of bright uptake then washout, for the right patients. A common contrast ultrasound method was removed after false alarms in a related bile duct cancer. Biopsy reading was strengthened with a three stain panel. Risk thresholds for starting surveillance were refined for hepatitis B and C. The full guideline lives on the association website.
europmc-pmc3219291:
Simon Finfer and colleagues surveyed resuscitation fluid use across three hundred ninety-one intensive care units in twenty-five countries, in this 2010 study in Critical Care. Which fluid doctors choose for a crashing patient, salt-based crystalloid or protein-like colloid, was under debate because the choice might affect survival. The study captured practice during a single day.

More than a third of the patients received resuscitation fluid, most often for poor circulation or abnormal vital signs. Colloids were given to more patients and in more episodes than crystalloids, despite costing more. After adjustment, the country a patient was treated in strongly predicted which fluid was used, while illness severity did not. Practice, the authors note, follows local habit more than patient need.
europmc-pmc3313891:
Guyot, Ades, Ouwens, and Welton presented a method in 2012 for recovering patient level survival data from published trial charts. Trials of time until an event, such as death, usually publish only summary figures and a survival curve. Those summaries are not enough for combining trials or judging whether a treatment is worth its cost, which blocks deeper follow up analysis.

Their algorithm works backward from a digitized survival curve, using reported numbers of events and patients still at risk, to rebuild data very close to the original. Several observers repeating the process got nearly identical results, with survival figures and median times matching closely. The authors recommend that trials always publish counts at risk and total events beside their curves, so others can reuse the data.
europmc-pmc3320591:
Kleemann and colleagues showed how a crop fungus delivers its attack proteins in carefully timed waves, in a 2012 study. The fungus infects the model plant arabidopsis in two acts, first feeding on living tissue and later killing it. It secretes effector proteins that manipulate the plant, and the team read which genes switch on at each stage of infection.

Deep sequencing showed most effector genes turn on only after contact with the host, arriving in consecutive waves tied to each stage. Glowing tagged proteins gathered in stage specific compartments where fungus meets plant. Some effectors were sprayed from the tiny pore of the entry structure before the fungus even broke in. In tests, different effectors pushed plant cells toward survival or death, matching the fungus's two feeding acts.
europmc-pmc3353191:
To and collaborators estimated how common asthma is among adults worldwide, using the World Health Organization's World Health Survey. Earlier global figures had stitched together studies with different methods; this survey asked the same questions in the same way across many countries at once.

Responses came from 178,215 adults aged 18 to 45 in seventy countries. Global rates were roughly four to five percent for doctor-diagnosed or treated asthma, and about nine percent for recent wheezing. Yet prevalence varied more than twentyfold between countries, with Australia highest. Many treated patients still smoked, and a fifth had never received treatment, gaps the authors highlight for policy.
europmc-pmc3372091:
Vauzour reviewed the brain effects of dietary polyphenols in 2012, the plant compounds found in tea, cocoa, and berries. Such foods have been linked with better memory and slower age-related decline. The older view credited simple antioxidant action for most of the benefit.

The review argues the compounds work mainly by tuning cell signals and switching on protective genes. Named routes include pathways tied to sirtuins, NF-kappaB, and Nrf-2, which raise defense enzymes and growth factors for neurons. Trials with tea, ginkgo, cocoa, and blueberry showed gains in learning in animals and people. Framing polyphenols as signal changers reshapes how brain-protective diets are studied.
europmc-pmc3466591:
Zhang and co-authors reported in eLife in 2012 that a hormone released during fasting can lengthen the lives of mice. The hormone, called FGF21, is made by the liver when food runs short. It helps the body burn fat, sharpens insulin action, and slows growth. The team bred mice that made extra FGF21 throughout life.

Those mice lived markedly longer than normal mice, even though they ate just as much. Gene activity data pointed to a quieter growth hormone pathway in the liver as the main route. Zhang's group notes the hormone did not act through the usual nutrient-sensing paths tied to aging. The result raises the chance that FGF21-based drugs could slow aging in other species.
europmc-pmc3468891:
Cooper and colleagues compared ways to clean up motion errors in a brain imaging method, in a 2012 Frontiers in Neuroscience paper. The method, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, shines light through the scalp to track blood flow in the brain. When a subject moves, the fibers shift and the signal jumps, often swamping the real brain response.

The team added a known fake signal to twenty real recordings full of motion errors, then tested four cleaning methods against simply dropping bad trials. All four methods recovered the signal far better than dropping trials. Spline interpolation cut the error the most, while wavelet analysis gave the cleanest contrast. Cooper's group recommends routine cleaning, naming those two methods as the best choices.
europmc-pmc3482391:
Zhang and co-authors cataloged the toxin systems bacteria use against each other, in Biology Direct in 2012. Many bacteria carry polymorphic toxin systems: delivery gear paired with a swappable toxin tip and a matching shield protein that protects the owner. Using genome comparisons across bacteria, the team traced how these weapons travel, fire, and vary.

They found the systems in all major bacterial groups, shipped by at least eight kinds of delivery machinery. The toxin tips spanned more than one hundred fifty kinds, from DNA cutters to pore formers, and shields numbered over ninety families. Some bacteria stack many shields in a row, guarding against whole arsenals. Zhang's survey also predicts new parts and roles, including effects on cooperation and cheating in microbial communities.

french-constitution-1791:
France adopted its first written constitution in September 1791, the work of the National Constituent Assembly. The Revolution had begun in hope two years before, and the Assembly tried to settle it into ordered liberty. The result was a constitutional monarchy: a king kept on his throne, ruling beside an elected Legislative Assembly.

The charter divides power, promises equality before the law, and guards property and speech, while limiting the vote to men who paid set taxes. The king accepted it under pressure after his failed flight to Varennes. War and radical anger swept the settlement away within a year, and the monarchy fell in 1792. The constitution remains the charter of the Revolution's hopeful phase, liberty under law before the Terror. It also records what the men of 1789 thought a free state should be.
frus-1861-d191:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Cassius Clay on 6 May 1861. Clay was the new American minister to Russia, bound for St. Petersburg. The letter is document 191 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Clay was a Kentucky emancipationist with a fighter's fame. Russia, under a young czar who had just freed the serfs, watched America with rare warmth. Seward's May letter sent Clay to the one great court that leaned toward the Union. Clay's fame as a duelist and emancipationist made him a marked man at any court. A marked man at court drew eyes, which Clay turned to the Union's gain.
frus-1861-d291:
Word from Mr. Harvey reached Washington on 28 July 1861, in a letter to William H. Seward. It stands as Document 291 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d91:
On 22 October 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in his firm autumn tone. The letter is document 91 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late October letters from Seward carry the feel of a man who has found his wartime stride. The orders are brief, the tone is firm, the goals are clear. This note to London shows the Secretary in full command of his far flung front. The orders assume Adams's full grasp, a trust the Secretary rarely gave so freely. Full command in the chief bred full effort in the man who served him.
frus-1862-d191:
Document 191 is the second Seward dispatch to Charles Francis Adams dated 18 November 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams served as American minister in London, the post his father and grandfather had also held in earlier years.

Paired letters on one date often mean one carried the Secretary's orders while the other passed papers or news. The Adams legation answered in kind, and the printed file grows thick. For readers tracing how the Union kept Britain at arm's length in late 1862, the paired dispatches of November are core evidence. British backing for the South would have brought Richmond credit, ships, and fresh hope at once.
frus-1862-d291:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 23 June 1862 in a letter printed as Document 291 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Dayton wrote two days before the Seven Days battles began, in the last quiet of the Richmond campaign. French observers expected the capital's fall to settle the war's foreign side. His report belongs to that expectant week, and its value lies partly in its timing. It preserves what Paris believed just before events proved it wrong. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d391:
Document 391 is the second Seward dispatch to Simon Cameron dated 6 September 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent both letters to St. Petersburg together.

Same-day pairs on the Russian route mattered because sailings were rare; a missed mail could cost a month. Clerks therefore batched the post's business carefully. This second letter completes the September brief for St. Petersburg, and the pair together shows Washington briefing its Russian envoy on the invasion crisis as it began. Letters to Russia favored broad lines of policy over fast-changing battle news. The czar's government had freed its own serfs in 1861 and watched America's struggle closely.
frus-1862-d491:
On 2 April 1862 James Shepherd Pike sent this report from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 491 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Pike wrote days before the battle of Shiloh, in a lull when European opinion was weighing the war's cost against its likely end. The Dutch, careful neutrals with worldwide trade, wanted the fighting stopped but would not move first. His report measured that mood for Washington. Ministers' letters in this season also carried the small change of diplomacy: visits, dinners, and remarks that hinted at policy. Pike's blunt style makes his contributions to the volume unusually readable.
frus-1862-d591:
Dated 2 June 1862, this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Thomas Corwin was printed after the order of 7 June in the volume's Mexican file. It is Document 591 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The two June instructions, read together by date, show Seward handling the Mexican question in successive layers as reports from Corwin arrived. France's advance in Mexico posed the Union a problem it could not solve by force that year. So it solved it by record. The record held clear protests, kept promises of sympathy, and a paper trail for the future. Corwin's post was where that trail was laid. The letter is a working part of the longest-range policy in the whole volume.
frus-1862-d691: On 3 April 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to a Mr. De Long. The letter is document 691 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, answering the run of dispatches De Long had sent that winter. The evidence names both men and the date, but it does not state De Long's post or the letter's topic.
frus-1862-d91:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 5 July 1862. It stands as Document 91 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d191:
Writing from London on 7 May 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 191 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

After the Emancipation Proclamation took effect on New Year's Day 1863, the war stood openly as a fight over slavery. That change made British support for the South harder to defend in public. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d291:
Washington's orders to London on 17 September 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 291 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Instructions like this one show how the Lincoln government ran a war abroad while fighting one at home. The paper trail is the diplomacy itself, order by order. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d391:
In Washington on 16 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 391 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons was the man Seward had to persuade, warn, or answer in person in Washington. Notes to him carried the American side of each dispute between the two governments. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d491:
The date 5 May 1863 heads a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d591:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 18 July 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d691:
Edwin M. Stanton, the Secretary of War, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 October 1863. The note is document 691 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863. Unlike most letters in this run, it comes from inside the Lincoln cabinet itself.

War and foreign affairs often met. Army and navy acts at sea or on the border could stir trouble with Britain at any time. Stanton's note brought the War Department's facts or views to the man who had to answer for them abroad. The reader sees the home side of diplomacy here. Before Seward spoke to foreign envoys, he needed word from his own team.
frus-1863p1-d91:
William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 25 February 1863, the second day in a row he wrote to London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 91 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Day-after-day letters from the secretary often chased a point that would not wait for the next steamer. For London, the points were steady ones: fair dealing from Britain, and a stop to warships for the South. This letter keeps that press on. It is a mid-run sheet, plain in form, whose weight comes from the chain of orders it belongs to.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d191:
Acting Secretary of State Edward Stettinius wrote to Wallace Murray, the State Department's adviser on political relations, on 5 November 1943. The short secret note passes on items from that day's meeting with President Roosevelt, some for Murray's information and some needing action.

Roosevelt admits he does not grasp the Middle East oil problem and asks for a two-page brief on it at once. He floats a trusteeship for the region shared by Russia, Britain, and America. He also wants a four-power commission for French West Africa, and he sounds annoyed with de Gaulle. A final item, on Turkey, is marked secret and passed on only in conversation, so its content stays off the page.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d291:
John Martin, Prime Minister Churchill's private secretary, sent a short secret covering note to Harry Hopkins at Cairo on 23 November 1943, enclosing a British telegram from Jedda dated 15 November. Churchill, writing as Colonel Warden, had asked Martin to show Hopkins the telegram and have it returned.

The enclosure reports King Ibn Saud's complaint from Mecca. An American representative in Jedda had put seven pointed questions to him about Saudi arms requests to Britain: what was asked, what was promised, and what had arrived. The king answered that fifty light reconnaissance cars were promised and none had come. The British minister calls the questions unfortunate, since they suggest distrust between the allies, and urges a quick joint agreement on arms for Saudi Arabia.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d391:
Three unrelated reports for the President at Tehran were gathered into a secret telegram Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt from Washington on 29 November 1943. It is a typical Hull digest, moving from China to Portugal in a few lines.

Chungking reports news from a Chinese source who had lately seen Japanese and puppet officials at Nanking. Japan keeps making unsuccessful peace offers to Chiang's government. Former foreign minister Matsuoka left Japan on 7 October. His errand was to try to arrange peace between Germany and the Soviet Union. A consul at Kweilin reports Changteh in flames and Changsha expected to fall with only token defense. Finally, Salazar's speech of 26 November stressed British and American assurances of Portuguese sovereignty over the Azores, and Portuguese press accounts set that American part in italics.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d491:
Madame Chiang Kai-shek wrote to President Roosevelt on December 5, 1943. She had stood beside her husband, Generalissimo Chiang, at the first Cairo Conference in November, serving as his voice in English, and China had won public pledges in the Cairo Declaration. The State Department printed her letter in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Few figures moved between the Chinese and American leadership as Madame Chiang did; she had addressed the United States Congress earlier in 1943. A letter from her to Roosevelt carried the weight of the China theater and of her own standing in Washington. It shows the personal diplomacy that held the Chinese alliance together.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d91: Roosevelt replied to Ambassador Winant in London on November 2, 1943, the same day Winant's dispatch in this series was written. The answer is Document 91 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. President-to-ambassador letters in wartime often carried guidance too sensitive for wider files. The record names the parties and the date only. The reply rests in the Foreign Relations volume with the other papers of that full day.
frus-1944-quebec-d191:
Mackenzie King's notes, reprinted by the editors, preserve his conversation with Roosevelt just before dinner at Quebec. King raised Canada's part in the Pacific war. Canada was prepared to fight Japan, he said, but in the northern or central regions. Roosevelt answered that a token representation should suffice, and that nothing might be needed for some time.

The president hinted Canadian men might be useful driving the Japanese from northern China toward the war's end. He also said Canada should have a token force to march into Berlin. On Russia, King asked directly what part Stalin would play against Japan. Roosevelt repeated what had been said earlier and added that Stalin had given his word himself.
frus-1944-quebec-d291:
An editors' note bridges Quebec and the Hyde Park meetings of September 17 to 19, 1944. Roosevelt reached home on the morning of September 17. Churchill arrived a day later with his wife, daughter Mary, and a party including Leathers, Ismay, and Moran, leaving on the night of September 19 for the Queen Mary and England. Guests included the Duke of Windsor at lunch and Morgenthau at dinner.

Because Churchill was a guest in Roosevelt's home, their conversations were informal and unminuted, as was the president's custom. Leahy's account lists the substance. There were political questions on Italy, Yugoslavia, and Russia. There was signature of the Octagon report, and drafting of a statement on Italy. Finally came a discussion of atomic energy, military and industrial, which produced an initialed aide-mémoire.
frus-1944-quebec-d91:
Treasury staff prepared a briefing book dated September 9, 1944. Briefing books gather facts and positions for busy leaders. The State Department printed this one in the Quebec 1944 volume. It appeared three days before the conference opened.

A briefing book aims to give one reader everything needed. Treasury officials packed figures and arguments into a single volume. Money questions awaited the leaders at Quebec that month. They included aid to Britain and Germany's economic future. For readers, the book shows how departments arm their chiefs. Pages of staff work stood behind each short summit discussion.
frus-1945-50-intel-d191:
The memorandum of 28 March 1947 is the work of the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence (Wright). In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 191, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d291:
On 17 June 1948, staff wrote up the discussion at the 13th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. Readers meet it as document 291 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time.

A memorandum of conversation is the note a participant or aide wrote after a talk, setting down who was there and what was said. For a reader, the gain is scene and voice, rare goods in a file of stiff forms. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d391:
A letter dated 29 July 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 391 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Reform talk filled the files that year, as the government weighed the Dulles team's harsh grades for the CIA.

A formal letter was a step above a memo: it put a request or a stance on record under the writer's signature. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d91:
Minutes of the eighth meeting of the Advisory Committee on Intelligence are dated 3 December 1946. The committee advised the State Department on its intelligence work. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A committee still meeting in December 1946 shows the State Department's intelligence function settling into a lasting, smaller form. The eighth meeting's minutes record routine where the autumn of 1945 had recorded upheaval. Readers can measure the change across the volume: from frantic memos about survival to numbered meetings about business. That settling is itself a result worth noting, the sound of a new order becoming normal inside an old department.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d191:
Hold everything on Italy, Stettinius cabled from Caserta on 30 January 1945. His top secret message to Acting Secretary Grew, sent from Allied Force Headquarters in Italy, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It concerns a joint statement he had not yet seen.

The Combined Civil Affairs Committee has prepared a proposed joint statement on Italy. Stettinius hopes Grew will hold up any action on it. He has not seen the text, but the feeling at headquarters is that issuing it in its present form would be most unfortunate. He asks Grew to cable the full text and its status. The message runs through a channel marked for the acting secretary's eyes alone at the far end.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d291:
The American chiefs met at Malta on 30 January 1945 and set their house in order first. These Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, open the staff conference that preceded the leaders' talks at Yalta. General Marshall leads the recorded business.

First comes the agenda paper for the combined talks, C. C. S. 765/8, which the chiefs agree to recommend for approval. Marshall points out its additions, among them the combined bomber offensive and planning dates for the end of both wars. Next, an overall review of cargo shipping wins approval of the Joint Staff Planners' recommendations. The third item turns to the fighting itself: strategy in northwest Europe, placed on the table for examination and discussion with the British.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d391:
General John Deane, head of the American Military Mission in Moscow, wrote the questions for the first staff meeting with the Soviets. His memorandum of February 7, 1945, lists what to ask. Had Soviet plans for operations in the Far East changed since October? Would the Soviets need a Pacific supply route once war with Japan began?

More questions follow. Would Moscow agree to American air forces operating from the Komsomolsk-Nikolaevsk area? Each question carried a negotiation inside it. Deane, who dealt with the Soviet staff daily, framed the asks that the chiefs carried into the secret February 8 meeting.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d491: Justice Byrnes would beat the communiqué home, and Stephen Early planned for it in this telegram to Jonathan Daniels of February 10, 1945. Byrnes should reach Washington early the next week, and the press would surely want a conference with him. Early and Byrnes had talked, and Byrnes understood the position. Early suggested Daniels and Walter Brown arrange it if the press wished. One condition held firm: the final communiqué must appear before Byrnes said anything. The wire shows the administration scripting a key homecoming.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d91:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson put his views on the peace machinery in writing on 23 January 1945. His memorandum to the Secretary of State is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It lists the points he had tried to make at their meeting the day before.

Stimson recalls that the Moscow Conference of 1943 had in view two bodies. One was a general body open to all peace-loving states, large and small. The other was a stopgap body of the four large powers, to guard security while order was restored. The powers that won the war, he argues, must keep the world safe until a lasting system stands. Their stopgap body should be formal, and hard at work.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d191:
Stalin agreed to take up the Trieste question at the summit in a message to President Truman dated July 6, 1945. The short note, printed in translation, is document 191 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It answers Truman's message of June 25 about Trieste, Istria, and Yugoslavia.

The matter has a number of questions demanding their mutual consideration, Stalin writes. He is prepared to discuss them at their meeting in Germany. The message reached Truman at sea, relayed by the White House Map Room on July 7, and Stalin sent Churchill a similar note the same day. Behind the calm wording stood a live dispute: Yugoslav forces held Trieste, the Western Allies had just forced a partial pullback, and the city's future was unsettled.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d291:
Acting Secretary Grew gave London the tentative American answer on the satellite treaties in a telegram dated June 23, 1945. The message to Ambassador Winant is document 291 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It responds to the British proposal to move straight to peace treaties with Hungary, Romania, and Bulgaria.

Washington fully agrees peace should come as soon as possible, Grew writes. But treaty talks, with their hard territorial questions, cannot finish quickly, and meanwhile the United States will not drop its demands for real participation in the control commissions. Nor is it convinced that peace with the present governments, above all in Romania and Bulgaria, would best serve democratic principles, even if it sped the Soviet troops' withdrawal. The plan: keep peace as the goal, demand a real voice now, and press the Yalta principles on governments and elections.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d391:
Destruction of the German battle fleet is urged in a Joint Chiefs of Staff memorandum to President Truman dated July 10, 1945. American policy, the chiefs recommend, should be that all German naval vessels be destroyed, sunk on the high seas or scrapped. Only a limited number would be kept for experiments and tests, plus auxiliaries still of use.

If the European Advisory Commission nations could not agree, Washington should still press for the destruction of all capital ships and submarines: battleships, pocket battleships, and cruisers named among them. Smaller craft would be divided. The memo, signed by General Marshall, shows the military mind set on ending German sea power outright.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d491:
General Anders and his Polish troops in Italy are the concern of Kirk's cable from Caserta of June 28, 1945. Broad, a British officer, had shown Kirk a Foreign Office telegram just received. It instructed Broad, if the supreme commander saw no objection, to proceed to the Polish general headquarters in Italy. There he was to explain to General Anders, in as favorable a manner as possible, why Poles abroad should welcome the formation of the new Polish government.

Broad was authorized to give Anders the story of the Moscow negotiations, much as Washington's circulars had outlined it. He was also to point out the obvious advantages accruing to Poland from the constitution of the new government. The cable shows London managing its Polish soldiers' reaction to the Warsaw settlement.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d591:
Top secret minutes record a meeting of the Committee of Three in Washington on June 26, 1945. They form document 591 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Present were Stimson of War, Forrestal of the Navy, and Grew, the acting head of State.

The three took up a proposed warning to Japan. Stimson read a draft memo he had written for the President, and the group weighed its effect at home and abroad. All agreed the tone was about right. Even if Japan did not yield, they felt, a clear warning could do no harm. It might firm U.S. resolve for an all-out fight if Japan held out. A joint subcommittee was tasked to draft the warning itself, with named men from each of the three departments.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d691:
Ambassador Wilson reported Turkey's minister's reply to Washington's cautious line on June 26, 1945. His urgent wire from Ankara is document 691 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Wilson had conveyed the final paragraph of the Department's June 23 instruction that morning.

The acting foreign minister thanked the U.S. for its interest and promised to keep Wilson fully informed. Turkey, he said, could hardly be expected to respect a Soviet view claiming Turkish land and bases. He pressed Wilson for Washington's reaction to Britain's proposed approach to Moscow. Told the U.S. view, he said he understood it, but hoped for more at the summit. At the Big Three meeting, he urged, the U.S. should back equal sovereignty and independence for all states. He added that Soviet units were leaving Poland and Hungary for Bulgaria, movements that looked like threats.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d91:
Major General Crawford reported General Parks's findings from Berlin to General Deane on June 23, 1945. The urgent telegram from SHAEF headquarters in Frankfurt is document 91 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. Parks had flown in the day before to inspect the ground the Soviets had picked for the conference.

The report is encouraging. The Crown Prince's palace at Potsdam suits the joint sessions well, and the Babelsberg housing area on the Griebnitz lake has been cleared of Germans and is being renovated. The American compound holds about 70 houses and some 500 people, with overflow space needed at Zehlendorf in Berlin. Parks was warmly received by General Kruglov. Crawford lists three permissions still needed, covering extra ground, free use of the supply highway, and a bigger working party.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1091:
American staff drafted this fuller version of the Italy policy paper at Babelsberg on July 20, 1945. It repeats the aims of the earlier draft: Italian independence, recovery, and free choice of government in time. A peace treaty, drafted fast by the new Council of Foreign Ministers, would end Italy's odd double status.

Three steps would meanwhile honor Italy's help in beating Germany. The powers would announce an early treaty, promise such economic aid as is practical, and back early Italian elections. The Allied Commission would hand duties to Rome faster. Outdated surrender clauses would be suspended, while Italy still pledges to meet Allied military needs and keep only the forces the Allies allow.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1191:
