A second memorandum from the United States Chiefs of Staff bears the date 19 July 1945. The flow of staff papers shows the chiefs feeding views to the team through the whole summit. Each note took up the questions from the armed forces' standpoint.

By the third day, the talks were moving from speeches to trades. The chiefs' staff kept pace, putting the services' needs and warnings in writing. This paper continues the series from the opening days. Read in a row, the memoranda form a military diary of the summit, kept by the men who would have to enforce its terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1291:
On 19 July 1945 the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. Someone had to think each question through on paper first; papers like this one are that thinking. The chiefs' staff supplied it in a steady flow through the talks.

A staff note from the third day belongs to the phase when stands were still soft. Facts and warnings could still move the envoys' minds. This memorandum carries the services' view at that open moment. It survives in the official record as part of the chiefs' near-daily counsel to the men who bargained for the United States.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1391:
Mikołajczyk's diary continues with an entry dated 29 July 1945. He was then in the middle of the Potsdam weeks, watching the settlement of Poland take shape around him. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

A diary kept day by day catches what later memoirs smooth away: rumor, waiting, and hope rising or falling on small news. This entry belongs to the summit's final stretch, when the leaders were drafting their closing texts. For readers, the value is closeness. The great questions of 1945 appear here at the scale of one man's day. Borders, armies, and governments fill a page written down before he knew how the story ended.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-91:
Minutes kept by a note-taker named Page record a Potsdam meeting on July 24, 1945. Several staff members took turns writing the American record of the conference sessions. Their sets of minutes were later printed side by side in the second Potsdam volume. Where wording mattered, having more than one set helped editors check the sense of a remark.

Page's record gives the meeting in direct, workmanlike form. Readers see points made, answers given, and the order in which topics came up. Such notes were never meant for print at the time. That is part of their worth: they show the talks as staff heard them, not as press offices later framed them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d791:
R. Borden Reams, information officer in the Secretary's office, wrote to Assistant Secretary Dunn on July 27, 1945. Document 791 concerns the conference's public face. An information officer handled the press side of a summit. Reams wrote inside the American team as the talks neared their close. The letter joined the second Potsdam volume.

Press work at Potsdam walked a fine line. The talks were secret; the world's papers were hungry. Readers see an officer managing that gap from inside. The document adds a rare strand to the volume: not what was decided, but how word of it would be handled. It shows secrecy as a task, not just a rule.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d891:
American members of the Economic Subcommittee reported to the Secretary of State on August 1, 1945. Their report covers the fight over Article 19 of the Economic Principles. That clause set the order for paying Germany's import and reparation bills.

All three sides in fact agreed on two sentences. Reparations must leave Germans enough to live on, and paying for approved imports ranks as a first charge on exports. The Americans still insisted on an added note about gear covered by the Reparations Agreement. The British agreed, but the Soviets refused. With that, the whole subject failed to reach agreement.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d991:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled the American minister in Switzerland on July 24, 1945. The same text went to the missions in Sweden, Portugal, and Turkey. Each envoy must formally notify his host government of a claim by the powers occupying Germany. They claim title to, or control of, all German-owned or German-run assets.

Host governments are asked to take no step that clashes with that control. Britain has agreed to the warning for neutral states, and France has signaled its missions will join. The Russians have been told their consent is assumed. Envoys should also urge their fellow occupying-power colleagues to deliver the same notice.
gao-gaoreports-b-296391: Photo Science took its July 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297291: Computer Cite doubled its December 2005 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-297691: Israel Aircraft Industries took its March 2006 contract fight to GAO — the TAMAM division — and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Foreign firms get the same full hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299291: MCS Portable Restroom Service took its March 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest. Even portable-toilet contracts get the full bid-law treatment.
gao-gaoreports-b-311391: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Eomax Corporation. The June 23, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-191: NIH and EPA research conflicts of interest needed tighter reviews in 2005, and GAO's report says the agencies had to improve their vetting. The review checks the lab-industry ties. The science deserved the clean hands. The reviews had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-291: Unemployment benefit receipt got a GAO information piece in 2005, and the report covers who got the checks. The review counts the recipients one by one. The jobless deserved the accurate count. The count was accurate. The checks were counted. The recipients were counted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-491: Pension paperwork delays got a GAO nudge in 2005, and the report says federal action could speed the forms. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the retirees deserved timely data. The retirees deserved timely data. The forms had to speed up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-391: Selected major weapons got GAO report cards in 2006, and the report assesses the programs' health. The findings grade the arsenal. The report warns that the big-ticket systems needed honest grades. The assessments had to be frank. The arsenal needed honest grades.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-491: Child support enforcement needed cost control in 2006, and GAO's report says more focus on labor costs and audits could cut federal spending. The findings target the expenses. The report warns that the collection machine should not cost more than it collected. The costs had to come down.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-91: Port risk management needed refining in 2006, and GAO's report says further refinements were required to assess risks and prioritize protections. The findings demand the upgrade. The report warns that the harbors' shields needed honest ranking. The refinements had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1091: The EPA's cleanup of downtown towers after 9/11 drew GAO's skeptical eye in 2007. Its test-and-clean program for the World Trade Center zone raised flags the report says needed answers. The findings press for better proof that the air and dust where New Yorkers lived and worked were truly safe.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-591: The Great Lakes' beaches were getting graded in 2007 — GAO's report says the EPA and states had moved on the beach-health law, with more to do. The findings track the cleanup. The report's standard: the world's largest freshwater shores deserve swimmable water.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-691: NASA's business software was thinking small in 2007 — GAO's report says the space agency had to weigh agency-wide needs to get its money's worth. The findings push for enterprise thinking over fiefdom buying. Rockets may fly solo, the report argues, but their back office should not.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-791: Old rules deserved second looks in 2007 — GAO's report says Washington could do better at reviewing whether regulations still earned their keep. The findings pitch retrospective review as good government hygiene. The report's motto: rules should have to re-audition for their jobs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-91: Fixed-up books got a GAO audit in 2007, and the report looks at how bureaus told the story of their redone numbers. The findings grade the honesty. The report warns that the mended ledgers needed plain talk. The do-overs had to be out in the open.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-291: The Government Accountability Office dug into yellowstone Bison: Interagency Plan and Agencies' Management Need Improvement to Better Address Bison-Cattle Brucellosis Controversy in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-691: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at oil and Gas Royalties: The Federal System for Collecting Oil and Gas Revenues Needs Comprehensive Reassessment. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-891: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on state Department: Comprehensive Strategy Needed to Improve Passport Operations. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-91: The Government Accountability Office dug into defense Acquisitions: Departmentwide Direction Is Needed for Implementation of the Anti-tamper Policy in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
garland-main-travelled-roads-1891:
Hamlin Garland's Main-Travelled Roads made his name when it appeared in 1891. Harper's later lists group it with Prairie Folks, Rose of Dutcher's Coolly, and The Eagle's Heart. A note from Garland dated March 1, 1922, fronts this printing.

The tales show farm life in the Middle West with no trace of romance. Mortgaged farms, brutal winters, worn-out women, and the slow crush of debt fill the pages. Under the Lion's Paw stands out as the most cutting farm story in American writing. Readers who hoped for cheerful pioneer tales got a shock, and a new realism in fiction was born.
gissing-new-grub-street-1891:
George Gissing published New Grub Street in 1891, his definitive novel of the writing life in London. Hack writers starve while mediocrities prosper, in the bitterest portrait of literary trade written. Gissing, who had starved, knew every rung of the ladder they climb and fall in London.

Edwin Reardon, a novelist of talent, cannot write the three-volume potboilers the market demands and sinks toward death in poverty. Jasper Milvain, his friend, treats literature as a trade, charms editors and widows, and rises by knowing the business of books. Amy, Reardon's wife, leaves him for failure and in time weds the rising Milvain, in Gissing's coldest turn of the screw. The title names the old Grub Street of hired pens, reborn in the magazine age. The book remains the set text for every writer who has feared the market's verdict.
grillandi-tractatus-de-sortilegiis-latin:
Paolo Grillandi, an Italian judge who served the papal court, wrote his treatise on sorcery in the earlier sixteenth century. It circulated here in the Frankfurt Tractatus duo of 1591, a standard gathering of witchcraft law. Grillandi writes from the bench, and his Latin sets out inquisitorial demonology at its most systematic.

He defines sorcery, divides its kinds, and lays down how courts should prove it. Confession, witnesses, and signs each get their rules. The treatise taught judges across Italy and beyond how to run a witch trial. Law for the witch courts is here written by a judge who knew them from inside. Its system is the point, and the terror, of the book.
guaita-essais-sciences-maudites-2-1891:
Stanislas de Guaita reads the Fall through Kabbalah in Le serpent de la Genese, first part, from 1891. The work forms the first part of the second series of his Essais de sciences maudites. De Guaita led the French occult revival with aristocratic learning and total conviction in magic as a hidden science of the soul.

The serpent of Genesis becomes, in his hands, a key to cosmic law. Hebrew letters, myths, and rites are weighed page by page here. He writes for initiates, dense with symbol and reference throughout. The book shows Paris occultism at its most erudite in the eighteen nineties, a world of salons, orders, and secret doctrine.
guaita-serpent-de-la-genese-1891:
Stanislas de Guaita published Le Serpent de la Genèse in 1891, the first part of a planned large work on evil and the occult. De Guaita was a French poet and Martinist who helped revive occult study in Paris. He read the Bible's serpent as a key to a hidden tradition.

Through Genesis and later lore, de Guaita traced the serpent as a symbol of secret knowledge, temptation, and hidden powers. He drew on Kabbalah, old grimoires, and tales of sorcery and poison. The work is dense, learned, and openly on the side of the occult against a purely material age. It shows French occultism at its most literary and ambitious.
guaita-temple-de-satan-1891:
De Guaita launches his Essais de sciences maudites with Le Temple de Satan, in French from 1891. The volume defends esoteric Christianity against two foes at once. Material science on one side and black magic on the other both draw his elegant, scornful fire in this cornerstone of the French occult revival.

He presents magic as a sacred science with strict moral law. Satan's temple, in his telling, is error built into a system. Parisian occultists took the book as a manifesto of their cause. It stands at the head of his life's work, the portal through which readers enter his grand design of essays.
hardy-tess-1891:
Thomas Hardy published Tess of the d'Urbervilles in 1891, a novel about a poor country girl in Wessex. Tess Durbeyfield learns her family claims kinship with an old noble line. Sent to claim kin, she meets Alec d'Urberville, who ruins her. She later finds love with Angel Clare, a parson's son learning farming.

Tess tells Angel her past on their wedding night, and he cannot forgive her. Hard work, desertion, and want follow before a final, fatal reunion. Hardy subtitled the book the story of a pure woman. Its attack on double standards shocked Victorian readers. It remains his most loved and argued-over novel.
hartland-science-fairy-tales-1891:
Edwin Sidney Hartland, an English man of law and lore, wrote this study of fairy tales in 1891. It was one of the first books to treat the tales as a theme for strict study. Hartland held that tales keep the marks of the old ways of the folk.

He traces one tale type, the swan maid, through land after land and age after age. The Melusine tale, the fairy bride who is part snake, stands at the heart of his case. The book shows how one tale can map the spread of lore round the world.
herbart-textbook-psychology-1891:
Johann Friedrich Herbart wrote his Lehrbuch zur Psychologie, Textbook of Psychology, in 1816, and Margaret K Smith translated it in 1891. Herbart, who held Kant's old chair, treated psychology as a science of the soul's mechanics. Ideas, in his picture, press, check, and lift each other like forces in a crowded field.

From that mechanics Herbart builds his accounts of perception, memory, feeling, and desire. The textbook is spare and ordered, meant to ground his famous pedagogy in the mind's real workings. His Science of Education grows straight from this root, as the evidence of the two books shows. Smith's English carried the system to American students of the mind.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol10-1891:
The tenth and last volume of the Guiding Symptoms closed the set in 1891, eleven years after Hering's death. A project begun from one man's proving notebooks had grown into the largest symptom record of its school. Volume X completes the alphabetical run of remedies.

Its pages follow the house style: symptoms by region, ranks marked, characteristic signs lifted clear. With the set whole, a prescriber could trace almost any proved sign to its remedy. Later abridgments drew heavily on these volumes, yet the full ten still reward anyone who wants Hering in his own fullness.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r: This edition of Gibbon's second volume covers Rome's age of chaos: the barracks emperors, the plague, the empire splitting and nearly dying in the third century. Gibbon narrates disaster with cool irony and unmatched style. For readers comparing printings, the history itself needs no introduction: it is the greatest work of English historiography.
how-to-read-heads-or-practical-lessons-o: How to Read Heads, 1891. The practical lessons. This book preserves that manual. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it.
husserl-philosophie-der-arithmetik-1891:
Husserl's Philosophy of Arithmetic, published in German in 1891, was his first book. He had trained as a mathematician in Vienna and Berlin, then turned to philosophy under Franz Brentano. The young scholar asked a deceptively plain question: how does the mind grasp number?

The book studies counting, collecting, and the signs we use for numbers, trying to ground arithmetic in acts of the mind. Its method leans on psychology, the very approach Husserl would attack nine years later in the Logical Investigations. A sharp review by Gottlob Frege helped push him toward that change. The debut already shows his care for exact description, straining against the limits of his teachers' psychology. It is the starting point of the long road to phenomenology.
ibsen-hedda-gabler-archer-1891:
Henrik Ibsen wrote Hedda Gabler in Norwegian, and William Archer made this English version in 1891. Archer, the critic who brought Ibsen to England, knew the playwright's aims at first hand. Hedda is often called his most dangerous heroine, a caged mind with pistols and pride.

Hedda, wed to the dull scholar Tesman, is bored, pregnant, and trapped in respectability. Her old flame Lövborg returns with a great book and a wild past of drink. Hedda burns his manuscript, lends him a pistol, and is trapped by Judge Brack's knowledge. She shoots herself rather than live under scandal and another man's power over her life. The play's cold grip and Hedda's mystery keep stages busy to this day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mizmor-shir-le-:
Mizmor Shir le-Yom ha-Shabbat — a psalm, a song for the Sabbath day — is the superscription of Psalm 92, and Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen trace its musical life in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The psalm opens the Sabbath at evening service, returns in the morning's verses of praise, and is read again after the Torah at afternoon service.

Musically, the article admits, the northern rite has no fixed tradition for it, so cantors and choirmasters filled the gap with settings of their own. One stands out: Schubert composed verses one to eight for baritone, solo quartet, and chorus, printed in Sulzer's Schir Zion and performed at the London Symphony Concerts. In practice the congregation reads the psalm and the cantor takes the closing verses in elaborate chant.
judge-letters-that-have-helped-me-1891:
Warm notes from a guide fill Letters That Have Helped Me, William Q. Judge's book of 1891. Judge wrote the notes to Julia Keightley, a keen fan of the creed. She set them in print with his leave, since they had helped her so much on the path.

Each note deals with doubt, grief, pride, or zeal in plain, kind words. There is no grand creed here, just close counsel. Fans call it the warm heart of the creed in the United States. Seekers still turn to it in hard times. Keightley, who got the notes, was a scribe in her own right. Her choice to share them gave the creed a warm, close text.
kennan-siberia-exile-vol1-1891: Siberia and the Exile System, volume one, George Kennan's 1891 exposé. The Tsar's prison land. This book preserves that classic. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
kennan-siberia-exile-vol2-1891: Siberia and the Exile System, volume two, George Kennan's 1891 exposé. The exile's tale continues. This book preserves that classic. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes.
lagerlof-gosta-berling-1891:
Selma Lagerlof published The Story of Gosta Berling in 1891, her first novel, set in Varmland in Sweden. Gosta Berling is a priest removed from his post for drinking. He joins a band of retired officers and idlers at Ekeby Manor. Their year of feasts, pranks, and loves drives the tale.

Legends, ghosts, and folk tales weave through the main story. The lady of the manor holds the cavaliers in check until a dark bargain unsettles all. Lagerlof writes in a rich, song-like style. The book made her famous at home and abroad. She later became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
leland-gypsy-sorcery-1891:
Charles Godfrey Leland wrote on the lore of the Romani folk for years. His Gypsy Sorcery and Fortune Telling came out in 1891. The book gathers charms, spells, and ways to read fate. Much of it came from Romani men and women he knew in England.

Love charms, cures, and signs for luck fill the pages in strong runs. Leland gives the words of the spells and the acts that go with them. He also tells of gods and fays the folk held dear. The book is a rich store of folk magic from its age.
liebeault-therapeutique-suggestive-1891:
Liebault puts suggestion to work in Therapeutique suggestive, in French from 1891, the clinical companion to his book on induced sleep. Case after case shows words curing the so-called incurable at Nancy. Pain, palsy, and nervous ills yield, in his reports, to calm speech and firm expectation in the waking and sleeping states alike.

He records failures beside successes with a practitioner's honesty throughout. The method asks for no drugs, no passes, no stage tricks at all. Colleagues came from abroad to watch the old doctor work. The book forms the practical birth record of the talking cure, a quiet landmark on the road to modern psychotherapy.
lobachevsky-theory-parallels-halsted-189:
Nicholas Lobachevsky broke Euclid's hold on geometry in his Geometrical Researches on the Theory of Parallels. George Bruce Halsted translated the work, first published in German in 1840, into English in 1891. For two thousand years, Euclid's parallel postulate had seemed beyond doubt. Lobachevsky denied it and built a new geometry on the denial.

In his system, many lines through a point can miss a given line entirely. Angles and areas then obey rules strange to school geometry. He shows the system hangs together without contradiction. The book founded non-Euclidean geometry as a field. Later physics found his strange space at work in the real world.
mooney-the-sacred-formulas-of-the-cherok:
James Mooney worked for the Bureau of American Ethnology and lived among the Cherokee, learning their language and gaining their trust. His 1891 report prints the sacred formulas that Cherokee shamans dictated to him, given in Cherokee with English translation.

The formulas are spoken cures and charms: words for healing sickness, for success in hunting and fishing, for war, and for winning love. Each text shows how the shaman named the disease spirit and called on stronger powers against it. Mooney added notes on herbs, rites, and the shamans' own explanations. Few early records preserve native ritual language this fully.
newes-from-scotland-1591:
Newes from Scotland appeared in 1591, a pamphlet reporting the North Berwick witch trials in Scotland. The accused, including schoolmaster John Fian, were charged with raising storms against King James VI at sea. Torture produced confessions, and the pamphlet spread the story in England.

Pages describe meetings with the Devil, charms, and plots against the king's ships, as the court claimed they happened. James himself took part in questioning the accused, and his interest shaped the case. The pamphlet is a primary source for a famous witch trial. It also shows how print turned a local panic into national news.
ochorowicz-mental-suggestion-1891:
Julian Ochorowicz links the trance to thought leaps in Mental Suggestion, his study in English from 1891. Ochorowicz was a sage of Poland who worked in Paris. He found that a mind in deep trance can take a mute bid from a far mind, with no word, sign, or touch to bear the thought from one to the next.

Tests with a young seer fill the book. He prints hits and fails with fair care. His work stands at the join of two fields. It helped turn trance craft to the study of thought leaps.
openalex-w1963107491: Archives need modern care — and Portuguese speakers lacked current guides. Funari's 2006 Portuguese-language work on permanent archives and document treatment grew from his 2003–2005 leadership of a UNICAMP working group on electronic document preservation. The book filled a gap in archival literature.
openalex-w2070221591: A perspective article — the viewpoint is unstated. This 2013 work titled 'PERSPECTIVE ARTICLE' offers some author's perspective on a field. The thin catalog record hides the topic entirely; the format promises opinion, not data, from an expert.
openalex-w2087628191: Malaria's disguise genes dodge immunity. A 2007 study mapped the gene maps of falciparum malaria's var genes. The work compared var gene diversity behind the parasite's disguise — up to 60 genes per genome, each a potential disguise.
openalex-w2138708491: A turtle genome decoded extreme survival. A 2013 paper described the western painted turtle genome, a model for tough living. The work mapped tooth loss, immune shifts, and long life features — a reptile's secrets, revealed.
openalex-w2169827291: Trade deals shape what nations eat. This 2013 paper warns that the Trans-Pacific Partnership — a sweeping trade agreement under negotiation since 2010 among Pacific-rim countries including Australia — could threaten diet-related health. The authors examine how the deal's rules on food trade, investment, and regulation might push diets toward processed foods, and argue that public-health voices were sidelined in the talks.
openalex-w2509252391: Antimatter raining from space could betray dark matter — or just ordinary cosmic-ray collisions. This 2016 Physical Review Letters paper presents the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer's precision measurement of the antiproton flux and antiproton-to-proton ratio from 1 to 450 GV, based on 349,000 antiproton events. The result is a crucial baseline for anyone hunting exotic physics in cosmic rays.
openalex-w2597376791: Instead of spraying pesticides, farmers can release beneficial insects and microbes to eat the pests — augmentative biological control, now used on over 30 million hectares. This 2017 BioControl review surveys new opportunities in the field, with Europe as the largest commercial market for invertebrate agents. The paper maps where biocontrol is headed next.
openalex-w2756512191: On August 14, 2017, three detectors — Advanced Virgo plus the two LIGOs — caught the same black-hole merger, GW170814, with a false-alarm rate below one in 27,000 years. This 2017 Physical Review Letters paper reports the first three-detector gravitational-wave observation. Triangulation shrank the source's sky location dramatically, a leap for follow-up astronomy.
openalex-w2789737791: How do particle spectra change from tiny proton collisions to massive lead ones? This 2018 Journal of High Energy Physics paper measures charged-particle transverse momentum spectra across pp, p-Pb, and Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV. The nuclear modification factors reveal how the quark-gluon plasma reshapes the debris.
openalex-w4391756091: Image analysis needs trustworthy validation — and metrics matter. This 2024 Nature Methods paper, by Maier-Hein, Reinke, Godau and colleagues, delivers Metrics Reloaded: recommendations for validating image analysis. The guidance standardizes how the field judges its algorithms.
openalex-w4406942591: Eczema's maddening itch starts deep in the skin. This review covers why atopic dermatitis itches so badly: broken skin walls plus haywire immune signals. The authors untangled the itch pathway step by step. A skin review of why scratching never brings relief.
openalex-w4409453391: Crystal surfaces can host strange electronic states. This theory paper models electron bands on different faces of a cubic lattice with eg orbitals, finding a flat surface state tied to an octupole moment. The authors mapped the band structures. A condensed-matter study of surfaces with exotic character.
openalex-w7172334291: Seeing whole organs in 3D takes clever optics. This paper presents a do-it-yourself light-sheet microscope for four-color volumetric imaging of intact specimens. The authors extended the design for complex samples. An imaging-methods paper democratizing deep tissue views.
openalex-w7204754091: Clean water and sewers shape public health, yet Brazil's Amazon region lags far behind. This comparative study looks at two cities in eastern Amazonia, Castanhal and Maraba, measuring sanitation, health, and income side by side. The authors document deep gaps within a single state. A data-driven portrait of how unequal basic services translate into unequal health.
pearson-fragments-zeno-cleanthes-1891:
Zeno of Citium founded the Stoic school at Athens around 300 BCE, and Cleanthes, his pupil, led it after him. The books of both men are lost. A. C. Pearson gathered what later writers quoted from them, and Cambridge University Press published his English collection in 1891, with an introduction and notes.

Each fragment comes with remarks that explain hard terms and point to the source that kept the words alive. Through these scraps readers can trace early Stoic teaching on fate, nature, and virtue. Pearson's book was the first English gathering of the pair. It still serves as a direct door into the first age of the Stoa.
plos-pbio-0020091:
Mark J. Dayel and R. Dyche Mullins worked out a trigger step in cell shape change for PLOS Biology in 2004. Cells crawl and divide by building filaments of actin. The Arp2/3 complex starts new filaments branching off old ones, and WASP proteins switch it on.

The authors show how adding the first piece of a new filament, delivered by WASP, fires up the complex. That detail explains how the cell keeps actin growth off until the right place and moment. Precise timing matters, since wild actin growth would wreck cell shape. The mechanism is a neat case of a machine that arms itself with its own first building block.
plos-pbio-0020391:
Alekos Athanasiadis, Alexander Rich, and Stefan Maas surveyed RNA editing in human gene messages in PLOS Biology in 2004. Editing swaps one RNA letter for another after the message is made. The most common swap turns A into I, which the cell reads as G.

The team found this editing is far more widespread than thought, mostly in Alu repeats, which are common stretches in human messages. Widespread editing in repeats may help the cell mark and manage them. It also means the final protein code can differ from the DNA more often than assumed. The survey redrew the scale of editing and set off searches for its roles in brain function and disease.
plos-pone-0000091:
Paul de Groot and R. W. Veldhuizen described artery change in heart disease in PLOS ONE in 2006. Atherosclerosis is the buildup of fatty plaques inside arteries. As a plaque grows, the artery can widen outward to keep the channel open, a process called remodeling. Late in the disease, that compensation fails.

The authors trace remodeling from the start of plaque growth to its end stage in human coronary arteries. Seeing the whole arc in real tissue matters for treatment timing. Drugs and stents work on arteries at particular stages. A map of the full process helps doctors judge which stage a patient's artery has reached and what can still be saved.
plos-pone-0000191:
Chung-Ming Liu, Shu-Hua Lin, Ying-Chen Chen, and colleagues published this influenza study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines the timing of severe avian influenza A H5N1 outbreaks, the bird flu strain feared for its lethality. The authors link the onset of outbreaks to drops in temperature.

Cold snaps may change bird behavior, virus survival, or both, in ways that spark outbreaks. The authors test that link across outbreak records. If temperature drops really do precede flare-ups, weather data could give health and farm authorities a short warning window for a dangerous virus.
plos-pone-0000291:
Silvia Díaz, Francisco Amaro, Daniel Rico, and colleagues published this cell biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Metallothioneins are small proteins that bind metals, protecting cells from toxic ones like cadmium. In Tetrahymena, a single-celled pond organism, the authors show these proteins fall into two discrete subfamilies.

Two subfamilies suggest two distinct jobs, perhaps handling different metals or stresses. Sorting the family in this model organism clarifies how cells across life manage metal danger. Tetrahymena is a standard lab subject, so the classification guides work on pollution response and metal biology.
plos-pone-0000391:
Komla Sobo and colleagues looked inside the cell's recycling stations in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Late endosomes are compartments that sort material the cell has taken in, and their membranes contain raft-like domains, patches rich in certain fats. The team asked how varied those patches are.

Finding real diversity among the raft-like domains suggests the compartments are not uniform bags but have organized zones with different jobs. Membrane organization affects how cells sort cargo, break down waste, and respond to signals. Mapping that variety gives cell biologists a finer picture of a basic piece of cell machinery.
plos-pone-0000491:
Shobha Broor and colleagues followed young children in rural India for three years to map chest infections, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Acute respiratory infections are among the top killers of small children worldwide. The prospective cohort study tracked the epidemiology and virology of these infections, recording which viruses caused them and when.

A three-year window captures seasonal cycles and year-to-year variation that a short study would miss. Knowing the local virus mix guides vaccine and treatment priorities for the region. The study gives rural India, often absent from such data, a baseline that health planners can actually use.
plos-pone-0000591:
Jonathan Carlson and colleagues used the family-like layering of human groups to sharpen gene hunts, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Gene hunts link DNA variants to disease. They are plagued by false hits when the groups being compared differ in ancestry. The team showed how to use layered population structure to clean up such studies.

Human groups nest inside each other: broad regions hold local groups, which hold smaller ones still. Using that layering lets the math split true disease links from mere ancestry gaps. Cleaner methods mean fewer wasted years chasing phantom genes. That was a real cost in the first wave of genome-wide scans.
plos-pone-0000691:
Andre Franke, Jochen Hampe, Philip Rosenstiel and colleagues used systematic association mapping to name a new disease gene, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Crohn disease is one form of inflammatory bowel disease, driven by many genes together. Recent studies had found several Crohn-linked variants. Together they explained only a fraction of the disease's heritability, so more genes remained hidden.

Their mapping identified NELL1 as a novel IBD disease gene. Each new susceptibility gene adds a piece to the inherited puzzle and a possible drug target. Systematic scans like this one replaced guesswork candidate-gene studies, and NELL1 is presented as a catch from casting the net widely.
plos-pone-0000791:
Christian B. Willberg, Scott M. Ward, Reginald F. Clayton and colleagues found that an immune signal can shield liver cells from immune attack. Cellular immunity plays a key role in the outcome of hepatitis C virus infection, yet most infections become persistent. The mechanisms behind that persistence were unclear, but the liver, the primary site of infection, may be critical, as their 2007 PLOS ONE study argues.

The title states the finding: interferon-alpha protects hepatocytes, liver cells, from killing by cytotoxic T cells. A signal meant to fight virus may also preserve infected cells, balancing damage against control. That trade-off could help explain why hepatitis C so often settles in for the long term.
plos-pone-0000891:
Ingo Meister and Marco Iacoboni asked whether language areas switch on when people watch actions with meaning, in PLOS ONE in 2007. One idea holds that language grew out of brain systems for movement. Front and side brain areas that react to watched actions are part of that story.

If language truly grew from those systems, watching an action with a clear message might wake language areas too. The authors tested that expectation and report no language specific activation in their setup. A negative result like this is useful: it sets limits on a popular theory. It pushes the field to say more exactly which systems language and action really share.
plos-pone-0000991:
Mark Tarnopolsky, Andrew Zimmer, Jeremy Paikin and colleagues tested two supplements with strength training in older adults, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Aging brings lower muscle mass and more body fat. The team asked whether creatine monohydrate and conjugated linoleic acid could add to the gains from resistance exercise.

Older volunteers trained while taking the supplements, and the team tracked strength and body composition, including fat free mass and body fat. Supplements are widely sold to this age group on thin evidence. A controlled trial in the exact population that buys them is the right test. The paper reports what the combination did and did not add.
plos-pone-0001091:
Anil Thakur, Gautier Robin, Gregor Guncar and colleagues improved protein crystallization screening with seed particles, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Growing crystals is a major bottleneck in reading protein structures by X-ray methods. A crystal must first nucleate, start from a seed, then grow to usable size, and that start is often the failure point.

Adding heterogeneous nucleating agents, foreign particles that invite nucleation, raised success in sparse matrix screening, the standard first pass test. A better first pass saves protein, time and money on every structure project. Structural biology feeds drug design, so a bench trick that lifts success rates has wide downstream value.
plos-pone-0001191:
Can a simple body tissue detect an image, the way an eye does? Catherine Tempel-Brami, Iddo Pinkas, and Avigdor Scherz explored that odd question in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They used a living rat and a pigment injected into the bloodstream.

Light absorbed through the body was translated by the tissue into a chemical signature, which the authors visualized using photosensitized magnetic resonance imaging. In effect, the tissue itself acted as the light sensor and the scanner read the picture. The study is a proof of principle for imaging methods that borrow the body's own chemistry.
plos-pone-0001291:
Many bacterial pathogens inject proteins into host cells using a type III secretion system, a molecular syringe. Lian Zhou, Jing Wang, and Lian-Hui Zhang found a control circuit for that syringe in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Screening a mutant library, they found that breaking the genes for a spermidine transporter changed secretion.

The authors describe modulation of the type III secretion system by a spermidine transporter dependent signaling pathway. Spermidine is a small molecule cells use in many processes. Linking its transport to the injection machinery reveals a new place where a pathogen's attack could be blocked.
plos-pone-0001391:
Hyun-Gwan Lee and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on alcohol and mating acts in fruit flies. In people, drinking is tied to bold and loose mating behavior. Hard proof for the body basis of that link was thin. The team sought a lab model where the link could be tested in a strict way.

They gave male flies repeat doses of alcohol vapor and watched their courtship of females. The males grew bold and kept courting even when it made little sense. A fly model like this lets labs probe the genes and brain paths at play. That may in time clarify how drink loosens restraint in people too.
plos-pone-0001491:
Ling Li and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on herpes virus infection in the cell nucleus. A helper protein called Hsc70 gathers in spots inside infected nuclei. Parts of the cell's waste system gather there too. The team had shown the virus's gene copying sites sit in those spots. They asked what viral part calls Hsc70 there.

They show a viral protein called ICP27 is needed for Hsc70 to form its spots. Those spots sit at the edge of the virus's copying zones. The finding ties a host helper to a key viral worker. Blocking that tie could be a route to curb herpes growth.
plos-pone-0001591:
Marc Mangel and Michael Bonsall published a 2008 PLOS ONE paper that brings evolution models to stem cell science. Such models have served well in much of biology, but had not been used for stem cells save for cancer work. The pair build a frame that lets these models run on stem cells in full. It covers cell replacement, rest states, and variation.

With the frame, labs can test how stem cell pools hold up over a life span. They can also test how faults grow into disease in a formal way. Math frames like this turn loose tales into claims that data can check. That is a gain for a fast, hype prone field.
plos-pone-0001691:
Adele M. Mount, Christopher M. Smith, Fiona Kupresanin, and their co-authors asked which immune sentinels start the response to viruses, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Dendritic cells link the fast innate immune response to the targeted adaptive one. One subset, CD8α dendritic cells, was known to drive the growth of killer T cells during viral infection, sometimes seemingly alone.

The team tested whether other dendritic cell populations also activate CD4 helper T cells after viral stimulation. They report that multiple populations can do this job. The full text gives the cell sorts, the stimulation tests, and the T-cell responses each subset raised. A wider cast of activating cells means vaccine designs have more levers to pull than the single-subset view suggested.
plos-pone-0001791:
Rajini Sreenivasan, Minnie Cai, Richard Bartfai, and their co-authors catalogued sex-biased genes in zebrafish in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Knowledge of zebrafish reproduction was very limited, though the fish is a major lab animal. The team built a gonad-derived cDNA microarray. They analyzed large-scale gene expression profiles in adult gonads and other organs, drawing on more than a hundred thousand gonad-derived sequences.

They report novel genes with sexually dimorphic expression in the gonad and the brain. The full text gives the gene lists and the tissue patterns. Sex-biased genes in the brain as well as the gonads hint at deep molecular differences between the sexes that behavior studies can build on.
plos-pone-0001891:
Anders Folkesson and co-authors asked why germs in biofilms shrug off attack, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A biofilm is a slimy mat where microbes live packed close, and such mats stand up to drugs far better than free cells do. The team focused on antimicrobial peptides, small proteins that kill germs and form part of natural defense.

They grew Escherichia coli biofilms built in unlike shapes, some loose and some dense. Then they tested how each shape changed the germs' power to survive the peptides. Linking mat shape to drug survival helps explain stubborn infections on implants and in lungs. It also points to shape as a target for new care.
plos-pone-0001991:
Shally Awasthi and co-authors ran a trial on antibiotics for child pneumonia with wheeze, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Pneumonia kills many children in poorer countries, and antibiotics are the standard care under world guidelines. Yet a large share of these cases are caused by viruses, not bacteria, and children with viral cases are more likely to wheeze.

The trial, run at many centers with random assignment, gave children with non-severe pneumonia and wheeze a three-day course of oral amoxycillin or a control. If the drug adds no gain in wheezy cases, scarce antibiotics can be spared. Trials like this test when less treatment is safe.
plos-pone-0002091:
Jeffrey Canter and co-authors tested a mitochondrial gene variant against a common eye disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Age-related macular degeneration is a leading cause of vision loss in older adults. The variant, A4917G in a mitochondrial gene, changes one building block of a protein. It had been tied to neurodegenerative traits, the kind seen in nerve disease.

The team asked whether carriers face a higher risk of macular degeneration. As the title states, the variant is independently associated with the disease. A gene carried in the cell's power units adds a fresh strand to the genetics of this eye illness.
plos-pone-0002191:
Takashi Shiraiwa studied a small smell organ of the fruit fly, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Drosophila melanogaster smells mainly with its antennae, but it also has a smaller organ, the maxillary palp, sitting near the mouthparts. What that organ does for behavior had long been unclear.

Because the palp sits so close to the mouth, Shiraiwa tested whether it helps with taste as well as smell. The study looks at how signals from the palp combine taste and odor input. A fly that can blend two senses at the point of eating gains a fuller picture of its food before the first bite.
plos-pone-0002291:
Andre Kalil and Junfeng Sun asked why doctors have been slow to adopt five trial-proven treatments for severe sepsis, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Five pivotal trials had shown lower mortality with intensive insulin therapy, activated protein C, low-tidal volume ventilation, low-dose steroids, and early goal-directed therapy. Expert guidelines recommended all five, yet uptake in practice lagged.

The authors used a Bayesian analysis, which weighs how strong each trial's evidence really is. Their reading helps explain clinician caution: some celebrated results rest on single trials with fragile statistics. The paper is a lesson in reading landmark trials with a cooler head.
plos-pone-0002391:
Abdoul joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Hendy Abdoul, Vincent Mallet, Stanislas Pol, among others. Its subject is serum Alpha-Fetoprotein Predicts Treatment Outcome in Chronic Hepatitis C Patients Regardless of HCV Genotype. We examined the association between serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level and sustained virological response (SVR) in 93 chronic hepatitis C patients.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002491:
Desikan led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Radhika Desikan, Jakub Horák, Christina Chaban, among others. Its subject is the Histidine Kinase AHK5 Integrates Endogenous and Environmental Signals in Arabidopsis Guard Cells. Stomatal guard cells monitor and respond to environmental and endogenous signals such that the stomatal aperture is continually optimised for water use efficiency.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002591:
Zetola and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Nicola M. Zetola, Carlos G. Grijalva, Sarah Gertler, among others. Its subject is simplifying Consent for HIV Testing Is Associated with an Increase in HIV Testing. The rest of the title points to Case Detection in Highest Risk Groups, San Francisco January 2003–June 2007. Populations at highest risk for HIV infection face multiple barriers to HIV testing.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002691:
Patricia Fabian and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on influenza virus in human exhaled breath: an observational study. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Patricia Fabian, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Recent studies suggest that humans exhale fine particles during tidal breathing but little is known of their composition, particularly during infection. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002791:
Michael Xavier Kirby and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was lower miocene stratigraphy along the panama canal and its bearing on the central american peninsula. The catalog record names Michael Xavier Kirby first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Before the formation of the Central American Isthmus, there was a Central American Peninsula. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002891:
Maria Ban, Joanna Elson, Amie Walton and co-authors tested in 2008 whether mitochondrial DNA shapes the risk of multiple sclerosis. Several lines of evidence had hinted that inherited factors in mitochondria, the cell's energy units, might play a part. Mitochondrial DNA passes mainly from the mother.

For the PLOS ONE study the team re-read the full mitochondrial genome from 159 patients and also grouped their DNA into haplogroups, sets of shared variants. That two-part check gives a thorough test of the idea. Neurologists studying the roots of multiple sclerosis can see how far this lead was followed.
plos-pone-0002991:
Zhao Zhang, Jian Chen, Fuzheng Guo and co-authors built a fast protein tracking method in 2008. Dynamic proteomics follows how protein levels change over time, and demand was growing for methods with both speed and scale. Their approach labels proteins in living cells with sulfur-35.

Named SiLAD, the method was designed and tested for high temporal resolution, meaning many time points close together. Published in PLOS ONE, it aims to catch quick protein rises and falls that slower methods blur. Cell biologists studying responses to drugs or signals need exactly that timing. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003091:
Hiroyasu Kamei, Ling Lu, Shuang Jiao and co-authors traced duplicated IGFBP-1 genes in zebrafish in 2008. Gene duplication is the primary force behind new gene evolution. Judging whether duplicated copies have split into divergent functions is often challenging, and zebrafish are well placed to show the process.

The duplicated genes are induced by hypoxia, low oxygen, and have diversified since duplication, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, the pair gives a worked example of how copies drift apart in role. Such cases anchor general theories of genome evolution. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003191:
Suhail Khoja, Peter Ojwang, Saeed Khan and colleagues analyse HIV-1 subtypes in Nairobi, Kenya, in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Genetic analysis of a viral infection helps follow its spread in a population, track routes of infection, and, where relevant, inform vaccine design. Sequence analysis of the viral genome also gives information about patterns of genetic divergence over time.

Readers get a subtype picture for the Kenyan capital at that date. Knowing which subtypes circulate matters because vaccines and tests can perform differently across subtypes. The study adds a dated, placed record to the wider map of HIV diversity in Africa.
plos-pone-0003291:
Dan-Qing Liu, Li-Min Li, Ya-Lan Guo and colleagues study a brake on monocyte movement in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Signal regulatory protein alpha, or SIRP alpha, is involved in many jobs of monocytes. The team study the role of SIRP alpha in regulating beta-2 integrin-mediated monocyte adhesion, transendothelial migration and phagocytosis. They use THP-1 monocytes and macrophages.

The title reports that SIRP alpha holds back all three processes. Readers see one surface protein restrain sticking, crossing vessel walls, and engulfing. Monocyte movement drives inflammation, so its brakes could be drug targets for such diseases. That makes this brake worth study in its own right.
plos-pone-0003391:
Petric Kuballa and co-authors studied a gene variant tied to Crohn's disease in this 2008 paper. Crohn's is a painful, long-term inflammation of the gut. Large gene scans had pointed to a variant in a gene called ATG16L1. That gene helps cells clean up and digest their own waste, a process called autophagy.

The team tested how cells with the variant handle a germ that lives inside cells. Cleanup of the invader was impaired in those cells. Poor cleanup may let gut microbes linger and drive inflammation. The finding gives Crohn's research a clear process to target.
plos-pone-0003491:
Nandi Siegfried and co-authors compared trial quality across continents in this 2008 paper. Good trials need fair random assignment and hidden allocation of treatments. Those steps keep bias out of results. No earlier work had focused on HIV/AIDS trials or African trials.

The team checked how trials reported random generation and allocation concealment. African HIV trials reported these steps adequately more often than North American ones. The verdict runs against common assumptions about research standards. It credits African trial teams for rigor often overlooked. Trial quality sets how much trust any drug result deserves at all.
plos-pone-0003591:
Jae Kwak, Alan Willse, and Koichi Matsumura studied mouse odor signatures in this 2008 paper. Each mouse carries a unique odor, or odortype, used for recognition. Genes shape odortypes in part, notably the major histocompatibility complex. Environment and diet can also shift an animal's scent.

The team showed genetically based odor signatures persist despite dietary variation. Changing food did not erase the inherited signature. Individual recognition by smell is thus written into DNA. The finding separates genetic identity signals from diet noise. Smell guides mating in mice, so a stable scent badge has real value.
plos-pone-0003691:
George Peck, Liam Smeeth, John Whittaker, and colleagues published this stroke genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Bleeding in the brain, whether as haemorrhagic stroke or from a burst aneurysm, has been hard to explain genetically. Single studies were small, and their results stayed shaky.

The authors ran a meta-analysis of all candidate gene studies of these conditions in adults. Pooling the data gave firmer ground for judging which gene variants truly raise risk. The combined picture helps doctors and researchers sort real genetic signals from noise in a deadly set of diseases.
plos-pone-0003791:
Thomas E. Sussan, Jonathan Jun, Rajesh Thimmulappa, and colleagues published this heart disease study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Oxidative stress and inflammation drive the plaques of atherosclerosis. Nrf2 is a switch that turns on a battery of antioxidant defenses in cells. Its role in plaque growth was tested in mice lacking ApoE.

Disrupting Nrf2 weakened the atherosclerosis that ApoE loss normally causes. The result is counterintuitive: removing an antioxidant master switch slowed plaque. It shows oxidative stress pathways pulling double duty in heart disease, not simple protection. Mouse work of this kind often reframes human disease hunts.
plos-pone-0003891:
Suresh Gopalan and Frederick M. Ausubel proposed a new study system for host and microbe change in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article starts from a modern trend. Industry and social change keep bringing microbes into contact with new hosts. Those contacts let both sides adapt fast, and new diseases can arise.

The authors set out a metasystem built from simple model organisms. Using several paired models lets labs watch adaptation as it emerges. That view is hard to get from a single host and microbe pair. The frame can help scientists foresee how new host-microbe pairs settle or turn harmful.
plos-pone-0003991:
Lisa M. Mullen, Janine T. Bossé, Sean P. Nair, and co-authors studied a bacterial protein with two talents in 2008. A protein in Pasteurella multocida had been shown to bind fibronectin. Fibronectin binding helps bacteria stick to host tissues. The protein also resembles DNA uptake proteins of competent bacteria.

Their PLOS ONE article covers the ComE1 family across the Pasteurellaceae. Family members combine adhesion and DNA binding traits in one design. One protein doing both jobs may aid survival in host airways. The work widens what competence proteins are thought to do. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004091:
Lee Smith, John Willan, Nick Warr, and co-authors removed a candidate sex gene in mice in 2008. The early gonad can become a testis or an ovary. Chromosomal sex normally decides which path it takes. The team had screened for new genes steering that choice.

Their PLOS ONE article reports the Maestro gene is not required. Mice lacking it showed normal sexual development and fertility. A clear negative narrows the search for true sex-determining factors. It also shows why each candidate needs a knockout test. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004191:
Anna Sawka and colleagues published this interview study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Radioactive iodine treatment, called RAI for short, is often considered after surgery for well-differentiated thyroid cancer. Numbers alone cannot say what that diagnosis and treatment feel like to live through.

The researchers interviewed thyroid cancer survivors about being diagnosed, about the iodine treatment, and about how choices were made. Their accounts show the uncertainty and isolation that the treatment can bring. The study gives clinicians a patient's-eye view to weigh alongside survival statistics when advising on this treatment.
plos-pone-0004291:
Rebecca Mercer and Rachel Wevrick published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. MAGEL2 is one of several genes typically inactivated in Prader-Willi syndrome, a developmental disorder marked by obesity. What the loss of MAGEL2 alone does, without the other syndrome genes, was not well understood.

The team studied mice with a targeted mutation of Magel2. They report that loss of Magel2 impairs reproductive function in these mice. Separating one gene's effects from the full syndrome helps doctors understand which features come from which gene. The syndrome takes its features from several genes lost together.
plos-pone-0004391:
Glowing tags let biologists watch living cells from the inside. Simone Kredel, Franz Oswald, Karin Nienhaus, and co-authors built a new red tag in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper describes mRuby, a single-unit red fluorescent protein. It comes from a variant of the protein eqFP611. The tag is meant for labeling parts inside cells.

mRuby takes in light at 558 nanometers and gives it back at 605. That 47-nanometer gap, called the Stokes shift, is large. A wide gap makes the glow easier to separate from the light used to excite it. The authors report the protein is bright and works as one unit. Those traits suit it for clear imaging of cell structures.
plos-pone-0004491:
Salmon hurt at dams show the same brain injury signal seen in mammals, report Ann Miracle, Nancy Denslow, Kevin Kroll, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Biomedical research has produced biomarker tests, measurable signals that flag disease or injury. One set of signals comes from a brain protein called alphaII-spectrin, which breaks down after traumatic brain injury.

The trigger here was new: salmon injured at spillways, the chutes that let dam water pass. The injured fish generated the same breakdown products as mammals with brain trauma. That cross-species match gives wildlife managers a tool to measure dam injury in fish. It also shows the injury signal is old in evolution, shared by fish and mammals alike.
plos-pone-0004591:
A fossil trackway catches a small meat-eating dinosaur in the act of crouching, report Andrew Milner, Jerald Harris, Martin Lockley, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fossil tracks of non-avian theropod dinosaurs usually reflect the upright, two-legged stance retained in living birds. Behaviors like crouching are rarely captured, since they might create impressions made by the hands.

The resting trace, from the Early Jurassic, preserves exactly that unusual posture. Its bird-like anatomy, posture, and behavior are read from the marks the animal left as it settled. Tracks are behavior frozen in stone: they show what an animal did, not just how it was built. This one documents a rest pose that bones alone could never prove.
plos-pone-0004691:
Frédéric Pagès and colleagues named the mosquito behind a 2007 chikungunya outbreak in Gabon, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Chikungunya is a virus spread by mosquito bites that causes fever and joint pain. The outbreak struck Libreville, the capital of Gabon, and its source vector was in doubt.

The team trapped mosquitoes near a French army camp close to the city. They found the virus in tiger mosquitoes and matched it to the human strain in cases. Naming the true vector guides spray and control work. It also warns nearby towns which mosquito to watch. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail.
plos-pone-0004791:
Gustavo Martínez-Mekler and colleagues tested whether rank ordering distributions share a universal form in arts and sciences, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Searching for generic behaviors has driven deep understanding across many fields. A starting point is often a phenomenology built from observations, as with power law distributions that appear in word use. City sizes, and many natural and social systems.

The team asked if one rank form fits many domains at once. A shared form would let scholars compare fields with one ruler. It could also reveal common forces behind success and fame. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings.
plos-pone-0004891:
Shibichakravarthy Kannan and colleagues showed alveolar lining type II cells activate macrophages and mitigate Pseudomonas infection, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Alveolar lining type II cells maintain alveolar integrity, but extent of roles to immune defense was poorly understood. The team shows lining cells activate alveolar macrophage functions such as microbe killing, improving control of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection in lung models of pneumonia.

Epithelium is an immune partner, not just barrier. Crosstalk amplifies macrophage performance substantially. Pneumonia therapies might boost lining signals. Lung defense is cooperative. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0004991:
Dengue virus is a serious mosquito-borne pathogen. It causes classic dengue fever and a severe hemorrhagic form. Nearly half the world's population is at risk. Wayne Crill and colleagues mapped patient antibody responses in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used virus-like particles carrying serotype-2 antigens. The antigens were built to present specific epitopes.

The study charted which viral targets patients' antibodies actually hit. That map shows what a real immune response looks like. It distinguishes responses in classic fever from severe disease. The work feeds the design of safer dengue vaccines. Knowing the targets helps avoid the responses that make second infections worse.
plos-pone-0005091:
The same gray patch can look light or dark. Its surroundings decide which. David Corney and colleagues studied a related trick in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked how a stimulus's color alters its brightness. This effect is less known than the classic context effect. It is equally important for understanding vision.

Color changed how bright the same stimulus appeared. Brightness is not a raw measurement by the eye. It is a construction built from context and color together. The study maps that construction more fully. Vision scientists use such effects to infer the brain's computations. What we see is the brain's best interpretation, not a camera's record. This paper adds color's vote to that interpretation.
plos-pone-0005191:
Chlamydia trachomatis is a common germ that infects human cells and cycles through distinct life stages. One of its surface proteins, PmpD, looks like transport proteins in other bacteria and may be a vaccine target. Kiselev and colleagues tracked that protein in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team followed how PmpD is made and trimmed after production across the germ's life cycle. They did so in three strains of the species, named A, D, and L2. Knowing when the protein is exposed on the surface helps vaccine designers pick the right moment and form to target.
plos-pone-0005291:
How much do predators and grazers shape whole ecosystems, beyond simply eating other species? Altieri and colleagues studied a natural marine ecosystem in PLOS ONE in 2009 and found consumers in charge of both its diversity and its functioning.

Earlier biodiversity work often counted species while ignoring who eats whom, and used artificial test communities. Working in a real system, the team showed consumer effects run deep. The result puts feeding interactions at the center of how marine communities are organized and kept diverse. The sea floor and salt marsh alike show this rule: who eats whom can matter as much as how many kinds of life a place holds at one time.
plos-pone-0005391:
In shock, blood vessels leak fluid and proteins into tissues, and extensive leak can kill. The barrier is built from contacts between endothelial cells, controlled by Rho-family switches. Gröger and colleagues tested a natural peptide, B-beta 15-42, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The peptide preserved endothelial barrier function during shock in their tests. Keeping vessel walls sealed holds fluid inside circulation where it belongs. A fragment of a natural blood protein acting as a barrier guard is a candidate for intensive care use. Vessel leak is a shared last path in burns, sepsis,. Bad wounds, so a guard that holds the wall in shock could find use far past one ward or one kind of case.
plos-pone-0005491:
Agnès Petit-Paitel and co-authors studied nerve cell death in a Parkinson model for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. In Parkinson's disease, nerve cells that make dopamine slowly die. A toxin called MPP plus, drawn from a drug that caused Parkinson-like illness, harms the energy centres of those cells.

The team tracked a protein called GSK-3 beta in both the cell body and its energy centres. They linked its activity in both places to the failure of those centres and to cell death. That makes the protein a possible target for drugs aiming to slow the disease.
plos-pone-0005591:
Xiaoning Peng and co-authors reviewed the link between male subfertility and testicular cancer in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Several studies had suggested that men who have trouble fathering children face a higher risk of testicular cancer. Other studies disagreed, leaving the claim unsettled.

The authors pooled the evidence across studies to get a sharper estimate of the risk. A pooled review can show whether the link is real and how strong it is. The answer matters for how doctors counsel and monitor subfertile men. Pooled results still cannot prove cause, but they can show whether doctors should watch this group more closely.
plos-pone-0005691:
Jeremy Goldhaber-Fiebert and co-authors weighed the cost of helping South African women stick with cervical cancer screening in 2009. A screening visit only helps if a woman returns for results and care. Home visits by community health workers can raise that return rate.

The team linked spending on home visits to how much adherence rose. They then asked what level of spending buys health gains worth their price. Cervical cancer is a major killer where screening is thin, so small gains in follow-through save lives. The study gives planners a way to set visit budgets with eyes open.
plos-pone-0005791:
Elisson Romanel and co-authors traced the family history of the B3 DNA-binding group in 2009. This superfamily includes five gene families that steer plant development, from hormone response to seed growth. With many plant genomes newly read, the team could rebuild how the families split and spread.

Their focus fell on the REM family, the least charted of the five. The analysis shows how REM genes multiplied and diversified across plant lineages. Such histories help breeders predict a gene's job in a new crop from its kin. The paper adds order to a large, tangled plant gene clan.
plos-pone-0005891:
Weijiang Luan and co-authors examined in 2009 how day length and temperature together set rice flowering time. Heading date decides whether rice matures before cold or drought ends the season. Day length effects were well studied; temperature control at the molecular level was not.

The team probed the crosstalk between the two signals in heading-date genes. Their interaction means a variety tuned for one climate may misfire in another. Breeders facing warming climates need exactly this wiring diagram. The study adds the temperature half of a trait that decides harvest success across Asia.
plos-pone-0005991:
Beyond rods and cones, the human eye holds a third kind of light sensor. Ludovic Mure, Pierre-Loic Cornut, Camille Rieux and colleagues studied its pigment, melanopsin, in 2009. Melanopsin sits in ganglion cells of the retina and helps set the body clock. Their PLOS ONE paper asks how the pigment answers light.

Like the pigments in a fly's eye, melanopsin turns out to be bistable: it flips between two states, each answering light in its own way. A two-state pigment can both sense light and reset itself. The fly-like design in a human pigment links insect and human vision, and it helps explain how the clock cells keep time by daylight.
plos-pone-0006091:
A parent's sense of safety on the street may reach into a child's lungs. Subramanian and Malinda Kennedy tested that reach in 2009 with a national survey. Their PLOS ONE paper links parental perception of neighborhood safety with reported lifetime asthma among children across the United States, against a backdrop of work tying psychosocial stress to asthma.

Neighborhoods can be a steady source of stress, and stress is a known asthma suspect. A link at national scale would widen asthma policy beyond air and allergens, into housing and street safety. The study asks doctors and planners to read a child's breathing as a sign of the place the child grows up in.
plos-pone-0006191:
Signals that guide embryo growth must be kept on a tight leash. Susie Zoltewicz and colleagues studied Wnt signals, which help build the front of the brain, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Too much Wnt activity in the wrong place causes severe brain defects, and a gene called oto normally prevents that loss.

The team shows the cell's protein factory, the endoplasmic reticulum, holds Wnt back as part of the control system. Retention inside the cell tunes how much signal gets out. The finding adds a new brake to a pathway used across development. It may also matter for diseases where Wnt signals run too hot.
plos-pone-0006291:
Automated systems now label the genes of new genomes at high speed, with little checking. Peter Bakke and colleagues compared three automated annotation systems on one genome in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their subject was Halorhabdus utahensis, a salt-loving microbe, and no systematic comparison had been done before.

Errors in annotations are routine and then spread into every study that reuses them. Measuring each system's mistakes shows where human review matters most. The comparison gives genome centres a basis for improving their pipelines. It also warns users to treat automated labels as drafts, not facts.
plos-pone-0006391:
Diverse immune genes are linked to fitness in many species, but humans are harder to test. Hanne Lie, Leigh Simmons, and Gillian Rhodes asked whether genetic diversity predicts health in humans in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Diversity at the Major Histocompatibility Complex, key immune genes, has been associated with disease resistance across species.

The study tests that association directly in people. Mate preference research had hinted at diversity benefits in humans too. Confirming or rejecting the link shapes evolutionary accounts of human immunity. Health is the outcome that matters most for the claim.
plos-pone-0006491:
Behnam Nabet, Arthur Tsai, John Tobias, and colleagues mapped proteins in kidney filter cells for PLOS ONE in 2009. The glomerular podocyte is a specialized kidney cell with major processes and foot processes. Those feet wrap capillaries and form the filter that keeps protein out of urine. Their shape depends on the actin skeleton inside the cell.

The team identified a putative network of actin-associated cytoskeletal proteins in podocytes. A defined network gives targets for explaining foot process failure in kidney disease. When the filter fails, protein leaks and kidneys scar. Mapping the skeleton is a step toward protecting it.
plos-pone-0006591:
Giuseppe Battaglia and co-authors tested a receptor target in brain cells for PLOS ONE in 2009. Metabotropic glutamate receptors have been considered potential targets for therapy of experimental parkinsonism. One hypothetical advantage of using them is avoiding side effects of standard drugs. The team focused on mGlu3 receptors in striatal neurons.

Their title reports that activation of mGlu3 receptors stimulates production of GDNF in striatal neurons. GDNF is a survival factor for dopamine neurons, the cells lost in Parkinson's disease. A drug that raises the brain's own GDNF could protect those cells. The study links a druggable receptor to a protective factor.
plos-pone-0006691:
Pål K. Selbo and co-authors combined light-based delivery with a fusion toxin in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many cancer drugs get trapped inside cell compartments after uptake. Trapped drugs cannot reach their targets in the cell's main space. The team used photochemical internalization to break that trap. Light activates a sensitizer that opens the compartments and frees the drug.

The freed drug here was a fusion toxin called scFvMEL/rGel. It pairs a targeting antibody fragment with a cell-killing enzyme. Combining the toxin with light treatment produced strong anti-tumor effects. The strategy amounts to multi-modality therapy, attacking cancer two ways at once. It may improve other drugs that suffer from the same trapping problem.
plos-pone-0006791:
Michael Linderman, Mikhail A. Lebedev, and Joseph S. Erlichman recognized handwriting from muscle signals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Handwriting matters culturally and as a scientific tool. It serves recognition research, graphology, and medical diagnostics. Earlier studies leaned on observing the finished writing or the pen. Muscle activity during writing was a less used signal.

The team recorded electromyography from the arm during writing. Patterns in those signals identified what was written. The approach works without watching the hand itself. It could aid people who cannot hold a pen conventionally. It also opens new ways to study the motor control of writing.
plos-pone-0006891:
Shawn C. Oppegard and colleagues built a device to control oxygen over cultured cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Oxygen modulates many cellular pathways. Existing devices for changing oxygen in vitro meet research needs poorly. Control over timing and spatial pattern is especially weak. Biomedical studies of oxygen sensing need better tools.

Their microfabricated insert fits standard multiwell plates. It modulates oxygenation over adherent cell cultures in time and space. Researchers can now mimic waves or patches of low oxygen. Such patterns occur in wounds, tumors, and exercising muscle. Better control should sharpen every experiment where oxygen is the variable.
plos-pone-0006991:
Elli Rosenberg, Amir Ben-Shmuel, Oshrit Shalev, and colleagues studied malaria parasite genes under stress in PLOS ONE in 2009. About one in a hundred genes of Plasmodium falciparum belongs to the var family. These genes build a surface protein that sticks infected red cells to vessel walls. That sticking is part of how malaria makes people so sick.

The team stressed the parasites and watched var gene activity. The response differed by each gene's position in the genome. Position-dependent switching helps the parasite vary its surface and dodge immunity. Understanding the pattern may expose weak points in that disguise system.
plos-pone-0007091:
Huchun Li, Masayuki Sekine, Seyha Seng, and colleagues studied a famous cancer gene in PLOS ONE in 2009. BRCA1 is a key guardian of the genome. It helps run cell cycle checkpoints and DNA damage repair. The growth signal TGF-beta is a potent regulator of cell growth and tissue form. Their crosstalk was the subject here.

The team showed BRCA1 interacts with Smad3, a carrier of the TGF-beta signal. BRCA1 then tunes that signaling during oxidative stress responses. The link joins two major protective systems. It may matter for breast and ovarian cancers where BRCA1 is lost.
plos-pone-0007191:
Rosanna Capparelli, Alessandra Romanelli, Marco Iannaccone, and colleagues studied frog skin peptides as infection fighters in PLOS ONE in 2009. The peptides are called temporins. The European red frog secretes them from glands in its skin, and they act mainly against gram-positive bacteria.
