The team tested temporin A together with a modified form of temporin B in living animals. They report that the pair showed combined antibacterial and anti-inflammatory activity. Their work suggests that pairing natural peptides can do more than either single peptide does alone against infection and inflammation.
plos-pone-0007291:
Zhanghan Wu, Hong-Wei Wang, Weihua Mu, and colleagues simulated building blocks of microtubules in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Microtubules are hollow tubes that shape cells and move chromosomes. Their assembly has been studied for decades, but the underlying molecular mechanism remained poorly understood at the time.

An artificial sheet polymer can convert directly into microtubules. That sheet may be a structural intermediate in natural assembly. The authors simulate tubulin sheet polymers to test that idea. Their simulations show possible steps in microtubule formation. Cell biologists can use those steps to interpret real assembly images.
plos-pone-0007391:
Albert Wong built growth-factor-sensing drug carriers in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Cancers often overexpress EGF and other growth factors. Those signals promote cell replication and migration, helping tumors grow and spread through surrounding tissue in many common cancers treated in clinics.

Previous work had not produced targeted carriers sensitive to abnormal growth factor amounts. Wong demonstrates liposomes bearing modified EGF receptors, called MRBLs. These fat bubbles carry receptors crosslinked onto their surface. They respond to EGF in solution. Such carriers could one day release drugs only where growth factor levels are abnormally high.
plos-pone-0007491:
Timothy Gershon and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on nerve tumors that arise in children. Peripheral neuroblastic tumors share an origin in the sympathetic nervous system. At one extreme, neuroblastoma is malignant and dangerous. At the other, ganglioneuroma is benign. What pushes a tumor toward the mild end was the team's question, with a focus on gut nerve development.

They found that tumors maturing toward ganglioneuroma show signs of enteric neural crest differentiation. That maturation program involves Hedgehog signaling, a pathway known from embryo development. The clue suggests the same signal helps decide which path these tumors take. If a signal guides tumors toward the benign state, boosting it could become a treatment idea. The study links developmental biology directly to cancer behavior.
plos-pone-0007591:
Shie Hong Chang and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a signaling pathway that sculpts hair and glands. The skin carries many appendages, from hair follicles to sweat and mammary glands. All develop under EDAR signaling. A gain-of-function version of the EDAR gene is common in East Asian populations, with signs of recent selection. The team boosted Edar signaling in mice and mapped the consequences.

Enhanced signaling had pleiotropic effects, touching many traits at once. Craniofacial features changed along with the cutaneous glands. One pathway thus reshapes a whole suite of visible traits. That breadth helps explain the human variant's spread and its linked differences in hair and glands. The mouse work shows what turning a single dial does to a face and skin. It connects a gene variant to the anatomy it builds.
plos-pone-0007691: Uganda's HIV got a family-planning angle. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Hladik's team measured family planning's contribution to preventing mother-to-child HIV in Uganda. The prevention share was estimated. The angle feeds HIV policy.
plos-pone-0007791:
Aner Gurvitz published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It builds a worm model for an enzyme system that makes fats inside mitochondria. Mitochondria are better known for burning fuel than building fat. Yet they run their own fatty acid synthase, called type II.

When that system falters in mammals, health suffers. The author identifies the worm gene W09H1.5, also called mecr-1, as coding a key enzyme in the system. The gene is also linked to longevity in the worm C. elegans. A simple worm model lets researchers probe mitochondrial fat synthesis and aging together.
plos-pone-0007891:
Bryan Kolaczkowski and Joseph Thornton published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It warns of a bias in a popular way to infer evolutionary trees. Bayesian inference builds trees using probability models of evolution. It was generally assumed to share the good statistical properties of maximum likelihood methods.

One known trap is long-branch attraction, where fast-evolving lineages get wrongly grouped. The authors show Bayesian inference can suffer this bias and inconsistency too. Their result matters because many published family trees rest on Bayesian methods. Knowing the trap tells researchers when to double-check a surprising tree.
plos-pone-0007991:
Guy Cheron and colleagues listened to rhythm cells deep in the movement brain of living mice for PLOS ONE in 2009. The cerebellum times fine movement, and two of its cell types, Purkinje and Golgi cells, fire in steady beats. Calcium signals help set those beats.

Channels called BK, which open in answer to calcium, proved to run the beat in both cell types. When the channels' work changed, the rhythm changed with it. The result names a part that keeps the movement brain's clock, with hints for disorders where that timing slips.
plos-pone-0008091:
Dionicia Gamboa and colleagues sounded an alarm about malaria tests in Peru's Amazon in PLOS ONE in 2010. Quick malaria tests look for a parasite protein called HRP2. Clinics across South America were adopting those tests as the front line for diagnosis.

Many parasite samples from the region lacked the genes for that protein and its sibling. A test hunting a missing protein will call sick people healthy. The share lacking the genes was large enough to threaten the whole plan. The authors urge checks of gene loss before tests are rolled out.
plos-pone-0008191:
Svetlana Sarantseva and colleagues tested a treatment idea for Alzheimer's disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some inherited forms of the disease stem from faults in the amyloid precursor protein gene. Those faults can raise production of amyloid-beta, a protein linked to the disease. The team used fruit flies changed to model this condition.

Compounds that mimic apolipoprotein E were given to the flies. In the model, these mimetics slowed nerve cell loss. They also restored cognitive functions in the flies. The results suggest a path worth testing further. They do not prove a human cure, but they mark a lead.
plos-pone-0008291:
Sonia Lacroix-Lamandé and her team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about the gut of the newborn. Shots that work through the mouth or nose could stop germs where they first enter the body. Such shots lack good boosters, which are added parts that make a shot work better. Short bits of lab-made DNA, called CpG ODNs, are one type of booster now in tests.

The team asked how the gut of a newborn mouse pup reacts to these DNA bits. Pups do not react to shots in the same way grown mice do, so age had to be part of the test. A clear gut response in pups would back use of this booster in shots for the very young. The work fills a gap in care for small babies.
plos-pone-0008391:
Tomonaga Ichikawa and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about a shield for heart cells. A cell switch called Nrf2 guards cells from harm done by oxygen stress. Drugs that turn this switch on could help a weak heart that grows stiff and thick with time. But such drug use in the heart and blood system was not yet firm ground. The team made a new compound, dh404, that turns Nrf2 on.

In heart muscle cells, dh404 cut the harm from oxygen stress by a wide mark. Cells kept safe in this way may hold up when the heart is strained. A new switch-turner gives labs a tool to probe this guard path. It may in time lead to new drugs for heart failure.
plos-pone-0008491:
Allen Day and co-authors present a tool for gene study in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. After the genome was read, a major goal was to learn what each gene does. Their tool is called the UCLA Gene Expression Tool, or UGET. It rests on Celsius, a very large dataset of gene activity measures. Those measures come from many lab samples, aligned in one system.

The tool looks at genes that switch on and off together. Such co-expression across many samples hints at shared roles. The team use it to characterize genes for diseases. The approach lets researchers form testable ideas about unknown genes at scale.
plos-pone-0008591:
Saikat Chakrabarti and co-authors study coevolved sites in proteins in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Residue covariations between positions in protein families are crucial signals. Simultaneous changes, or residue coevolution, let a protein maintain its structure and function. When one site mutates, a partner site may change to compensate. The team examine structural and functional roles of such coevolved sites. They use data from many protein families.

They show coevolved sites cluster at key structural and active regions. Those sites help design protein engineering experiments. Predicting them can guide mutations that preserve function. The work turns an evolutionary pattern into a practical engineering tool.
plos-pone-0008691:
Ruth Krebs, Marty Woldorff, Claus Tempelmann, and colleagues peered at a small brain hub that steers the eyes. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used a strong form of brain scanning. The hub, the superior colliculus, helps launch quick eye jumps called saccades. Most earlier knowledge came from animal studies with fine electrodes. Human evidence was thin.

Volunteers made eye movements while the scanner watched their brains. High-field imaging gave a sharper view of this deep, small structure. The scans showed which parts lit up during a saccade. A human map of the hub helps link animal findings to vision science in people.
plos-pone-0008791:
Elise Glattard, Ingeborg Welters, Thomas Lavaux, and colleagues measured the body's own morphine during severe infection. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human cells can make small amounts of morphine themselves. Neutrophils, front-line white blood cells, release it when fed its building blocks. What that homemade morphine does in inflammation was unclear. Sepsis, a runaway infection response, offered a strong test case.

Morphine levels rose in patients with sepsis. Neutrophils accounted for part of that rise. The finding hints the body doses itself during crisis. Whether that self-dosing calms or harms sepsis patients remains an open question.
plos-pone-0008891:
Jianfang Hu, Qian Qi, and Avery August traced how a signal amplifier steers young T cells toward one fate. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. T cells mature in the thymus under receptor signals and surroundings. A kinase called Itk amplifies the receptor's messages. Losing Itk disturbs most stages of that maturation. One decision sends cells toward the CD4 helper line. A switch protein, Th-POK, enforces that decision.

Signals through Itk controlled how much Th-POK the cells made. That control, in turn, shaped CD4 T cell development. A named chain from receptor to fate switch clarifies immune development. It may help correct T cell defects.
plos-pone-0008991:
Harald Striegl, Miguel Andrade-Navarro, and Udo Heinemann reviewed a family of building-block proteins that move cell cargo, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Armadillo repeat proteins are built from a repeated sequence that folds into a sturdy shape. Cells use them in several jobs, including ferrying cargo in tiny membrane bubbles. They also help tether those vesicles where they need to dock.

The paper gathers what is known about armadillo motifs in vesicular transport. It compares family members and the transport steps each one supports. Sorting cargo correctly keeps cells fed, tidy, and able to send signals. A clear map of the players helps researchers spot what breaks in transport diseases.
plos-pone-0009091:
Angel Moreno-Torres and co-authors probed aching forearms in musicians who play for a living, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Repetitive light work often brings non-specific pain in upper limb muscles. The finger extensor muscles open the hand and work constantly in instrumentalists. Little was known about the chemistry inside those sore muscles.

The team compared muscle energy metabolism during exercise. Sore muscles split their acidity into compartments oddly as they worked. That pH compartmentation tracked with the players' work-related pain. Hidden chemistry, not visible damage, may explain this common occupational complaint.
plos-pone-0009191:
Irina Druzhinina and colleagues published this fungal evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Its subject is Trichoderma reesei, a green mould used in factories worldwide. The mould makes cellulases, enzymes that break down plant fiber. Industry has relied on it since a single sample was found in the Solomon Islands during World War II.

The mould is the asexual stage of a common tropical fungus called Hypocrea jecorina. The authors traced how the species evolved and how it lives in nature. They also describe a new close relative that lives in the same places but never mates. Together, the work explains the family history behind a workhorse of the enzyme industry.
plos-pone-0009291:
Joo Chuan Tong and co-authors published this virus evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chikungunya fever, spread by mosquitoes, came roaring back after two quiet decades. Outbreaks swept Africa, Indian Ocean islands, and Asia, making many people ill. Early family trees of the virus, built from partial sequences, raised questions about what drove its spread.

The authors proposed that human HLA genes help steer the virus's evolution. HLA proteins show virus pieces to the immune system, and they vary between people. If the virus adapts to common HLA types, that pressure could shape its family tree. The idea links a population's immune genes to the path an epidemic takes.
plos-pone-0009391:
Venkataramanan Soundararajan and co-authors published this protein structure study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Proteins with wildly different sequences often fold into the same shape. What stays constant across such a family was the puzzle. The authors examined proteins fold by fold across the whole protein universe.

They report that networks of atomic contacts in a domain's core are conserved. Even when sequences drift, the inner web of touches holds its pattern. That conserved core is like the frame of a house under many different facades. Knowing it helps predict structure and understand how folds survive evolution.
plos-pone-0009491:
Laila Woc-Colburn and co-authors checked a key immune task in people with HIV in PLOS ONE in 2010. Helper T cells need other cells to show them pieces of germs before they act. That showing uses a system called MHC class II. HIV can harm many immune tasks. The team tested whether monocytes from infected people could still process and present such pieces.

They found that this task stayed intact in the monocytes they studied. So not every part of the immune display system fails in HIV. A working pathway is good news for vaccine and treatment design. Therapies could build on the parts that the virus leaves standing.
plos-pone-0009591:
Hasmik Mkrtchyan and colleagues looked at single cells in human tissues in PLOS ONE in 2010. People differ in how many copies of some DNA stretches they carry. Those copy number differences were thought to come from inheritance. This team checked single cells from several tissues of the same persons. They found copy differences arising early in the embryo.

Such early changes leave a mosaic pattern that lasts in adult tissues. In a mosaic, neighboring cells carry slightly different genomes. The finding shifts the origin of much copy variation to before birth. It may help explain some disorders where only part of the body is affected.
plos-pone-0009691:
c-Myc is a protein that switches genes on and helps drive several cancers when it runs too hot. JinShui Fan and colleagues mapped its targets over time in human B cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. They used a method called array-based nuclear run-on to catch genes as they switched on.

The maps grouped Myc's targets into modules, sets of genes that rise and fall together. Watching the timing showed which genes Myc hits first and which follow later. A wiring diagram like this helps explain how one protein can steer cell growth so widely. It also points to steps where cancer drugs might intervene.
plos-pone-0009791:
Water voles are being returned to rivers where they had vanished. Merryl Gelling and colleagues asked whether captive housing before release harms the animals' welfare. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The species is Arvicola terrestris, a large riverside rodent.

Reintroduction programs often house wild animals together for a short time first. The team tested whether that short-term social stress hurt the voles. Welfare checks matter because stressed animals may fare worse after release. The findings help programs house voles in ways that protect them. Short stays in captivity are hard to avoid in such programs.
plos-pone-0009891:
In ulcerative colitis, gut inflammation flares and then should settle, but settling can lag. Farooq Rahman and colleagues traced why resolution is delayed in this bowel disease. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ulcerative colitis attacks the lining of the large intestine.

Delayed resolution was tied to elevated cytokine release downstream of TLR4. Cytokines are immune signal proteins, and TLR4 is a sensor that detects bacterial molecules. A stuck sensor can keep sending alarm signals after the trigger fades. The pathway points to targets for calming the gut. Slow settling means longer bouts of damage to the gut lining.
plos-pone-0009991:
How corn handles carbon at its core can hinge on one changed building block in one enzyme. Nengyi Zhang and colleagues traced such a change through maize metabolism. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. An amino acid is one of the building blocks of proteins.

Central carbon metabolism is the core chemistry that turns sugar into energy and materials. Genetic analysis unveiled an amino acid substitution that alters one enzyme's activity. The enzyme is maize NAD-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase. A single swap changing enzyme activity shows how finely metabolism is tuned.
plos-pone-0010191:
The authors were Andrea von Groll, Anandi Martin, Matthias Stehr, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study compared tuberculosis strains by their fitness. Multidrug-resistant TB is a major threat to global control efforts. One genotype, called W-Beijing, has been linked to drug resistance in many places. That raises a question: are those strains simply fitter than others?

The team measured fitness in W-Beijing and non-Beijing strains directly. Fitness here means how well a strain grows and competes against rivals. If resistant strains pay no fitness cost, they can spread even without drug pressure, which changes control strategy.
plos-pone-0010391:
Ulrich Leischner and co-workers reported a simple imaging trick for tissue samples in PLOS ONE in 2010. Viewing fine 3-D structure in large samples usually needs advanced microscopy. The team noticed that formalin, the common preserving fluid, changes how tissue glows. It makes spaces outside cells glow more, leaving cells as dark shapes. That contrast outlines cell shape clearly.

A preservative side effect thus became a staining method of sorts. Cells could be picked out by their dark silhouettes against bright surroundings. Cheap tricks matter in labs that cannot afford top-end scopes. They also remind researchers to look closely at familiar tools. Sometimes the sample jar already holds the method. The finding may ease shape studies in many tissue types.
plos-pone-0010491:
Stefan Bernhard and Frank Noé improved a method for finding semi-rigid parts inside large molecules in PLOS ONE in 2010. Proteins do their jobs by changing shape. Those changes move blocks of the molecule that stay fairly rigid inside. Spotting those blocks reliably from simulations is a standing challenge. The authors used molecular dynamics simulations, which track atoms over time.

Their method aims to identify the moving domains in an optimal way. Better domain maps help explain how proteins act as machines. They also guide drug design, since pockets often open at domain borders. The study is computational, tested on simulated motion. It offers other modelers a sharper tool for reading protein movement.
plos-pone-0010591:
Kaare Engkilde and colleagues ran an unexpected diabetes experiment in mice, published in PLOS ONE in 2010. NOD mice develop type 1 diabetes because their immune system attacks the pancreas. The team repeatedly exposed the mice to a chemical that causes a mild skin allergy.

Mice that got the skin treatment developed diabetes far less often. The mild, ongoing skin reaction seemed to steer the immune system away from the pancreas. No strong rash was needed, only repeated low-level exposure. The result suggests that carefully redirecting immune attention might one day help prevent autoimmune disease.
plos-pone-0010691:
Brett Crawford and colleagues studied a sugar-chain enzyme in mouse breast tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Branching ducts form many organs, and sugar chains called heparan sulfate guide that branching. The enzyme Ndst1 trims those chains in a key step.

When mammary cells lacked Ndst1, the gland's milk-making lobes failed to develop properly. Other parts of the gland formed as usual. So one trimming step controls one stage of growth, not the whole program. Stage-by-stage control like this helps explain how organs build complex shapes from simple tubes, one timed step at a time.
plos-pone-0010791:
Shimrit Perkol-Finkel and Laura Airoldi studied how underwater algal forests recover from loss, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Forests of large algae shelter fish and young sea life worldwide. These forests are shrinking under pollution, grazing, and warming. On the Adriatic coast, the team tested what lets a cleared patch regrow.

Experiments in the subtidal zone varied the state of the surrounding forest. Recovery was strongest where healthy forest stood nearby to supply spores and shade young growth. Isolated clearings recovered poorly, even when conditions improved. The lesson for restoration is plain: protect the remaining forest first, because it is the seed bank for everything else.
plos-pone-0010891:
Matthew Alkaitis, Carlos Solorzano, Russell Landry and co-authors published this pain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many patients keep hurting long after surgery heals, and the switch from short-term to chronic pain is poorly understood. The authors studied the body's own cannabis-like chemicals, which normally dampen pain signaling through two receptor types.

Working with rats that had a paw incision, a model of surgical pain that fades on its own, they tracked how these chemicals and spinal cord support cells behave over time. Earlier work showed that boosting one receptor type reversed both pain sensitivity and signs of glial activation. The new results point to the body's own system helping pain resolve by calming inflammatory signaling in spinal glia. Alkaitis and colleagues suggest aiding that natural shut-off could prevent chronic post-surgical pain.
plos-pone-0010991:
Viviane Lima, Robert Hogg and Julio Montaner published this HIV policy modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. New global guidelines in 2008 greatly widened who should start HIV therapy. British Columbia faced the question of what full use of them would buy. Its epidemic is concentrated among gay men and people who inject drugs.

The authors built a transmission model comparing treatment coverage levels under the new guidelines against the existing baseline. Scenarios ranged from half to full coverage of everyone medically eligible. Drug costs were counted in Canadian dollars. The model also allowed for the large share of infected people unaware of their status. Lima and colleagues estimate the effects on new infections, illness, and deaths. Their analysis supports treating earlier and wider as both a clinical and a prevention strategy.
plos-pone-0011091:
Makela, Koivuniemi, Korhonen and colleagues published brain cell research in PLOS ONE in 2010. They studied young nerve cells that can grow into new brain tissue. Two signals acted on those cells in the brain: one made by immune cells there, and a small protective peptide.

The immune signal harmed the young cells and lowered their survival. The peptide, called PACAP, had the opposite effect and helped keep them alive. Together the results show a tug of war over cells needed for brain repair. Knowing both sides could guide efforts to protect or rebuild brain tissue after injury.
plos-pone-0011191:
Brumm, Farrington and Petren studied a rare finch in PLOS ONE in 2010. On the Galapagos Islands, one of Darwin's finches has dwindled to very low numbers. The team examined how its mating signals, especially song, have diverged from its close relatives over time.

That divergence may now trap the species, since split signals can block mating with any partner group. The authors frame the case as an evolutionary dead end. It warns conservation teams that saving a species may require managing genes and signals, not just habitat. The rarest finch thus teaches a broader lesson about small populations.
plos-pone-0011291:
Ahmad and Lim defined a protein's built in brake in PLOS ONE in 2010. Intersectin helps cells pull cargo inward and also acts as an exchange factor that switches on other proteins. Left unchecked, that activity would fire at the wrong times. The protein restrains itself through an internal inhibited state.

The team found the smallest unit of the protein that still carries that self restraint. Defining the minimal unit clarifies how the brake works at molecular level. That explains part of how cells control cargo uptake. Such self regulation is a recurring theme in cell biology, and precise borders help future drug and mutant studies.
plos-pone-0011391:
Lise Madsen and co-authors reported in 2010 on what it takes to recruit heat-making fat cells inside ordinary white fat. Brown fat burns energy as heat, and coaxing white fat to grow brown-like cells is a hoped-for route to weight control. The switch depends on a heat protein that must be turned on during the change.

The team found that turning on that protein during recruitment requires active cyclooxygenase enzymes, the same enzymes that common pain drugs block. That dependence links a familiar drug target to the body's energy-burning machinery. It raises a practical caution and an opportunity. Pain drug use might affect fat browning, while tuning the same pathway might one day help grow more heat-making cells. Either way, fat research must now reckon with this enzyme step.
plos-pone-0011491:
Mirela Kuka and co-authors found in 2010 that a family of enzymes is required to keep two immune alarms in balance. Dendritic cells, the sentries that start immune responses, release IL-12 and IL-23 when their Toll-like receptors are triggered. The balance between the two alarms shapes what kind of response follows, steering defense toward different threats.

Without Src kinases, the dendritic cells could not produce the two alarms in their normal balanced output. The kinases thus act as a control point where the flavor of immunity is set. That control point interests drug designers, since many diseases involve too much of one alarm relative to the other. Tuning a shared upstream kinase might rebalance the response more gently than blocking either alarm outright, preserving defense while easing disease.
plos-pone-0011591:
Scott Lane and colleagues used brain scans to study choice-making in cocaine dependence for PLOS ONE in 2010. Long-term stimulant use is linked to poor decisions and to changes in both grey and white matter in the brain. The team wondered whether damage to the brain's wiring helps explain the faulty choices.

They used diffusion tensor imaging, a scan that maps the fibre tracts linking brain regions, in a small group of cocaine-dependent adults. They then related the wiring measures to how those adults made decisions. The work links the physical state of brain connections to a behaviour that helps keep addiction going.
plos-pone-0011691:
Nan-Hua Chang and co-authors studied how immune tolerance breaks down in lupus-prone mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. New Zealand Black mice develop autoantibodies, a sign their B cells attack the body's own tissues as happens in lupus. Whether a failure of B cell silencing, called anergy, lies behind that defect was unknown.

The team showed that a B cell growth signal, BAFF, together with T cells, breaches that tolerance. Neither factor acting in the usual protected setting fully explained the breakdown, but their cooperation did. The two-hit picture helps explain how self-attack gets its green light in autoimmune disease.
plos-pone-0011791:
Lili Zhang and co-authors studied fast estrogen signals in lab-grown neurons, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Estrogens are used a lot to treat hot flashes in menopause. Some of the brain gains from hormone therapy may come from quick, non-gene effects, such as sparking calcium waves in neurons. Most past work had looked at other estrogen receptors.

Drugs that pick out estrogen receptor beta set off calcium waves in neurons grown from stem cells of both humans and mice. The rhythmic waves show a fast signal route at work in young neurons. That route may help explain how estrogen acts on the brain.
plos-pone-0011891:
Carol Devney, Julian Caley, and Bradley Congdon studied in 2010 how a tropical seabird copes when the sea runs unusually warm. The black noddy nests on islands and feeds offshore, so warm surface water can push its prey deeper or farther away. The team watched adult foraging and chick growth across two breeding seasons with different conditions.

Parents adjusted their foraging behavior, and chicks developed differently, when warm anomalies struck. Such flexibility, called plasticity, can buffer a species against climate swings, but only up to a point. Recording where that buffer holds in noddies helps forecast which seabirds are most exposed as ocean heat events grow more common.
plos-pone-0011991:
Barak Rotblat and co-workers showed in 2010 that the stability of tiny protein clusters on the cell surface sets the strength of a growth signal. H-Ras is a switch protein that triggers several pathways, including the MAPK pathway that drives cell division. Active H-Ras gathers into nanoclusters in the cell membrane, and their arrangement shapes the output.

The team found that how long those clusters hold together regulates how much MAPK signal comes out. Signal strength, not just on or off, decides cell behavior, so a physical cluster becomes a volume dial. That mechanism is relevant to cancer, where Ras switches are among the most common faulty parts.
plos-pone-0012091:
Alison Chow, Jocelyn Liang, Janice Wong, and colleagues examined human airway cells in a PLOS ONE study from 2010. They used a lab-grown airway cell line and challenged it with charged protein pieces like those released by immune cells during asthma attacks. The question was how the airway lining answers such an attack, and whether its answer goes out in all directions or only some.

The team tracked two signal proteins the cells release when stressed. They found the release is uneven, aimed more toward one side of the cell layer than the other. That aim may shape where swelling and mucus build up in an inflamed airway, a detail that matters for understanding asthma at the tissue level.
plos-pone-0012191:
Shengli Ding, Michael Chi, Brooks Scull, and co-authors traced how a fatty diet inflames the gut in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Obesity from rich diets travels with inflammation that dulls the body's response to insulin, a step toward diabetes. Most research blamed fat tissue itself for that inflammation, but gut bacteria had begun to look like an earlier trigger.

The team found gut inflammation arriving before obesity and insulin trouble, closely tracking both. An early gut signal changes where prevention should aim: calm the intestine and the later steps may never start. It also strengthens the case that the microbes we feed shape metabolic disease from the very beginning.
plos-pone-0012291:
Tatia Lee, Tiffany Lee, Adrian Raine, and co-authors scanned the brains of men asked to lie about feelings, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Thirteen healthy volunteers viewed pictures that were pleasant or unpleasant and, on cue, misreported which kind each was. Brain imaging during this small, deliberate dishonesty can show which regions work when a true emotional judgment is overridden by a false one.

Lying about emotion is not the same as lying about facts, and this design separates the two. The regions involved likely serve self-control and conflict monitoring as much as deceit itself. Studies this focused give lie-detection claims a needed reality check: the brain activity of lying is entangled with ordinary effort, not a single dishonesty center.
plos-pone-0012391:
Timothy York, Jerome Strauss, Michael Neale and colleagues weighed genes and environment in early birth in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Babies born too early face high risks, and in the United States the burden falls much more heavily on African American families. Social factors alone do not explain the gap, and gene studies had not yet pinned down the mix of causes.

Using family and population data, the authors split the risk into genetic and environmental parts for each group. Both parts mattered, and their balance differed between groups. That split matters for prevention: it argues against one-size programs and for research that measures genes and living conditions together.
plos-pone-0012491:
Nigel Brothers, Alan Duckworth, Carl Safina and colleagues showed that seabird deaths in longline fisheries are badly undercounted, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Hundreds of thousands of seabirds drown on baited hooks each year. Official counts usually come from hauling the line in, but most birds are caught while the line is being set, and many fall off before hauling.

By observing the setting process directly, the team found true mortality far above haul-based figures. Undercounting hides the scale of a threat that is pushing some albatross species toward extinction. Honest counts strengthen the case for simple fixes, like weighted lines and night setting, that fleets resist without proof.
plos-pone-0012591:
Yanlong Cong, Guangmei Wang, Zhenhong Guan and colleagues reported a mixed flu virus in pigs, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Human-like H3N2 influenza viruses have repeatedly jumped into domestic pigs around the world. Pigs can host both human and bird flu strains at once, giving the viruses a chance to swap gene segments and create new combinations, called reassortants.

The team identified a reassortant carrying human-like H3N2 and avian H5 segments in pigs and flagged it as a potential public health risk. An H5-bearing virus adapted to mammals is precisely what pandemic watchers fear. Surveillance of pig herds is therefore front-line defense, not a veterinary side issue.
plos-pone-0012691:
Pham, Fazio, Cucullo and co-authors tested whether sources outside the brain muddy a blood marker of brain injury. The protein S100B leaks from the brain when the blood-brain barrier breaks, and doctors read it in blood. Their 2010 study asked if tissues outside the skull also release it and distort the reading.

They report that these outside sources do not in fact change blood levels in a meaningful way. That clears a doubt hanging over a handy test for brain injury and barrier damage. Cleaner markers mean faster, surer calls in emergency care.
plos-pone-0012891:
Vagenas, Aravantinou, Williams and co-authors tested a therapeutic vaccine meant to hold the monkey AIDS virus down after drugs stop. HIV patients depend on antiretroviral therapy for life, since the virus rebounds when drugs pause. A vaccine that keeps levels low after stopping would ease that dependence.

Their 2010 study gave a tonsil-delivered vaccine, combining a PolyICLC adjuvant with inactivated SIV, to treated animals. After therapy stopped, vaccinated animals kept low virus levels. Holding a virus down without daily drugs is a long-standing goal this result supports.  Virus levels were followed for months after drugs stopped.
plos-pone-0332491:
Eszter Holub and four colleagues compare two chemotherapy drugs in a 2026 cell study. Both drugs block thymidylate synthase, an enzyme cancer cells need to copy DNA. Blocking it corrupts the DNA building blocks and triggers cell death. The drugs studied are a fluorouridine compound and raltitrexed. The team used human colon cancer cells, including lines with damaged DNA repair systems.

Both drugs switched on DNA damage responses, as expected. Yet their wider effects on gene activity differed sharply. The fluorouridine drug strongly activated genes tied to p53, the cell's damage guardian, in every cell line. The other drug did not lean on that pathway in the same way. Protein tests confirmed the difference. Two drugs with the same main target can thus kill cells through partly different routes, which matters for choosing treatments and combinations.
plos-pone-0339691:
Ilhan Yoo and colleagues tested a deep learning system that reads needle electromyography signals, the electrical traces from muscles used to diagnose nerve and muscle disease. Human reading of these traces is slow and swayed by bias. Using three hundred seventy-six signals from fifty-seven patients at a university hospital, the model sorted patients into healthy, muscle disease, or nerve disease.

The model beat six experienced electromyographers on accuracy and every other score, reaching about seventy percent patient-level accuracy against the physicians' mid-fifties. Inspection showed it leaned on genuinely relevant signal features. One caution stood out: when the model was wrong, it was wrong in unison more often than the doctors, whose errors scattered. The study argues for AI as a second reader, not a replacement.
plos-pone-0341491:
Tobías Alfonso Parodi Camaño, Jhon Víctor Vidal Durango, and Ivan Portnoy ask whether a chief executive's self-love helps or harms a small firm's power to innovate. Their 2026 study surveys eighty-five companies in Colombia across many sectors. One survey measured bosses' self-admiring traits, and another rated each firm's innovation across products, processes, marketing, knowledge handling, and research spending.

Certain self-admiring traits lined up with stronger innovation in some areas and weaker showings in others. The pattern suggests such traits carry both spark and risk for a business. For owners and boards, the message is practical: pick and coach leaders with eyes open to which habits push new ideas and which ones crowd out other voices.
plos-pone-0343191:
Khondakar Shahriar proposes in 2026 a personalised system for estimating Parkinson's severity from speech recordings taken over time. Rating severity normally needs an in person visit and expert judgement, which limits how often patients can be checked. Speech changes early in the disease, so voice offers a remote window. The system learns each patient's own pattern and states its uncertainty openly.

On a held back set of unseen patients, severity estimates landed very close to expert scores, and a three stage grouping was sorted with high accuracy. The method beat standard learning and global time based rivals. Frequent home monitoring could become practical if wider tests confirm the result.
plos-pone-0343591:
Sanjiv Singh and colleagues asked what gets husbands involved in family planning in two districts of Uttar Pradesh, India, for this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The survey covered households of more than twelve hundred married women of childbearing age, and the authors argue a husband's role should mean joint decisions and support, not just using contraception himself.

About two-thirds of husbands joined decisions on family size, and over half backed their wives' contraceptive use. A positive attitude toward family planning and exposure to media messages were the strongest predictors of both, outweighing factors like religion or having a son. The authors suggest programs recruit supportive husbands as visible champions in their communities.
plos-pone-0343891:
Lin, Parry, and Killackey set out a review plan in 2026 on training needs for nurses who care for adults born with heart defects. Better childhood surgery means many more such patients now reach adult life, where nurses may lack specialist grounding. Under the plan, five databases plus grey sources will be searched without limits on date, place, or language.

Two reviewers will screen and chart the evidence on what nurses need to learn for this care. A clear map of training gaps can shape courses for a fast-growing patient group. Adult congenital care sits between children's and adult services, so nurses often fall between training systems.
plos-pone-0344291:
Shabana Urooj, Kiran Napte, and Najah Alsubaie present this 2026 PLOS One deep learning paper on brain tumors. It detects tumors in MRI scans without a biopsy. Their system reads each scan two ways at once. One network studies the raw image. A second studies hand-computed texture and shape features drawn from it. A swarm-based step trims the feature list to keep computation manageable.

On a standard brain MRI dataset, the combined model sorted scans into four classes. Its accuracy topped ninety-six percent. Precision, recall, and combined scores were just as high. The authors say the dual design fixes weaknesses of earlier systems, like poor explanation and weak generalization. They position it as a fast, noninvasive aid for glioma screening. Clinical testing is still needed.
plos-pone-0344691:
Allen Duong and colleagues mapped the immune cells that invade pig lungs after transplant injury caused by blood flow being stopped and restarted. This ischemia-reperfusion injury is a leading cause of early graft failure in human lung transplantation, and pigs mimic human physiology closely. Two transplant setups were studied, one sampled after hours and one after three days.

Neutrophils and one class of monocyte surged into the graft within hours and held steady, while other monocyte types and dendritic cells kept rising through day three. T cells grew more activated even though their total numbers barely changed. A detailed cell timeline like this shows which defenders arrive when, guiding drugs that might calm the earliest wave.
plos-pone-0346391:
Zachary Kerr and colleagues measured imposter feelings, the fear of being exposed as a fraud, among two hundred eighty-nine sport science undergraduates at a university in the American Southeast. They also recorded competitiveness and background details, looking for which combinations of identity and temperament track with the strongest self-doubt. A standard imposter scale and a competitiveness index supplied the scores.

Just over half the students reported frequent or intense imposter traits. Seniors scored higher than younger students, and students who disliked the combative side of competition scored higher too. Among first-generation students, those who did not identify as men reported notably stronger imposter feelings than men, a gap absent in other students. The findings tell advisors where self-doubt concentrates in this degree path, and that it grows, not shrinks, near graduation.
plos-pone-0346991:
Suzannah D'Hooghe and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Set in Flanders, Belgium, it studies the perceived obesogenic environment, surroundings people feel push them toward weight gain. The adults involved live in socioeconomically disadvantaged situations, where healthy choices are often the hardest to make.

The findings come from a Group Model Building process in which residents take part themselves, helping to draw the system of causes. Complex systems thinking suits obesity, which grows from food prices, transport, stress, and shops acting together. Local health policymakers gain a cause map drawn with the community, not just about it.
plos-pone-0347491:
Jennifer Miller and colleagues report new excavations at Panga ya Saidi, a cave near Kenya's coast holding at least seventy-eight thousand years of human history. The cave is central to understanding early modern humans in eastern Africa. Using fresh digging, three-dimensional scanning, radiocarbon dating, and sediment analysis, the team reconstructed how the cave floor itself formed and changed.

Deposits in the sheltered main chamber run more than five meters deep with strong artifact densities, while open areas mostly accumulated washed-in soil with little cultural material. Shifts in where sediment came from trace how the living space inside the cave evolved from the late Ice Age into recent millennia. Knowing which layers are trustworthy sharpens every claim made from the cave's famous finds.
plos-pone-0347591:
Someyo Kamal Utsho, Md Rawjatul Fahim, and Ruhaidah Samsudin published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE asking how well machine learning can estimate fine particle air pollution across different climates. They trained models on tens of thousands of monthly satellite-based samples from five climate zones, then tested each model on a climate zone it had never seen. A tuned gradient-boosting model did the predicting, and an explanation technique ranked which inputs mattered most.

Accuracy varied sharply by zone: subtropical regions were predicted fairly well, while tropical regions were barely predictable from weather data alone. Geographic coordinates did most of the work, far outweighing weather, because location stands in for where pollution is emitted and how air carries it. Removing coordinates collapsed performance entirely. Their open framework is offered as a benchmark, and a warning that pollution models cannot simply be carried between climates.
plos-pone-0347891:
Nathan J. Hansen and colleagues present a protocol for detecting tongue nerve damage without needles in survivors of throat cancer. Radiation for HPV-related cancers often injures the hypoglossal nerve years later, weakening the tongue and swallowing, but the standard test drives a needle into the tongue. Their study instead lays a dense grid of surface electrodes on the tongue to record its electrical chatter.

Thirty-six patients treated at MD Anderson will undergo the surface test alongside clinical exams, symptom reports, and needle testing for comparison. Machine learning will judge how well surface signals classify nerve damage severity. The aim is a painless screening tool for a common late effect of treatment.
plos-pone-0348091:
Yu-Shan Chang and colleagues followed children conceived with fertility help in Taiwan from birth to age twelve in 2026 work. Parents and doctors have long wondered whether such children grow differently, and past studies disagreed, especially for twins.

The national birth cohort covered more than twenty thousand singletons and about a thousand multiples, conceived naturally, by insemination, or by IVF. Treated groups looked smaller in combined figures, but the gap largely reflected the higher share of multiples, who start smaller. Separated properly, growth paths were reassuringly close. The study is among the longest looks at growth after fertility treatment in Asia.
plos-pone-0348191:
Ji Hyeon Seo and Ji Hye Lim set out to improve predictions of which hospital patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a serious lung condition, will die during their stay. Doctors often adjust such predictions with a general illness score, but that score was not built for lung disease. The team used a large Korean hospital registry covering more than thirteen thousand patients.

Drawing on discharge records from 2011 to 2023, they built a severity adjustment model tuned to the illness patterns that travel with this lung disease. A tailored score should sort patients more fairly than a general one. Hospitals could use it to compare outcomes honestly and to spot patients who need closer attention early.
plos-pone-0348291:
Cindy Phan Vu and Lauren Saling tested a question at the heart of social media policy: can ordinary users fact-check as well as experts? One hundred two participants were shown misinformation and then either an expert correction or a crowdsourced note of the kind used on the platform X. Confidence in the false claims and willingness to share them were measured before and after.

Both kinds of correction worked. Confidence in the misinformation fell, and willingness to pass it on fell, with no meaningful advantage for the experts. Platforms face far more falsehoods than experts can check, so evidence that vetted crowd notes perform equally is significant. The study supports scaling community checking while keeping quality safeguards.
plos-pone-0348391:
Diana Carbone, Francesco Marcatto, and Donatella Ferrante tested whether arguing in a group makes people better at spotting fake news than reflecting alone. Their 2026 study had one hundred eleven college students judge news stories, then either discuss them in groups or write individual reflections, then judge again.

Accuracy improved only for fake stories that had been discussed in groups. Solo reflection produced no gain. Intriguingly, group discussion seemed to teach a transferable skill: afterward, students also judged new, undiscussed fake stories better, provided those came after the discussed ones. Even groups containing members who were initially wrong improved. The authors link the result to the theory that reasoning evolved for argument, so structured debate sharpens truth detection.
plos-pone-0348591:
Aymene Youcef Krachni and colleagues spent a year testing whether adding artificial plants to laboratory zebrafish tanks helps or harms. Zebrafish are a workhorse of biomedical research and are usually kept in bare tanks, a practice welfare science questions. Sixteen tanks, half enriched with plastic plants and half not, were compared on survival during rearing, sex balance, fertility, and pathogen load.

No significant differences appeared in any health or breeding measure. Behavior analysis in the small home tanks showed the plants mainly cost the fish swimming room. The null result cuts both ways: enrichment of this simple kind is safe, but in small tanks it buys the fish nothing measurable. Facilities can decide with evidence rather than fashion.
plos-pone-0348791:
Meinolf Wonnemann and Jost Langhorst led a lab test of an old herbal mix. The mix holds myrrh, chamomile, and coffee charcoal. It is sold for gut complaints. The team dosed a machine that mimics the human colon. The gut microbes came from patients with irritable bowel syndrome of the loose type. Dosing ran for eight days.

The mix stirred the microbes to make more helpful acids. It also boosted groups of gut bacteria tied to good health. Brew from the dosed machine then shielded gut cells in a dish. It kept their walls tight and nudged immune signals toward calm. The team says the signs look good, but proof in patients is still to come.
plos-pone-0348891:
Alvaro F Montalvo-Peralta and co-authors surveyed medical students in Lima, Peru, in 2026 about reflux and sleep. Poor sleep is rife in medical training. Reflux is a plausible cause that can be treated, yet earlier work had handled the link loosely.

One hundred seventy-one students completed standard sleep and reflux scales. Adjusted modelling then counted other factors that shape sleep. Reflux burden and poor sleep were both strikingly common. Students with reflux burden had a notably higher rate of poor sleep than those without. The design cannot prove which came first. Still, it flags reflux screening as a cheap step in student health.
plos-pone-0349091:
Rikako Shimizu and co-workers read Japan's web searches to learn how the public thinks about major depression. Early care matters because the illness raises suicide risk and harms work life. Their 2026 study uses three years of search data from the country's most visited search engine, sorting the most common depression-related queries by the symptoms they name.

Searches pairing depression with symptom words outnumbered searches for depression alone. Sleep trouble was the symptom people searched alongside depression most often. Most searched symptoms matched the official signs doctors use to diagnose the illness. Public understanding online seems broadly in line with clinical views, which may help health messages meet people where they already look.
plos-pone-0349191:
Ellie Maynard, Ruth H Thurstan, and Ciarán McLaverty led a deep look at carbon buried in the sea floor. Ports must be dredged to stay open. Firms also dig sand and gravel from the sea. Both acts stir up stored carbon. Some of that carbon may return to the air. The team used old records, firm data, and sea floor maps for northwest Europe.

Port dredging stirred a bit over two million tonnes of carbon per year. Sand and gravel digging stirred far less, near four hundred thousand tonnes a year. In British waters both were dwarfed by fishing trawls, by a factor near one thousand. But the harm is packed into small zones. The team says managers should now count this source too.
plos-pone-0349291:
David Buil-Gil and a large international team asked whether teenagers with lots of unstructured free time get into more trouble, testing the idea across twenty-one countries in Europe and the Americas. Survey answers came from more than fifty-eight thousand young people aged thirteen to seventeen, covering time spent hanging out away from home, loose time at home, and organised or family time.

Unstructured time away from home stood out as a strong, steady companion of self-reported offending, outweighing most classic risk factors the team controlled for. Structured time at home pointed the other way, toward less offending. The pattern held in most countries, and simulations suggested that modest cuts in loose out-of-home time could trim youth crime. The authors argue that prevention should shape teenagers' everyday environments, not only their attitudes.
plos-pone-0349391:
Thomas F Denson, Michelle L Moulds, and Jessica R Grisham surveyed a representative sample of nearly five hundred British adults about co-rumination. The habit means chewing over problems together in long, speculative, gloomy conversations. Most earlier research chased this habit in teenagers. The team measured it alongside personality, social life, and emotional wellbeing to see whether the adult version carries the same trade-off.

The paradox survived into adulthood. Co-rumination sat between traits such as extraversion and anxiety on one side and outcomes on the other, linked at once to warmer relationships and lower loneliness, and to higher anxiety. Effects were generally small, and older adults co-ruminated less than younger ones. The authors describe a habit that genuinely comforts and quietly costs, sometimes in the same friendship.
plos-pone-0349591:
Wang and colleagues, in a 2026 study, trace a control loop that limits blood vessel growth in the brain after a stroke. New vessels help repair stroke damage, and an enzyme called 15-PGDH supports that growth. The team suspected a long noncoding RNA, a gene-like stretch that makes no protein, of holding the enzyme back.

Using mice with a blocked brain artery and vessel cells starved of oxygen in dishes, the team found both the enzyme and the RNA rose after injury. Yet they pulled in opposite ways. Silencing the enzyme slowed vessel cell growth, movement, and tube building. Raising the RNA lowered the enzyme and also slowed vessel growth, and restoring the enzyme undid that effect. The authors describe a feedback loop: injury raises a brake and an accelerator together, which may keep post-stroke vessel growth from running too far.
plos-pone-0349791:
Ida Arentz Taraldsen and colleagues present the protocol for a trial testing how much oxygen patients with acute heart failure should receive. Extra oxygen is routine for breathless patients, yet no clear evidence says whether aiming high or keeping oxygen modest works better. The trial will run at several centers with patients randomly assigned to one of two targets.

One group will be kept at a higher blood oxygen target and the other at a lower, restrictive one, delivered by an automatic device so neither patients nor staff know the assignment. Acute heart failure drives one in twenty hospital admissions, so even a small difference between strategies would affect huge numbers of patients. No results are reported in this protocol.
plos-pone-0350091:
Ala' Hawa and colleagues asked whether tear size changes what predicts failure after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair, the keyhole surgery that reattaches torn shoulder tendons. They followed more than eleven hundred repairs, sorted into small, medium, and large tears. Six months after surgery, ultrasound checks showed whether each repair had torn again, and patients rated satisfaction and function.

The risk factors for retear were not the same across sizes. In small tears, older age, longer surgery, a wider tear front-to-back, and stiffness before surgery each raised the risk. Knowing that predictors shift with tear size helps surgeons counsel patients more honestly and tailor technique and follow-up to the tear in front of them.
plos-pone-0350191:
Nearly all living things need molybdenum, and a molecular machine called an insertase installs it into enzymes. Tim Julian Schmidt and colleagues traced this machine's family tree across plants, fungi, and animals, in this 2026 PLOS One evolutionary study.

Most lineages fused the machine's two parts into one protein, but the order of the parts differs between groups, a clue to separate histories. The working site stayed remarkably unchanged, tolerating few substitutions. One animal version, gephyrin, also props up nerve signal receptors in the brain, and its surface is conserved in ways its chemistry alone cannot explain. The authors suspect extra, undiscovered jobs.
plos-pone-0350291:
Andrea M Zurek-Ost and Mark Sorensen tested a simple idea for estimating age at death from skeletons: weigh one hip bone. Bone loses mineral and mass with age, especially in women, so dry weight might carry an age signal. Their 2026 study measured nearly four hundred hip bones from people aged sixteen to ninety-three, recording height, weight, and sex.

Statistical models using those measures explained about a third of age variation, missing the true age by roughly nine years on average. Most estimates landed within twenty years of the known age. Results weakened on a smaller modern test group, a warning the authors state plainly. They conclude hip bone weight can support age estimates, but only cautiously and alongside proven methods.
plos-pone-0350391:
Even when HIV treatment works well, the virus sometimes lingers at very low levels. Eunmi Yang and colleagues reviewed ten years of records from two South Korean hospitals to learn who experiences this low-level viremia and whether it harms them, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Of about three hundred eighty patients, fifteen met the study's strict definition. Those patients far more often had started treatment with extremely high virus counts. Yet their later rates of virus rebound, new AIDS-defining illness, and death looked no worse than fully suppressed patients. Starting viral load was the one clear predictor the analysis found.
plos-pone-0350991:
Qarin Lood and colleagues mapped studies on training for care leaders. The training goal is care centred on each person. Twenty two papers met the review rules. Most courses ran in northern Europe. Nurse leaders formed the main audience. Content covered leadership styles and coaching skills. It also covered values for person centred work.

Teaching leaned on long work based learning. Gains were mostly self reported shifts in practice. Culture on wards was said to improve. Hard outcome measures stayed rare. Standard tools were seldom used. Leaders shape how care feels each day. Proof of training impact still needs stronger study designs.
plos-pone-0351691:
Néhémie Nzoyikorera and seven colleagues sequence measles virus from a 2024 outbreak in Burundi. Cases had resurged since 2019 despite progress toward elimination. Investigators could not tell whether outbreaks formed one linked chain or several separate introductions. Throat swabs came from four neighbouring health districts. The team generated whole genomes from eighteen isolates, then compared them with public sequences.

Every new genome belonged to genotype B3, the regionally common type. The sequences split into two clusters rather than one family tree. That pattern means Burundi's outbreak was not a single chain of spread. A diverse virus population was circulating, including one previously unrecognized cluster. The results show why genetic surveillance matters alongside case counts. It reveals hidden transmission structure that ordinary outbreak investigation cannot see.
plos-pone-0352091:
Ghulam Muhammad Abro and colleagues studied how local leadership shapes development in Hyderabad Cantonment, a military-run urban community in Pakistan. Their research asks whether building a community's own skills and organization, with leadership at the center, helps residents improve their area. The team mixed survey numbers with interviews to hear how people judge their leaders.

Residents reported clear gaps. Women took little part in leadership, money and materials were hard to gather, and ordinary people had small roles in decisions. The authors suggest practical steps to widen who leads and how choices get made. They are careful to note the results show what residents perceive, not measured proof of cause, which still makes them useful for planners in similar towns.
plos-pone-0352191:
Deeksha Shama and Archana Venkataraman tackled a dirty-data problem in automatic seizure detection: the human labels used to train detectors are often wrong about when a seizure starts and ends. Scalp recordings are noisy, so even experts disagree, and standard training treats every label as truth. Their method, BUNDL, instead teaches the network how uncertain each label is, inside a Bayesian frame.

A new training rule built on that idea lets the model lean on confident labels and discount shaky ones, without adding any new parts to the network. Tests on simulated recordings and the follow-on job of locating where seizures begin checked whether cleaner learning follows. For hospitals short on expert annotators, a detector that expects label noise is far more realistic than one that demands perfect teachers.
plos-pone-0352591:
Liangxiao Xiong and colleagues studied how rock containing crossing cracks weakens under repeated two-way squeezing. Their 2026 paper reports compression tests on rock-like samples with built-in cross fractures. The team varied crack angles, side pressure, and the number of loading cycles, then tracked strength and crack growth.

Repeated loading steadily lowered the samples' strength, and more groups of crossing cracks lowered it further. The main crack mattered most: it controlled both strength and how new cracks spread. The angle between main and secondary cracks changed strength very little on its own. Where several crack groups met, stress patterns grew tangled and cracks spread in complex ways. The results help engineers judge fractured rock around mines and tunnels.
plos-pone-0352691:
Bassolas, Birello, and Vicens examined how energy change is discussed on YouTube in a 2026 study. Video platforms now shape what many people learn about power, climate, and new technology. The team studied themes, wording, and feelings in energy videos, then ran a live test with two matching channels that differed only in how formal the language sounded.

Casual wording drew a broader crowd than formal wording did. Viewers stayed longer at the start of casual videos, while formal videos held people better in later parts. Counts from the platform and ad tools backed that mixed pattern. For teachers and advocates, the lesson is that tone changes both who shows up and who stays.
plos-pone-0352991:
Sikandar Hussain led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study teaching computers to recognize Dravet syndrome from brain wave recordings. This rare childhood epilepsy is hard to spot, and few patient recordings exist. Using records from nine affected children plus healthy and other-epilepsy controls, they trained hybrid deep learning models and tested them one child at a time.

Models pre-trained on brain wave data classified children more steadily than models trained from nothing. Hussain calls the work a proof of concept, and says larger multi-center collections must test whether the method can help real diagnosis.
plos-pone-0353291:
Xiangyu Zhu and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One paper on spotting defects in manufactured products with computer vision. Factory inspection systems often miss faint, subtle flaws, and training data for rare defects is scarce. Their method first sharpens suspicious image regions with super-resolution, then combines information across image scales using a graph-based network that weighs how regions relate to each other.

Tested on public benchmark datasets with only a few example images, or none at all, the method beat leading alternatives at finding defects and pinpointing their exact location. It performed especially well on fine textures and held up when moved to new domains. The authors present it as a practical step toward inspection systems that catch the flaws human eyes and older models overlook.
plos-pone-0353391:
Basile Garcia, Crystal Qian, and Stefano Palminteri run in 2026 a moral Turing test on how people judge explanations written by humans or by large language models. Participants read justifications for moral and non moral choices, guessed who wrote each, and said whether they agreed. Belief about the source was expected to sway judgement apart from the true source.

Guessing beat chance but stayed far from perfect. People showed no overall liking for human texts, and model texts even won in hard moral cases. Yet people agreed less with anything they believed came from a model. Length, typos, and cost benefit wording swayed both guessing and agreement.
plos-pone-0353691:
Guimarães and colleagues, in a 2026 study, look at how often tuberculosis appeared in people treated with biologic drugs in Pernambuco, Brazil, over ten years. Biologic drugs calm the immune system and help diseases driven by immune attack, but they can also raise infection risk. The region already carries a heavy load of tuberculosis.

Records covered more than eight thousand patients in rheumatology, gut, and skin care. About two in every hundred patients developed tuberculosis, and the rate was highest in gut disease patients, at more than double the rate in joint disease patients. Lung disease was the most common form. Rates did not differ much before versus during treatment, which led the authors to point at exposure in daily life as a key driver. They call for larger regional studies to sharpen safety rules.
plos-pone-0353991:
Yuuki Shichi and eight colleagues compare how pancreatic cancer cells behave grown flat in a dish versus grown in three-dimensional clusters, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The focus is mucins, slippery protective proteins that tumours exploit to grow and resist treatment. Eight cancer cell lines — some orderly and epithelial in character, others loose and mesenchymal — were grown both ways and their proteins catalogued.

Far more mucin types appeared in the three-dimensional cultures. One mucin, absent entirely in flat growth, switched on robustly in every orderly cell line when grown in 3D. The authors argue flat dishes hide the very molecules drug hunters need to see, and 3D culture should be the default for biomarker work.
plos-pone-0354091:
Francisca Olajide, Frithjof Lutscher, and Stacey R Smith? published this 2026 modeling study of early warning signals for emerging epidemics. Signals like rising variance can hint a disease is about to take off, but noise and delays weaken them. The authors built a model coupling infection spread with social media chatter, generated simulated outbreaks, and tested which signals warned earliest.

The compartment of reported infections proved most trustworthy, and variance beat autocorrelation when noise ran high. Signals inside the social media stream itself predicted poorly. Olajide offers the framework for sharpening outbreak preparedness.
plos-pone-0354591: The prisoner’s dilemma — with conservative versus aggressive cooperators — evolves in analyzable dynamics. This paper modeled those dynamics. The game-theoretic findings reveal when caution versus boldness wins in the evolution of cooperation.
plos-pone-0354691:
Choi and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask what helps stroke survivors in Korea rejoin everyday social life a year after their stroke. Returning to work, family roles, and community is a core goal of rehabilitation, yet the drivers may differ for the most and least impaired. Nearly twenty-seven hundred survivors from a national cohort were sorted into five levels of movement ability.

For the most impaired group, the surroundings mattered most: an accessible home and the age and closeness of their caregiver. For higher-functioning survivors, thinking, language, mood, and having a job mattered more. Across every group, being able to do daily activities and rating life quality highly supported participation. Caregiver strain dragged participation down everywhere. The authors argue rehabilitation should be matched to function level: fix the home and support the caregiver first for the most impaired, and build skills and work paths for the rest.
plos-pone-0354891:
Tanbin Jahan Ferdousy led a team of eight authors on this 2026 computer-designed dengue vaccine study. Dengue's four virus types make vaccine design tricky, and no perfect antiviral exists. Working entirely in software, the team stitched chosen virus fragments with a human immune-boosting adjuvant into a single candidate meant to cover all four types, then simulated its behavior and immune response.

Simulations predicted strong worldwide population coverage and stable binding to immune sensors. Ferdousy is explicit that laboratory and animal testing must come next before any claim about a real vaccine.
plos-pone-0355191:
Binta Maria Aleogho, Rikuou Yokosawa, and Kentaro Noma demonstrate a gentler way to watch chemical messengers at work inside a living worm, in this 2026 study. Neuropeptides carry signals through the nervous system, but standard labeling either relies on antibodies of uneven quality or attaches a bulky glowing protein that can distort the peptide's behavior. Their alternative uses a split glowing protein: only a tiny tag rides on the peptide itself.

When the tagged peptide is released and meets its partner fragment anchored outside cells, the two halves join and light up. They modeled which personal traits, illnesses, lifestyle factors, and air pollution exposures preceded a pacemaker for this block.

plos-pone-0356691:

Two immune genes kept pointing in the same direction in both diseases and sat in inflammation-heavy cells, but they did not pass the toughest significance tests. The authors present the overlap as a partial, testable lead rather than a proven shared pathway.
plos-pone-0356791:
