polish-constitution-3-may-1791:
The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth adopted its constitution on 3 May 1791, the first written national constitution in Europe. Reformers in the Great Sejm pushed it through as the Commonwealth weakened and its neighbors circled. The charter was a rescue attempt: strengthen the state before Russia and Prussia could finish dividing it.

The text ends the nobles' right to block all business with a single veto, makes the monarchy hereditary, and gives towns a voice in the state. Catholic faith is kept, with toleration promised to others. Russia answered with invasion, and the partitions wiped Poland from the map within four years. The charter of a nation's last hope, adopted too late, is still honored in Poland's national day.
ponzinibio-de-lamiis-latin-1591:
Gianfrancesco Ponzinibio, a jurist of Piacenza, wrote De lamiis, on witches, early in the sixteenth century. This text comes from the Frankfurt Tractatus duo of 1591, which revived his daring argument. Ponzinibio holds that the witches' flight and sabbath are illusions, not bodily events.

As a lawyer, he attacks the evidence itself. Dreams and torture, he argues, cannot build a capital case. His tract is the daring precursor that Johann Weyer later built upon. Skeptics across Europe cited Ponzinibio as their early authority. The book's courage is plain: a working jurist told the witch courts, in Latin, that their central scene never happened.
prestwich-chalk-plateau-1891:
Joseph Prestwich, a great English rock scholar, staked his name on the Kent flint claims in this paper of 1891. Benjamin Harrison, a Kent shop man, had found rough flints on the chalk hills that he held to be tools. Prestwich backed him in print, with the talk that came next in full.

The flints, called eoliths, were said to show man at work before the ice age in Britain. Prestwich tells of their beds, depth, and worn forms as proof of true tools, not chance stones. The paper is a grand man's bold bet, held in the full record of its day.
ripley-compound-of-alchymy-1591:
George Ripley was an English canon and alchemist of the 1400s. His Compound of Alchymy is a poem in twelve gates. The print here is the 1591 dress of the work. It is the chief poem of English alchemy.

Each gate is a step in the Great Work, from first rot to the red stone. Ripley veils his craft in rich signs: kings, beasts, and baths of dew. He warns the false hand and cheers the true son of the art. The poem's fame kept it in print for two hundred years.
russell-studies-scriptures-vol3-1891:
Russell's Thy Kingdom Come, published in 1891, is volume three of Studies in the Scriptures. The book turns from chronology to the papacy, prophecy, and the coming kingdom itself. Russell's followers read it as the sequel that showed what the dates would bring.

He reads the book of Revelation and the parables as a coded history of the church age ending in harvest. The great pyramid of Egypt even enters his argument as a stone witness to the divine plan. The volume deepened the movement's sense of living at the turn of the ages. Russell treats prophecy as a timetable that careful Bible study can read.
russell-thy-kingdom-come-1891:
Charles Taze Russell issued Thy Kingdom Come in 1891 as the third volume of Millennial Dawn. The series, also called Studies in the Scriptures, set out his reading of prophecy. Bible Students, his movement, awaited Christ's kingdom on a dated scheme. This volume carries that scheme toward its climax.

Its Great Pyramid chapters made pyramidology a doctrine of the movement. Russell read the pyramid's passages as a stone calendar of sacred history. Measurements in inches became years in his prophetic sums. The book is a document of record for the Bible Student faith. It is preserved as history, not as endorsement. Its influence built a lasting movement.
saussaye-manual-science-religion-1891:
Pieter Daniel Chantepie de la Saussaye was an Amsterdam professor whose Manual of the Science of Religion, in this 1891 English edition, helped name a field. The science of religion was then new, split between history and philosophy. His manual gave it a method and a map.

De la Saussaye sets out phenomenology, the ordered description of rites, myths, and ideas, before judging any of them. He treats prayer, sacrifice, priesthood, and sacred books as forms that recur across the world. Textbook writers across Europe built on his scheme, and his terms still echo in the field.
sbe-32-vedic-hymns-1-1891:
F. Max Muller gave the Vedic Hymns, Part One, English dress in 1891. The work is Book Thirty-Two of the Sacred Books of the East. The hymns come from the Rig Veda, the most old text of India. Muller spent his life on the Vedas at Oxford.

The hymns here praise the Maruts, the storm gods who ride with Rudra. Rudra, Vayu, and Vata get hymns of their own in the set. Wild winds, rain, and the crash of the storm fill the old songs. Muller's notes weigh each hard word and old rite in the text.
sbe-40-taoist-texts-2-1891:
James Legge gave the Texts of Taoism English dress in the Sacred Books of the East. Book Forty, from 1891, is Part Two of that work. It holds the last books of the Writings of Kwang-dze, known now as Zhuangzi. Zhuangzi is the great wit and sage of the Taoist line.

Books Eighteen to Thirty-Three close the vast, wild text here. Tales of a butterfly dream, a huge fish, and free roams of the mind fill the pages. Zhuangzi mocks stiff rites and the praise of the crowd. Legge's dress was the first full one of the work in English.
schiller-riddles-sphinx-1891:
Writing under the name A. Troglodyte, F. C. S. Schiller issued Riddles of the Sphinx in 1891. The subtitle calls the work a study in the philosophy of evolution. Schiller was a young Oxford thinker at the time. His book fired an early shot in a long campaign.

The riddles are the old puzzles of life: mind, matter, God, and human worth after Darwin. Schiller argues that thought must start from human needs and acts, not from cold abstraction. That stance grew into his humanist form of pragmatism. The book stands as the founding statement of that program. Its bold tone still startles.
schopenhauer-fourfold-root-1891:
Arthur Schopenhauer wrote On the Fourfold Root as his doctoral dissertation in 1813. Mme. Karl Hillebrand translated the German essay into English in 1891. Its subject is the principle of sufficient reason, the rule that everything has a ground. Schopenhauer claimed the rule takes four distinct forms.

He sorts those forms by the kinds of objects minds can know. Causes in nature, grounds of judgment, and motives for action each follow their own version. Sorting them clears up, he thought, much muddle in older philosophy. The essay lays the base for his whole later system. Readers often start his work here.
stargate-program-summary-1991:
The Defense Intelligence Agency summed up its psychic spy program in a short paper of May 15, 1991. The STAR GATE Program Summary is the program's own official overview, freed for release years later. STAR GATE was the last name of the long remote viewing effort.

The summary tells what the program sought, how its viewers worked, and what its chiefs claimed for it. Viewers were tasked to describe far and hidden targets by mind alone. The paper is brief, dry, and strange in equal parts. It is the first file to read on the whole remote viewing affair.
tao-te-ching-legge-1891:
James Legge published his complete translation of the Tao Teh King in 1891, as part one of The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East thirty-nine. The Tao Te Ching, ascribed to Lao Tzu, holds eighty-one short chapters of verse-like counsel. It is the founding book of Taoism and one of the most translated texts on earth.

The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao, the book begins, then teaches rule by softness and non-action. Legge adds his introduction and notes, weighing the text's age and meaning with care. His rendering favored exact study over poetic dress. Generations of English students of Chinese thought began with Legge's Lao Tzu. The little book still rewards slow reading.
tob-0191:
Max Muller placed his translation of the Upanishads in the Sacred Books of the East, the series he founded and edited. The Upanishads close the Vedas with dialogues on Brahman, the world's ground, and the Self that knows it. Forest sages teach kings and sons in question and answer.

Famous passages ask what the eye cannot see but by which eyes see. Muller's Victorian English is stately and exact. The evidence notes this translation is not on Gutenberg and no text is attached to this entry. The edition's historical place is secure: it carried Hindu philosophy to the general reader of the West.
tob-10091:
Alexander Whyte, a Protestant minister, wrote Santa Teresa as an appreciation rather than a strict biography. Teresa of Avila was the sixteenth-century Spanish nun whose mystical writings and reform of the Carmelite order made her one of Catholicism's most beloved saints. Whyte admired her across a deep church divide.

He dwells on her courage, humor, and practical wisdom as much as on her visions and prayers. Teresa appears as a working reformer who founded convents, handled money and opposition, and still wrote about the inner life with rare clarity. Whyte's warm tribute invites Protestant and general readers to take her seriously.
tob-10791:
Thomas Thomson was a working chemist who wrote in the early 1800s, when the science was still young. His History of Chemistry, in this first volume, runs from the old arts of Egypt and Greece through the phlogiston age to the atomic views of his own day. He knew some of the founders of the new chemistry in person.

Old crafts, alchemy, and early drug lore give way to the study of gases and the fall of phlogiston. The book is dated in spots, as any such tale told from inside must be. Still, it is worth much for its closeness. A science tells its own past while that past is still in living memory.
tob-4191:
Sri Lanka's oldest history comes down in the Dipavamsa, the Chronicle of the Island, kept by Buddhist monks. Hermann Oldenberg edited and translated it in 1879. The verse chronicle tells how the Buddha visited the island, how King Vijaya founded its line, and how the faith took root.

Councils, relics, and the planting of the sacred Bo tree receive careful record. Later chronicles drew on its lists of kings and elders. As the oldest historical record of Buddhism's southern school, the Dipavamsa anchors the island's memory of itself. Verified from the 1919 edition, Oldenberg's version remains the scholar's entry to the chronicle tradition.
tob-4291:
James George Frazer published the first edition of The Golden Bough in 1890, in just two volumes. Volume one opens with a strange scene at Nemi in Italy, where a priest kept guard and could be killed and replaced by his successor. Frazer asks what could explain so grim a custom.

To answer, he gathers cases of magic, taboo, and dying gods from peoples all over the world. He argues that human thought moved from magic toward religion and then science. Shorter than the later twelve-volume edition, the first version states his big idea plainly, and it helped launch the modern study of human cultures.
un-sc-res-1091:
The Council paid tribute to its outgoing Secretary-General on 13 December 1996. Boutros Boutros-Ghali's single five-year term was ending that month. The Council met in closed session for the text. It recognized the central part he had played in guiding the Organization in its Charter duties. His work for peace had spanned the post-Cold War world's first hard years.

The Council acknowledged his contribution to international peace, security, and development. It praised his exceptional efforts to solve problems in the economic, social, and cultural fields. His work to meet humanitarian needs won the same thanks. So did his push for respect for human rights and basic freedoms for all. The Council voiced its deep appreciation for his dedication to the Charter's purposes and principles. It thanked him also for fostering friendly relations among nations. The tribute closed his tenure.
un-sc-res-1191: United Nations Security Council Resolution 1191, adopted on 27 August 1998, is a short procedural text on judges for the war crimes court for the former Yugoslavia. The Council had gathered names put forward for the court by 4 August 1998. It sends nine nominees, from nine different countries, on to the General Assembly. The Assembly then elects from that list under the court's statute.
un-sc-res-1291:
War in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is the subject of Resolution 1291 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 24 February 2000. Several African states had troops inside the Congo, and the 1999 Lusaka cease-fire was barely holding.

The text extends and expands the United Nations mission there, called MONUC, to 5,537 troops. MONUC would watch the cease-fire, check violations, and track the pullback of forces. It would help disarm armed groups and back the return of foreign troops to their home countries. The Council also let the mission use force to protect civilians under direct threat of attack.
un-sc-res-1391: The formal record of the Security Council includes the text numbered 1391, catalogued for 1973. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1491: In 2003 the Council voted Resolution 1491 into its official record, and this entry preserves that record through English Wikisource. The document follows the house style of such acts: earlier resolutions recalled, facts noted, then numbered paragraphs that decide the matter. Its value is the primary wording itself, not any summary of it.
un-sc-res-1591:
Darfur sanctions are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1591, adopted in March 2005. Both Sudan's government and rebel groups had broken the cease-fire again and again. Air strikes and village attacks went on, and the Janjaweed militias had not been disarmed. Algeria, China, and Russia abstained.

The text sets up a sanctions committee and a team of four experts based in Addis Ababa. People named by the committee face travel bans and frozen assets worldwide. The named include those who block peace, break the arms embargo, or commit atrocities. The Council also bars attack flights over Darfur and tightens control on arms moving into the region.
un-sc-res-1691:
Security Council Resolution 1691, adopted on June 21, 2006, recommended Montenegro for membership in the United Nations. The catalog year repeats the resolution number and is plainly wrong. Montenegro had voted for independence from its union with Serbia weeks earlier, and its people chose to leave by a narrow margin in a peaceful referendum watched by foreign observers.

The council acted without a dissenting vote, and the General Assembly seated Montenegro on June 28 as the 192nd member state. The short resolution closed the last chapter of the old Yugoslavia's breakup, which had started with wars in the early 1990s. Montenegro's calm path to a seat stood out against that violent past.
un-sc-res-1791:
Burundi's peacebuilding office was extended on 19 December 2007. A government of national unity had formed on 14 November. The Peacebuilding Commission had adopted a strategic framework with Burundi and a way to track it. The last rebel group, the Palipehutu-FNL, still stood outside the peace. Human rights abuses continued to draw concern.

The Council extended BINUB's mandate, as set by resolution 1719 (2006), until 31 December 2008. Burundi's leaders won praise for holding to the peace despite its strains. The FNL was urged to return to the joint verification body and finish the peace process without delay. The South African facilitation and the regional initiative were encouraged to keep pressing the talks. BINUB and the facilitation were told to speed their joint work. The government was urged to press on with governance changes and security reform. The office carried the United Nations role from peacekeeping into peacebuilding.
un-sc-res-1891: Kept under number 1891, a formal Security Council decision is preserved through a Wikisource copy of the UN record. The document's readers in its own day were governments and missions who had to act on it. Its readers now get the same complete text: what the members found, what they decided, and what they asked to be reported.
un-sc-res-191:
Apartheid's own expert report was endorsed on 18 June 1964. Fifty-eight states had brought South Africa's race conflict to the Council in April. The group of experts named under resolution 182 (1963) had reported. Their main finding called for all South Africa's people to be brought into consultation on the country's future. The Council judged the situation a grave disturbance of the peace.

The Council condemned apartheid and the laws behind it, above all the ninety-day detention clause of the General Law Amendment Act. It repeated its urgent appeal for every person jailed or restricted for opposing apartheid to be freed. The experts' recommendations and conclusions were noted, and their main conclusion was endorsed and backed in full. South Africa was invited to accept that conclusion and join the consultations. The Secretary-General had to consider what help the United Nations could give to bring such talks about.
un-sc-res-291:
The end of 1970 brought the Cyprus force its next term, on the advice of a report dated 2 December. The report said the peacekeeping force was still needed to maintain peace on the island. Cyprus's government agreed it should continue beyond 15 December 1970. Resolution 291 was adopted unanimously on 10 December 1970.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to show the utmost restraint. They had to keep working together toward the Council's goals, and use the calmer climate on the island well. The force's stationing was extended for a further period, ending on 15 June 1971. The renewal kept the mission in place, as others had done since 1964, while a final settlement remained out of reach.
un-sc-res-391:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was extended in the summer quiet of 15 June 1976. The Secretary-General's report of 5 June held that the force remained essential to the island's calm. Its freedom of movement in the north was still restricted, though talks were mending the problem. Talks between the two communities offered the best hope of a settlement, he judged, if both sides showed flexibility. The parties had agreed to six more months.

The Council restated resolution 186 (1964) and its endorsement of the General Assembly's settlement terms. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. Any act that could spoil the search for peace was barred. The stationing of the force in Cyprus was extended for six months, to 15 December 1976. All parties were asked to give the force their fullest cooperation. The Secretary-General would continue his good offices mission and report on the talks.
un-sc-res-91:
Kashmir's mediator resigned and the Council reset its course on 30 March 1951. Sir Owen Dixon had reported on his mission under resolution 80 (1950). India and Pakistan had both restated their wish for a free and impartial plebiscite under United Nations auspices. A plan in Kashmir to call a constituent assembly threatened to prejudge the outcome.

The Council accepted Dixon's resignation at his request, with thanks. It decided to appoint a successor as United Nations representative. The new envoy had to go to the subcontinent, consult both governments, and work for demilitarization of the state. He must report within three months of arrival. If talks failed, the parties were called to accept arbitration on the points still in dispute. The Council also affirmed that a constituent assembly could not settle the state's future, and the military observer group would keep watching the cease-fire.
un-sc-res-991:
El Salvador's civil war had ended, and the Council marked the change in 1995. On 28 April 1995 it paid tribute to ONUSAL, its observer mission there. The country, the text says, had moved from conflict to democracy and peace. The Secretary-General and his representatives had guided the mission. Member states that sent personnel earned thanks. Reports from the mission and its human rights division informed the vote.

The government, the FMLN, and all Salvadorans had to speed up the peace accords. Outstanding promises needed finishing so the gains would last. The Council welcomed their stated commitment to reconciliation. It called on states and world bodies to keep aiding El Salvador. The mission was winding down as a rare success story.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Resolution 1091, adopted at a closed meeting on 13 December 1996, is the Security Council's farewell tribute to outgoing Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali. It thanks him for guiding the UN, for seeking lasting answers to conflicts worldwide, and for reforms meant to strengthen the UN system. It also honors his work on economic and social problems, aid for people in need, and respect for human rights.

Resolution 1191, adopted on 27 August 1998, is a short procedural text on the International Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. Recalling the resolutions that created the tribunal and added a third trial chamber, the Council states its decision. It will consider the nominations for the tribunal's judges received by the Secretary-General by 4 August 1998. It then forwards nine nominations to the General Assembly, as the tribunal's Statute requires, for the Assembly's election of the judges.

The war in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement anchor Resolution 1291, adopted on 24 February 2000. The Council backed the deal as the best path to peace and called for all foreign forces to leave in an orderly way. It noted worry over illegal mining of Congo's wealth and over blocked aid access to refugees and displaced people.

The Council extends the UN Organization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, MONUC, until 31 August 2000. It expands it to up to 5,537 military staff, including up to 500 observers. MONUC is to watch the ceasefire, probe breaches, and work with the Joint Military Commission. Within 45 days it must draft a plan covering troop pullback, disarmament of armed groups, and foreign withdrawal. Under Chapter VII it may guard UN staff and sites and shield civilians under direct threat of attack.

At Lebanon's request, UNIFIL is renewed again on 28 January 2002. As in the previous renewal, the force had finished most of its original tasks after Israel's withdrawal. Its remaining work centred on restoring peace and security in the south of the country.

The mandate was extended for six months, until 31 July 2002, and the ongoing reshaping of the force was backed. Lebanon was called on to keep restoring its authority in the south, including through army deployments. The parties were told to ensure the force could move freely across its area, respect the withdrawal line, and show restraint, and violence was condemned.

Bosnia and Herzegovina's multinational stabilization force, SFOR, is renewed on 11 July 2003 for another planned 12 months. The force underpins the 1995 peace agreement, and full support is voiced for the High Representative's continued role. Refugee return across the region is stressed as part of completing the peace.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized states working through the alliance structure named in the peace agreement to keep SFOR running under unified command. Those states could take all necessary measures to carry out the force's peace-agreement tasks and defend themselves. The situation would be reviewed, and the authorization extended further if the state of the peace required it.

Targeted sanctions on Darfur's spoilers are created by Resolution 1591, adopted in March 2005. Every side had broken the N'Djamena ceasefire and the Abuja protocols: Sudan's air strikes, rebel attacks on villages, and the failure to disarm the Janjaweed all drew blame. The International Commission of Inquiry had reported, and the north-south peace deal risked being undermined by Darfur's war.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council sets up a Sanctions Committee and a four-member Panel of Experts, based in Addis Ababa, to watch compliance. The Committee will name individuals who block peace, commit atrocities, break the arms embargo, or order offensive military flights. Those named face a travel ban and a freeze of funds and assets, with narrow exemptions for basic and humanitarian needs. Sudan must get Committee approval before moving military equipment into Darfur. It presses all sides back to the Abuja talks, saying there is no military solution.

Montenegro broke away from Serbia in 2006. Its people voted to go their own way. The new state then asked to join the United Nations. Resolution 1691, passed on 22 June 2006, is the Council's reply. The members had read the request with care. They told the General Assembly to admit Montenegro as a member state.

Burundi's peace was young and still frail in December 2007. Resolution 1791, passed on 19 December that year, kept the UN peace team there for one more year. The land had made real strides toward calm. Yet hard tasks stayed on the list. Talks with the last rebel band, the FNL, had to end. Fighters had to lay down their arms for good. The guard forces had to be reshaped. Courts and troops had to learn to guard rights and law. A broad new cabinet had been named that November.

The team, known as BINUB, won a term to the end of 2008. The Council stressed that Burundi's own hands must steer its peace and growth. It cheered a new donor group that lined up aid for the land. It backed the joint plan drawn up by the UN team and the state as well.

Sudan sanctions get their expert panel extended until 15 October 2010 on 13 October 2009. The panel watches the arms embargo and targeted measures tied to Darfur. Commitment to full carrying out of the 2005 north-south peace deal and to a political end to the Darfur conflict, which the 2006 Darfur agreement had failed to deliver, is restated.

The panel is told to report by 31 March 2010 and to coordinate with the joint African Union-United Nations mediation and the Darfur mission, UNAMID. All states and bodies are urged to cooperate with the panel and the sanctions committee. Rebel groups that had stayed out of talks are also pressed to join them at once and constructively, and the sanctions regime stays under active review.

Security Council Resolution 191, adopted on 18 June 1964, deals with apartheid in South Africa. Fifty-eight member states had brought the race conflict to the Council's attention. The Council said apartheid broke the principles of the UN Charter and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It also noted that South Africa had refused to follow earlier resolutions on the subject.

The resolution condemns apartheid and the laws behind it, including the ninety-day detention rule. It urges South Africa to free people jailed for opposing apartheid, spare those sentenced to death, and grant amnesty to detainees and defendants. It also sets up an expert committee to study what measures the Council could take. It asks for an education and training program abroad for South Africans. It repeats the call to stop arms sales to South Africa.

Seven years of Cyprus duty closed with this renewal of December 1970. On the tenth, the Council adopted Resolution 291 without dissent. The Secretary-General reported that the force was still needed. Cyprus agreed it should stay past mid-December.

The text restates the Cyprus decisions, now with Resolution 281 added. It urges the utmost restraint from all parties. It asks for steady joint effort toward the Council's goals. The posting then runs to 15 June 1971. The usual hope closes the text. Progress by then might let the force shrink or withdraw. The mission had begun in 1964 with a three-month term.

Resolution 391, adopted on 15 June 1976, keeps UN peacekeepers in Cyprus for another six months. The Secretary-General reported that the United Nations Peace-keeping Force in Cyprus was still needed to keep the island quiet and to help the search for a settlement. The force's movement in the north was still limited, and talks between the two communities were the best hope for a lasting deal.

The Council extends the force's stay until 15 December 1976, hoping progress by then might allow it to shrink or leave. It urges both sides to show restraint, stick to past agreements, and keep working toward the Council's goals. It also asks the Secretary-General to keep his good offices mission going and to report back by 30 October 1976.

Belize joined the United Nations through Resolution 491. The Council passed it by a full vote on 23 September 1981. Belize, once called British Honduras, had won its freedom from Britain two days before. Guatemala still claimed its land, so the new state needed friends fast.

The text makes one request: the General Assembly should admit Belize as a member. That step gave the small state the shield of UN membership while the border claim went on. For Belize, this short text carried real weight. A seat in the Assembly was proof to the world, and to its large neighbor, that the new country was here to stay.

Resolution 91, passed on 30 March 1951, resets the UN's work on Kashmir. Eight members backed it, and three did not vote either way. Sir Owen Dixon, sent the year before, had filed his report with no breakthrough. Both India and Pakistan still backed a free vote on Kashmir's fate, held under UN eyes. But a plan to call a law-making body in one part of the state risked fixing the end in advance.

The Council chose a new envoy for India and Pakistan. His charge was to strip troops from the state so the vote could be held. The text warns that a part-state body can not settle Kashmir's fate. Both states were urged to take their last gaps to a judge if the envoy so advised.

El Salvador, not the Golan Heights, closes its UN chapter here. Resolution 991 was adopted unanimously on 28 April 1995. The country had moved from civil war to democracy. ONUSAL, the UN observer mission, had verified the peace accords. Its human rights chief reported on 18 April 1995.

Members paid warm tribute to the mission's work. They urged the government and the FMLN rebels to finish the peace accords' leftover tasks. More outside aid was requested for rebuilding. Then comes the formal ending. ONUSAL's mandate would terminate on 30 April 1995. The resolution reads as a graduation ceremony. A UN success story was being formally signed off.
volney-ruins-1791: The Ruins, or Meditation on the Revolutions of Empires, Volney's 1791 classic. The empires' ruins. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
waite-the-occult-sciences-1891:
A. E. Waite mapped the whole field of lore in The Occult Sciences, his survey of 1891. One book takes in magic, the great art of gold, and the arts that read fate. Waite sorts high creed from low trick. He gives each art its roots, chief books, and claims in brief.

The survey is calm, fair, and plain in speech. New fans could grasp the whole map from it at once. It is Waite's one tome guide to the field. Few guides of its age hold up so well for a first read. Waite knew the bands and book shops of the field at first hand. That range lets him weigh each art with a calm, fair hand.
walker-pronouncing-1791:
John Walker published his Critical Pronouncing Dictionary in 1791, setting out how English words ought to sound. Walker, once an actor, had become the leading teacher of elocution in London. His book marked the sounds of tens of thousands of words so that any reader could aim at approved speech.

Each entry gives spelling, pronunciation, and meaning, with rules and remarks where usage was in dispute. The dictionary served strivers who knew that accent could open or close doors in British society. For a century it was the authority on respectable pronunciation on both sides of the Atlantic. Its influence lingered in schools and pulpits long after newer guides appeared.
wedekind-spring-awakening-1891: Wedekind's 1891 Spring Awakening shows teens crushed by sexual repression. It was long banned. The Tower library holds the full text. It bared youth. Morals choked. Tragedy bloomed. Truth shocked. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
westermarck-the-history-of-human-marriag:
Edward Westermarck, a Finnish scholar working in England, published this Darwinian history of marriage in 1891. It was a large claim for its time: that marriage and the family rest on instincts shaped by natural selection, not on late invention.

Westermarck argues against the idea that early humans lived without marriage rules. He examines exogamy and the incest taboo, proposing that children raised together lose desire for each other, a claim still debated as the Westermarck effect. His evidence spans animals, early peoples, and civilized law. The book became a standard reference in the study of the family.
wilde-house-pomegranates-1891:
Oscar Wilde wrote these four tales for grown readers, and the set came out in 1891. Its name plays on the rich red fruit of the pomegranate tree. Wilde was then at the height of his fame in the London world of art.

Among the tales stands 'The Fisherman and his Soul,' a long tale of a man and a mermaid. He cuts his soul from his body to wed the maid of the sea, and pays a high price. The set shows Wilde's tale craft at its most rich and grave.
zola-money-1891:
Caxton issued Money at London in 1900, in Vizetelly's English version. Chapter heads run from The Temple of Mammon through Dreams and Schemes. Saccard Makes a Start and The Bank Is Founded follow in order.

Aristide Saccard returns, and this time his weapon is the stock market itself. His Universal Bank turns into a machine for breeding greed in all Paris. Fortunes rise in a morning and vanish by nightfall in the frenzy. A frontispiece shows the ruined Mazaud with a bullet through his head. Furious and prophetic, the 1891 novel reads like later headlines written a full century early.
